statement: The household labour force survey showed that the unemployment rate increased from 4.6 to 4.8 percent in the quarter, and the quarterly employment survey showed that average hourly earnings increased 3.9 percent over the previous year.
criterion: Stats NZ labour market statistics for the September 2024 quarter: true if the HLFS unemployment rate is reported as rising from 4.6% to 4.8% and the QES average hourly earnings annual increase is 3.9%; false if either figure differs materially.
reasoning: Stats NZ Labour Market Statistics for the September 2024 quarter confirm both figures. The HLFS unemployment rate rose from 4.6% (June 2024 quarter) to 4.8% (September 2024 quarter). The QES average ordinary time hourly earnings rose 3.9% in the year to the September 2024 quarter (down from 5.0% the previous quarter). Both figures match the criterion exactly.

statement: To give some historical context, I would also point out to members that over the last 15 years, the average unemployment rate in New Zealand has been 5 percent.
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS quarterly unemployment rate series, mean of the quarters from late 2009 to late 2024: true if the mean is approximately 5.0% (within rounding), false if materially different.
reasoning: Stats NZ HLFS-based annual unemployment rates (via ycharts): 2010 6.56, 2011 6.49, 2012 6.93, 2013 5.84, 2014 5.43, 2015 5.42, 2016 5.15, 2017 4.74, 2018 4.34, 2019 4.11, 2020 4.60, 2021 3.78, 2022 3.30, 2023 3.73, 2024 4.72. The mean of the 15 full years 2010–2024 is ~5.01%; adding the elevated late-2009 quarters (~6.1–6.5%) to make a Nov-2009→Nov-2024 window raises it only to ~5.05–5.08%. The quarterly mean over the last 15 years is therefore approximately 5.0% within rounding, matching Willis's statement. Trading Economics independently gives a 1985–2026 all-time average of 5.73% (inflated by the ~11% early-1990s peak), consistent with a lower ~5.0% average over the more recent 15-year window.

statement: The increase from 4.6 percent to 4.8 percent was lower than forecasters had been predicting. In its August Monetary Policy Statement, the Reserve Bank had forecast 5 percent unemployment and the Treasury had forecast 5.2 percent in the Budget update in May.
criterion: The RBNZ August 2024 Monetary Policy Statement forecast table and the Treasury May 2024 BEFU forecast table: true if they show unemployment forecasts of approximately 5.0% and 5.2% respectively for the period referenced, false if either figure is materially different or not attributable to those documents.
reasoning: The Sept 2024 quarter unemployment rate of 4.8% (up from 4.6%) is confirmed, and it came in below forecasters' predictions — the direction of the claim is independently well-established. The RBNZ August 2024 MPS confirms the 4.6% June-quarter starting point and projected unemployment rising above 5% toward a ~5.4% peak in 2025; the Treasury May 2024 BEFU projected a peak around 5.3-5.4%. Multiple independent secondary sources reproduce exactly the figures Willis cited (5.0% RBNZ, 5.2% Treasury, 4.8% actual), and no disconfirming evidence appeared. Caveat: the RBNZ MPS PDF, Treasury BEFU page and BERL all returned HTTP 403, so I could not open the primary forecast tables directly; confirmation rests on the RBNZ statement text plus consistent secondary reporting rather than cell-level verification of both tables.

statement: I haven’t seen that advice, but what I would say is that the Treaty is not changing and Treaty settlements are not changing.
criterion: The text of the Treaty Principles Bill as introduced, plus its regulatory impact statement and departmental advice: true if the bill contains no provision amending the text of the Treaty of Waitangi or the Treaty of Waitangi Act schedules, and no provision altering or reopening any concluded settlement Act or deed; false if it amends either.
reasoning: The Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill (94-1, 2024) as introduced contains Clause 9 ('Nothing in this Act amends the text of the Treaty of Waitangi/te Tiriti o Waitangi') and Clause 8, which excludes the bill from applying to the interpretation of any Treaty settlement Act or the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 in relation to historical settlements. It amends neither the Treaty text nor the Act's schedules, and it does not alter or reopen any concluded settlement Act or deed. Luxon's statement that 'the Treaty is not changing and Treaty settlements are not changing' matches the criterion as written. Critics' claims that the bill 'rewrites' the Treaty concern its interpretive effect on principles, not an amendment to the Treaty text or settlements.

statement: Now, there are clear indications that the economy has turned upwards, but even so, I would expect the unemployment rate to rise a bit further before beginning to fall.
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS quarterly unemployment rate series after the September 2024 quarter: true if the rate rises above 4.8% and then records a sustained decline from its peak before the resolve-by date; false if it falls immediately without rising, or if it is still rising with no peak reached by that date.
reasoning: Stats NZ HLFS seasonally-adjusted rate: Sep 2024 4.8%, Dec 2024 5.1%, Mar 2025 5.1%, Jun 2025 5.2%, Sep 2025 5.3% (8-year high). The rate rose above 4.8% as predicted, but by the 2025-12-31 resolve-by date it was still rising with no peak reached and no sustained decline. The Dec 2025 figure (5.4%) was released Feb 2026, after cutoff; easing only came in early 2026. The criterion explicitly makes 'still rising with no peak reached by that date' a false/wrong outcome.

statement: In the last year, wage growth has outpaced the cost of living in the first year of our new Government—compare that to the 13 quarters in a row under Labour, where wages grew slower than inflation.
criterion: Stats NZ wage growth series (Labour Cost Index and/or QES average hourly earnings) against the CPI annual rate: true if the annual wage measure exceeds CPI for the year to the September 2024 quarter, and if there are 13 consecutive quarters during the 2017-2023 Labour government where the wage measure was below CPI; false if the recent year shows wages below CPI, or if the longest such run under Labour is not 13 quarters on a consistent measure.
reasoning: First half confirmed: for the year to the Sept 2024 quarter, the Labour Cost Index (all salary/wage rates) rose 3.8% annually vs CPI inflation of 2.2%, and average ordinary time hourly earnings rose ~5% — wage growth outpaced the cost of living on every standard Stats NZ measure. Second half is overstated: real wages (LCI annual growth below CPI) did fall for a long consecutive run starting around Q2 2021 (CPI peaked 7.3% in Jun 2022 vs LCI ~3.4%), but that run straddled the change of government — Labour left office Nov 2023 and real wages stayed negative into early 2024 under the current government. The stretch falling entirely within the 2017-2023 Labour government is nearer ~11-12 quarters; reaching '13 quarters' requires counting quarter(s) that occurred under National, and the count also varies by measure. Core comparison holds; the '13 quarters under Labour' figure is materially generous in attribution.

statement: Yes, and in particular I stand by this Government’s action to conclude negotiations on a trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council which will deliver duty-free access for 99 percent of New Zealand’s exports over 10 years.
criterion: MFAT's published NZ–GCC free trade agreement text and accompanying national interest analysis: true if negotiations were concluded before 5 November 2024 and the agreement provides for tariff elimination on ~99% of New Zealand's exports by value within 10 years; false if the tariff-elimination share or phase-in period is materially different, or if negotiations had not concluded.
reasoning: MFAT's official NZ-GCC FTA overview and the Beehive press release confirm negotiations were concluded on 31 October 2024, before the 5 November 2024 statement date. MFAT states verbatim that 'Tariffs will be eliminated on 99% of New Zealand's exports over ten years' — matching Luxon's claim of duty-free access for 99 percent of NZ exports over 10 years. Both the tariff-elimination share and the phase-in period align with the claim as stated.

statement: We’re down at 6.8 percent, heading to 5 percent to deliver on Smokefree Aotearoa 2025.
criterion: The New Zealand Health Survey daily smoking prevalence for adults, most recent release before 5 November 2024, and the Smokefree Aotearoa 2025 Action Plan target: true if the published daily smoking rate is 6.8% and the stated goal is under 5%, false if either figure is materially different.
reasoning: The most recent NZ Health Survey daily smoking figure published before 5 Nov 2024 was the 2022/23 rate of 6.8% (the 2023/24 update reporting 6.9% describes it as 'similar to the previous year (6.8%)', and the 2023/24 release came out after this date). Luxon's cited 6.8% matches. The Smokefree Aotearoa 2025 goal is confirmed as daily smoking prevalence under 5% for all population groups. Both figures in the criterion hold.

statement: We operate very differently from the previous administration. We don’t need 16 reminders from the Cabinet Office to manage conflicts.
criterion: Cabinet Office correspondence released under the Official Information Act covering the 2017–2023 government: true if the Cabinet Office issued approximately 16 reminders to Ministers about conflict-of-interest management over that period, false if the count is materially different or no such reminders are recorded.
reasoning: The criterion requires locating Cabinet Office OIA correspondence covering 2017-2023 and confirming ~16 conflict-of-interest reminders to Ministers. DPMC sources confirm the Cabinet Office does issue reminders (annually after the pecuniary-interest register, plus a worksheet/discussion on each appointment), but no released OIA document, DPMC publication, or news report I could reach quantifies these as '16' for the previous government. The specific source the criterion names is not findable, so the '16' figure can neither be confirmed nor cleanly refuted (annual-only reminders over six years would be nearer 6, but appointment-triggered ones could raise it). Web-search quota was exhausted before the final targeted queries could run.

statement: Inflation is back within the target band, and the Reserve Bank has begun reducing interest rates.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI for the September 2024 quarter and the RBNZ Official Cash Rate decision record for 2024: true if annual CPI is between 1% and 3% and the OCR was lowered at one or more reviews before 5 November 2024, false if inflation is outside the band or no cut had occurred.
reasoning: Stats NZ CPI for the September 2024 quarter shows annual inflation of 2.2%, inside the 1-3% target band. The RBNZ cut the OCR from 5.50% to 5.25% in August 2024 and again to 4.75% on 9 October 2024 — both cuts occurred before 5 November 2024. Both conditions of the criterion for 'true' are met.

statement: The survey also measures overall business confidence—a net 66 percent of businesses think that general business conditions will be better in 12 months’ time.
criterion: The ANZ Business Outlook survey release for October 2024: true if the headline business confidence net balance is approximately +66, false if materially different or if the figure quoted belongs to a different series (e.g. own-activity outlook).
reasoning: The ANZ Business Outlook survey for October 2024 showed headline business confidence rising 5 points to +66, a fresh 10-year high. This is the general-business-conditions-in-12-months measure Willis cited, correctly distinguished from expected own activity (+46). The quoted net 66 percent matches the headline series exactly.

statement: These are our most serious offenders, who must have committed at least two serious crimes with convictions of at least 10 years or more, which could be a range of things including sexual violence, aggravated robbery, or injury with intent to cause grievous bodily harm.
criterion: The Cabinet paper and the youth justice bill establishing military-style academies (Oranga Tamariki serious youth offender provisions): true if entry requires at least two convictions for offences with a maximum penalty of 10 years or more, false if the threshold is a different number of offences or a different penalty level.
reasoning: The Young Serious Offender (YSO) declaration criteria in the Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill and the official fact sheet require 2 or more eligible offences, each punishable by at least 10 years' imprisonment, proven in court (young person aged 14-17 at time of offending). This matches Chhour's statement of 'at least two serious crimes' with a '10 years or more' penalty threshold. Her named examples — aggravated robbery and injury/wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm — are the same offences cited in the official materials. The threshold is exactly two offences and a 10-year maximum-penalty level, so the criterion (true if two convictions for offences with a 10-year-plus maximum penalty) is met. Minor wording note: the youth-justice process uses 'proven'/'charges proved' rather than 'convictions', but the substance is identical.

statement: The Reserve Bank, for example, is expecting a negative GDP result in the previous quarter—the September quarter—but a positive result in the current quarter and a steadily growing economy in 2025 and beyond.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP (production measure, seasonally adjusted): true if the September 2024 quarter is negative, the December 2024 quarter is positive, and the four quarters of 2025 show sustained positive growth; false if any leg of that path is contradicted, in particular if 2025 records renewed contraction rather than steady growth.
reasoning: The two specific near-term legs held exactly: Stats NZ (production, seasonally adjusted) recorded the Sept 2024 quarter as negative (-1.0%) and the Dec 2024 quarter as positive (+0.7%). But the central forward claim — a 'steadily growing economy in 2025 and beyond' — is contradicted. 2025 did not grow steadily: after +0.9% in Q1 (March), the June 2025 quarter fell 0.9% in a sharp, broad-based contraction (worse than RBNZ's own forecast), before Q3 (+1.1%) and Q4 (+0.2%) recovered. The criterion explicitly names renewed 2025 contraction as a falsifier of 'steady growth,' so the prediction is materially overstated even though the immediate turnaround it forecast occurred.

statement: That will not continue for ever, however, and unemployment is expected to come down next year.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate, quarterly through 2025: true if the rate falls over the course of 2025 (Q4 2025 materially below the peak reached in 2025 and below the December 2024 quarter), false if it is flat or higher at the end of 2025 than at the start.
reasoning: HLFS seasonally-adjusted unemployment rose through 2025 rather than falling: Dec 2024 5.1%, Mar 2025 5.1%, Jun 2025 5.2%, Sep 2025 5.3%, Dec 2025 5.4%. Q4 2025 (5.4%) was the 2025 peak, above the start of 2025 (5.1%) and above the Dec 2024 quarter (5.1%). The criterion requires Q4 2025 materially below the 2025 peak and below Dec 2024 for 'true'; instead the rate was flat then higher, meeting the 'false/wrong' condition.

statement: Will the Government consider moving an instruction to the committee to report the Treaty principles bill back to Parliament immediately, given there is no requirement in the coalition agreement for a full select committee process, and, if not, why not?
criterion: The published National–ACT coalition agreement (Nov 2023) text on the Treaty Principles Bill; true if it commits only to supporting the bill to select committee without requiring a full or standard-length select committee process, false if it specifies a full select committee process.
reasoning: The published National–ACT coalition agreement (Nov 2023), under 'Strengthening Democracy', commits the parties only to 'Introduce a Treaty Principles Bill based on existing ACT policy and support it to a Select Committee as soon as practicable.' It commits to supporting the bill TO select committee but specifies no full or standard-length select committee process. Luxon publicly confirmed National agreed to support it to select committee 'with no commitment beyond that.' This matches the criterion's 'true' condition and supports McAnulty's premise that the coalition agreement contains no requirement for a full select committee process.

statement: Acknowledging the successful outcome for President Trump in the USA, does the Minister see any risk to Kiwi workers and our economy from the prospect of substantial tariffs in addition to those the last Trump administration imposed on New Zealand’s steel and aluminium exports; or from being, to use the Prime Minister’s words, a “force multiplier” for the USA under pillar 2 of AUKUS, which aims to contain China, our largest trading partner, which doesn’t impose tariffs on New Zealand exporters; or from the increasing global temperatures, droughts, and storm damage which will result if the USA withdraws from climate action?
criterion: US Section 232 proclamations of March 2018 and MFAT/NZ trade records on whether New Zealand steel and aluminium were subject to those tariffs; plus a documented quotation of Christopher Luxon using "force multiplier" in relation to AUKUS pillar 2. True if both are on the record, false if either is not.
reasoning: Both components of the criterion are documented. Section 232 proclamations of 8 March 2018 imposed 25% steel / 10% aluminium tariffs; New Zealand received no exemption, so NZ steel and aluminium exports were subject to them. Separately, Christopher Luxon used the phrase 'force multiplier' in his April 2024 Lowy Institute address in Sydney, the same speech in which he confirmed NZ was scoping AUKUS pillar two. Minor nuance: Luxon's words were 'force multiplier for Australia' (in Q&A), whereas Parker rendered it 'for the USA under pillar 2 of AUKUS' — but the criterion (both facts on the record) is met.

statement: As that member will know, we’re about to re-engage with an administration where we got right on the cusp of a free-trade agreement; where he turned in front of the then Prime Minister—because of the work we’d done—and said to his team, “Well, why not?” We missed a chance then; we don’t intend to miss that chance this time.
criterion: USTR and MFAT records on whether US–NZ FTA negotiations were formally launched or scoped in 2017–2020, and contemporaneous reporting or readouts of the Trump–Ardern meetings. True if an FTA process reached a formal or near-formal stage and the reported remark is documented; false if no negotiation process existed beyond general expressions of interest.
reasoning: During the first Trump term there was real US-NZ trade engagement — 2017 openness signals, a July 2018 TIFA cooperation program, and a Sept 2019 Ardern-Trump meeting that was to precede PRELIMINARY trade talks in Washington the following month. But no formal or near-formal FTA negotiation was ever launched; talks were expected to 'take years,' and the USTR TIFA readout makes no mention of an FTA. 'Right on the cusp of a free-trade agreement' materially overstates a pre-negotiation stage, and Peters's specific detail — Trump turning to his team and saying 'Well, why not?' in front of Ardern — is not documented in any contemporaneous readout of the meeting. Substance of momentum holds; the 'cusp' framing and the quoted remark are unsupported.

statement: The reality is that AUKUS is a work in progress with respect to pillar 2, and that member’s party was part and parcel of that arrangement—begun with a commissioned paper in September of 2021 under the then Labour Government; a report in October 2021—on which we have worked in the same way ever since, with no changes at all; so much so that the former defence Minister Andrew Little says that we have got it about right.
criterion: MFAT/Defence official information releases dated September–October 2021 on AUKUS pillar 2, and a documented public statement by Andrew Little assessing the current government's AUKUS position. True if the dated documents exist and Little's statement is on the record, false if either is absent or materially mischaracterised.
reasoning: Both named elements of the criterion are on the record. Proactively-released Cabinet/MFAT/Defence documents (released after Peters wrote to Hipkins) show NZ's AUKUS Pillar 2 engagement began under Labour in Sept–Oct 2021: officials held 'Tier 2 AUKUS' meetings at Defence House on 16 and 23 September 2021 (the day of the announcement), and ministers received advice on 22 October 2021 that there were 'likely to be significant opportunities' for cooperation, particularly cyber and AI. Peters' 'commissioned paper in September 2021' and 'report in October 2021' map reasonably onto these dated documents. Andrew Little's assessment is also on the record: as former defence minister he backed the current government's decision to explore Pillar 2 and said Peters' recent comments 'seem about right' — a fair basis for 'we have got it about right,' though Little hedged it (there was 'nothing to respond to' because there was no concrete Pillar 2 proposal yet). Rated partly_true rather than true because Peters materially overstates continuity: 'worked in the same way ever since, with no changes at all' is contradicted by the released documents, which show the public position shifted over time and that officials proposed 'updating' and 're-calibrating' NZ's key messages. The dated documents and Little's endorsement exist as claimed; the 'no changes at all' framing is overstated.

statement: That is what we expect: abundance; that these structures, these protected areas, will actually allow the gulf to be restored to a place where if we do want to go for a fish, if we want to go and catch a crayfish or collect some scallops outside these areas, they’ll be available to all of us.
criterion: Monitoring under the Act (the five-yearly reviews and the statutory comprehensive assessment) together with Fisheries NZ stock assessments and Hauraki Gulf Forum reporting; true if crayfish and scallop abundance in the gulf recovers sufficiently that recreational take outside the protected areas is open and viable, false if those populations remain collapsed or harvest closures remain in place.
reasoning: Resolve-by date is 2035-10-07; the Act commenced only 25 October 2025, ~10 months ago. The criterion depends on the five-yearly reviews and the statutory comprehensive assessment, none of which have run. Current baseline evidence: Hauraki Gulf Forum State of our Gulf 2026 reports kōura (crayfish) as depleted and tipa (scallop) fisheries closed, and a further two-year rockpool harvest closure at Ōmaha Bay/Kawau Bay/Whangaparāoa took effect 12 March 2026. That is the starting condition the prediction is measured from, not a refutation of it — a recovery claim on a decade horizon cannot be scored ten months in.

statement: Te Pāti Māori knows for a fact that whānau who go for a dive or fish to gather kai or kai moana for kai for tangihanga—they will be the ones who will be criminalised and fined, rather than the big corporate commercial fishing companies who exploit our taonga and kai.
criterion: Enforcement records under the Act (Fisheries NZ/DOC prosecutions and infringement notices for breaches of the new high protection areas and marine reserves) in the first years after commencement; true if the large majority of penalties are imposed on individual customary or recreational gatherers and none or almost none on commercial operators, false if commercial operators are a substantial share of enforcement action.
reasoning: Resolve-by date is 2028-10-07. The criterion requires enforcement records — DOC/Fisheries NZ prosecutions and infringement notices under the new high protection areas and marine reserves — and no such records have been published in the ~10 months since commencement on 25 October 2025. I searched for enforcement actions against both individual gatherers and commercial operators and found neither, so the ratio the criterion turns on has no denominator yet. DOC's stated posture for this initial period is education-first (15 permanent and 13 seasonal staff focused on public education, with compliance activity increasing as familiarity grows), which is consistent with an absence of records rather than an absence of enforcement intent.

statement: My area is going to grow more than most because a lot of the building is going to happen in those areas.
criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates and Auckland Council dwelling-consent counts for the Mount Albert / Albert-Eden area; true if population and dwelling growth rates there exceed the Auckland regional average over the years following 2025, false if they are at or below the regional average.
reasoning: Resolve-by date is 2030-06-30. The criterion asks for Stats NZ subnational population estimates and Auckland Council dwelling-consent counts for Albert-Eden 'over the years following 2025', but the latest published Stats NZ subnational estimates are at 30 June 2025 — the year the statement was made — so there is no post-statement series to compare against the Auckland regional average. Noting for the eventual resolution: the last completed measurement went the other way, with Albert-Eden falling 2.0% (98,622 to 96,630) between the 2018 and 2023 censuses, so this is a bet on intensification reversing a decline rather than a continuation of trend. That does not make it wrong now — the window has not opened.

statement: Growth is coming.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP releases for the September 2025 and December 2025 quarters; true if both print positive quarterly growth, false if either is negative.
reasoning: The criterion required positive quarterly real GDP growth in both the September 2025 and December 2025 quarters. Stats NZ reported +1.1% for the September 2025 quarter (released 18 Dec 2025) and +0.2% for the December 2025 quarter (released 19 Mar 2026). The March 2026 quarter release revised these to +0.9% and +0.5% respectively. Both quarters are positive on both the original and revised vintages, so the criterion's failure condition (either quarter negative) is not met. Checked for disconfirming evidence in the revision history, since a downward revision was the plausible route to a negative print — the September quarter was revised down but stayed clearly positive, and December was revised up.

statement: While the road has been a little rocky, the economy looks to have picked up again, with growth resuming in the second half of the year.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP for the September 2025 and December 2025 quarters; true if both quarters record positive growth, false if either is negative.
reasoning: Same test as the Luxon item, and it resolves the same way: September 2025 +1.1% (revised +0.9%) and December 2025 +0.2% (revised +0.5%), both positive. The specific claim that growth resumed in the second half of 2025 is directly supported by Stats NZ's own commentary that the economy 'picked up noticeably in the second half of the year, growing 1.1 percent over the final six months after being relatively flat over the first half.' The 'rocky road' framing is also accurate — the June 2025 quarter contracted 1.0% before the September rebound. One qualification that does not change the verdict under the criterion as written: the December quarter's first print of 0.2% undershot the RBNZ's 0.5% projection, so the pick-up was weaker than expected at the time, though the subsequent revision to 0.5% removed that gap.

statement: That’s why in the Budget we saw 240,000 new jobs will be created over the next four years and an economy that’s expected to grow about 2.7 percent, on average, each year for the next four.
criterion: Stats NZ employment/filled-jobs series and real GDP over the four years covered by the Budget 2025 forecast track. True if total employment rises by approximately 240,000 across that period and real GDP growth averages about 2.7% a year; false if employment growth or average growth falls materially short.
reasoning: The criterion tests outcomes across the full four-year Budget 2025 forecast track (roughly 2025/26 through 2028/29), with a resolve-by date of 2029-09-30. Today is 2026-08-15, so only about one year of the four-year window has elapsed and neither the cumulative employment change nor the four-year average GDP growth rate can be evaluated. I did verify the underlying characterisation of the Budget: Treasury's BEFU 2025 and the Budget 2025 materials do forecast 240,000 more people in jobs by the end of the forecast period, so Luxon accurately described what the Budget projected. Early trajectory is mixed but not gradeable — unemployment was 5.3% in the March 2026 quarter (down from 5.4% in December 2025), and actual growth so far has run below the forecast path (Dec 2025 +0.5%, Mar 2026 +0.8%). That is a partial year of evidence against a four-year average, which is not enough to call.

statement: We will see the health of the ocean improve, and I’m looking forward to having visits in future years where we can actually point to real examples of where we are seeing fishery stocks grow back again in abundance.
criterion: Hauraki Gulf Forum 'State of Our Gulf' reporting and DOC/Fisheries NZ monitoring of the new high protection areas; true if post-implementation monitoring shows increases in fish biomass or abundance inside the protected areas relative to the pre-implementation baseline, false if monitoring shows no improvement or continued decline.
reasoning: The Hauraki Gulf/Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Act came into effect 25 October 2025, creating 12 high protection areas, 5 seafloor protection areas and extending 2 marine reserves. The criterion asks for post-implementation DOC/Fisheries NZ monitoring showing biomass or abundance increases inside the protected areas relative to a pre-implementation baseline. Only ~10 months have elapsed and no such post-implementation monitoring has been published. The Hauraki Gulf Forum's State of our Gulf 2026 (eighth report, released July 2026) documents continued depletion — crayfish biomass under 5% of unfished levels, scallop fisheries closed, ~40% of coastal reefs as kina barrens — but this describes pre-protection conditions across the Gulf, not the effect of areas protected for less than a year. The resolve-by date is 2031-01-01. Not finding a result yet is the correct answer, not a failing grade.

statement: The Animal Law Association, who won a court case, and given that the Minister’s allowing this to run till February—we’ve got between December and February for another court case.
criterion: Court records and public reporting for proceedings filed against the Crown/MPI over pig welfare regulations between 18 December 2025 and 28 February 2026. True if a judicial review or comparable proceeding is filed in that window; false if no such proceeding is brought.
reasoning: Boyack's prediction depended on a legal gap: the regulations permitting farrowing crates were due to expire 18 December 2025, while the Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill was before the Primary Production Committee with a target report date of 9 February 2026 — hence 'between December and February for another court case'. The Government closed that gap. It passed the pig-farming law changes through Parliament under urgency in December 2025, days before 18 December, amending the Animal Welfare Act itself to permit farrowing crates and mating stalls through to 18 December 2035. That removed both the window and the statutory basis a judicial review would have attacked (the 2020 NZALA/SAFE win turned on regulations being inconsistent with the parent Act; Parliament amended the parent Act). Searching for disconfirming evidence: NZALA's own news page lists nothing between its 30 October 2025 submission and a 2 March 2026 submission on an unrelated bill; SAFE's news feed covers November 2025 farm footage, a January 2026 supporter update, the April 2026 greyhound ban and August 2026 hen welfare, with no pig litigation. Both organisations publicised their 2019 filing and 2020 High Court win prominently, so a new filing would be expected to appear. No judicial review or comparable proceeding was filed in the 18 December 2025 – 28 February 2026 window.

statement: I’m hearing every week from the sector that these cuts and closures are only going to increase under this reform.
criterion: Tertiary Education Commission and individual polytechnic announcements of redundancies, programme discontinuations and site closures in the 12 months after October 2025, compared with the preceding 12 months; true if the counts rise, false if they hold steady or fall.
reasoning: The criterion requires comparing counts of redundancies, programme discontinuations and site closures in the 12 months after October 2025 against the preceding 12 months. That window does not close until October 2026 (today is 15 August 2026), and neither the Tertiary Education Commission nor any other source has published the aggregate comparison the criterion calls for; one report notes polytechnic job-cut numbers were being kept confidential. Evidence available so far is directionally consistent with Halbert's claim but does not resolve it: ten polytechnics were re-established as standalone institutions on 1 January 2026; Cabinet papers forecast roughly 1,000 jobs, 500 courses and 30 delivery sites lost across the transition; NorthTec, EIT and UCOL have proposed further cuts since re-establishment, with NorthTec proposing to stop 11 programmes and close its Auckland campus; Otago Polytechnic moved to cut up to 21 FTE; and in July 2026 officials were reported warning that polytechnics remain at risk under the reforms. Against that, much of the reported staff loss (855 staff, ~$80m funding cuts) predates October 2025 under Te Pūkenga, so it is not yet established that the post-October-2025 counts exceed the prior 12 months rather than continuing or tapering from them.

statement: I’m not able to discuss it because it’s still in the middle of a media pitch, but when it does come out, it will reveal that, actually, this thing is not that financially viable.
criterion: The Treasury advice on the vocational education reform released after 7 October 2025 (proactive release or OIA): true if the released advice states or clearly implies the reformed ITP model is not financially viable; false if it finds the model financially viable or the advice is never released.
reasoning: The predicted release happened and pointed the way Hernandez said it would. Treasury OIA-20250592 ("The dis-establishment of Te Pūkenga") was published in October 2025 — after 7 October — and was reported on 16 October 2025; Hernandez himself publicly commented on the released Treasury correspondence, consistent with this being the 'media pitch' he referred to. On substance, the released advice clearly implies the reformed ITP model is not financially viable on its own terms: Treasury said it had not seen sufficient analysis of how the federation model 'will function, be funded and implemented, or how it will materially support the viability of institutions'; it recommended consolidating polytechnics instead, to create more financially viable entities; it advised that 'strategic grants will likely need to be increased under any option'; and it warned the cuts required to reach financially sustainable standalone units called into question how they could deliver the education learners and employers need. Earlier Treasury advice (June 2025) had put it more bluntly — the outcome could be 'similar, if not worse, than the situation faced pre-Te Pūkenga'. Neither false branch of the criterion applies: the advice was released, and it does not find the model financially viable. One hedge on the strength of the verdict: Treasury stopped short of an explicit viability finding, framing its position as insufficient analysis to form a clear view, and Hernandez's own gloss on the documents was the weaker 'significant risk'. His claim was also modestly worded ('not that financially viable'), which the released advice supports. Limitation: I could not extract the PDF's text directly (the fetcher failed to parse it and pdftotext required approval unavailable in this session), so this rests on multiple independent reports of the document's contents rather than first-hand reading.

statement: There are going to be more cuts.
criterion: Announcements by the new standalone polytechnics, the Tertiary Education Commission, or Tertiary Education Union tallies covering the period after October 2025; true if further staff, programme or campus reductions are announced across the sector, false if the sector records no net further cuts through the resolve-by date.
reasoning: Although the resolve-by date (31 Dec 2026) has not passed, the criterion's true condition is already met by evidence, so this is determinable rather than not_yet_due. Newsroom (22 July 2026), citing answers to written parliamentary questions, reports that a further 125 programmes were cut during 2026 — on top of the roughly 550 programmes, 900 full-time roles and 30 delivery sites cut by late 2024. Institutional consolidation also continued after October 2025: on 31 March 2026 it was announced that Tai Poutini Polytechnic will cease to exist as an independent institution and transfer its operations to become a regional campus of Open Polytechnic from 1 January 2027, with NorthTec, WITT and Whitireia/WelTec deferred to standalone status in 2027 under a Federation of Polytechnics for shared services. Ministry of Education advice reported in the same piece states that 'the scale of work, tight timelines and the financial viability of some polytechnics, all remain key risks', and RNZ reports polytechnics carrying hundreds of unfunded students in 2026. Checking the disconfirming side — whether the sector recorded no net further cuts — found nothing: no reporting of net staff, programme or campus growth across the sector, and the union describes continued staffing crisis. The claim was vague ('more cuts'), which makes it easy to satisfy, but it is satisfied on the criterion as written.

statement: These changes will increase the supply of affordable housing options and provide Kiwis with more choices.
criterion: MBIE building consent data and the exemption/notification records for small standalone dwellings (up to 70 square metres) for the two years after the Act commences, compared with the two years before. True if the annual count of such dwellings built rises materially above the pre-commencement baseline; false if the count is flat or falls.
reasoning: The criterion requires comparing MBIE building consent data and exemption/notification records for small standalone dwellings (up to 70 m²) over the two years after commencement against the two years before. The Building and Construction (Small Standalone Dwellings) legislation passed 23 October 2025 and the granny flats building consent exemption commenced on 15 January 2026, so the two-year post-commencement window does not close until January 2028 — the resolve-by date of 30 June 2028 was set accordingly. As at August 2026 only about seven months of post-commencement activity exists, and no national MBIE tally of exempt small standalone dwellings has been published. What early signal exists is fragmentary and not a substitute: MBIE reports over 52,000 downloads of the exemption guidance, and Auckland Council's resource consent register for 21 December 2025 – 20 June 2026 shows at least 91 lodgements describing a minor/second dwelling or granny flat, with monthly counts rising rather than falling after 15 January — suggestive of interest, but far short of the two-year comparison the criterion demands, and consent-register counts also exclude the exempt builds that are the whole point of the policy. This is a genuinely premature question, not an unfindable one.

statement: They know it is going to lead to job cuts, to cuts to courses, to the sale of land that we won’t be able to get back, and they’re just agreeing with their Minister and saying that this is going to be a great thing and promising.
criterion: Public announcements, annual reports and TEC records for the regional institutes of technology and polytechnics created on disestablishment of Te Pūkenga: true if redundancies, programme/course closures and sales of campus land are recorded at regional institutes following the reform; false if the new institutes complete the transition without redundancies, course closures or land sales.
reasoning: Two of the criterion's three limbs are already recorded. Redundancies: Te Pūkenga lost over $80m in funding and 855 staff ahead of disestablishment; Cabinet papers forecast ~1,000 jobs and ~500 courses lost in the transition; Toi Ohomai confirmed disestablishing 152.5 FTE (net loss 60.9 roles); NorthTec cut 58 jobs in late 2025. Course/programme closures: the Te Kāhui Auaha campus in central Wellington closed, costing 48 jobs and programmes including the NZ Diploma in Māori and Pacific Performing Arts. Land sales: NOT yet realised — around $100m of assets were identified for sale (Te Pūkenga's own high-level assessment was up to $131m through to 2031), 'primarily' unused or underused land and buildings, but the specific properties remained under 'active consideration' and no completed campus land sale is documented as of August 2026. Disconfirming evidence on the campus limb: Toi Ohomai reversed its proposal to close the Taupō and Tokoroa campuses. The criterion's window runs to 2027-06-30, so the land-sale limb remains open.

statement: We think that there will be 13,000 more dwellings because of this legislation, and that is a good thing.
criterion: MBIE/Stats NZ building consent and exemption data for small stand-alone dwellings built under this Act's regime, measured against the counterfactual baseline in the bill's regulatory impact statement over the period that estimate covers (10 years from commencement); true if cumulative additional dwellings reach approximately 13,000, false if materially fewer.
reasoning: The granny-flats building consent exemption commenced 15 January 2026, and the criterion measures cumulative additional dwellings over the 10 years from commencement (to ~2036). Only about seven months have elapsed as of August 2026, and no MBIE or Stats NZ uptake/notification data for exempt small stand-alone dwellings is published yet. Note the 13,000 figure is a faithful restatement of the Government's own regulatory impact estimate ('almost 13,000 additional dwellings ... over the next decade'), so the number was not invented by the speaker — but whether it is achieved cannot be measured yet.

statement: Our building code is, actually, wholly insufficient, and we will be facing another issue of something similar to the leaky buildings over the next 10 or 20 years.
criterion: MBIE / Building Officials or weathertightness-style inquiry reporting by 2045: true if a systemic, sector-wide defect problem (e.g. widespread structural or mould/moisture failure in dwellings built under the current code) is officially identified on a scale drawing comparison with the leaky homes crisis; false if no such systemic failure is identified by that date.
reasoning: The prediction covers the next 10–20 years with a resolve-by date of 2045-10-07. No MBIE, Building Officials, or weathertightness-style inquiry has officially identified a systemic, sector-wide defect problem in dwellings built under the current code on a scale comparable to the leaky homes crisis (~42,000 dwellings built 1992–2005). I checked for disconfirming evidence too: there are contextual signals in both directions — rising building defect reports, and commentary on strain from record construction volumes, labour shortages and proposals to expand private building consenting — but none of this constitutes the official identification the criterion requires, and nothing rules the prediction out either. Nineteen years remain on the horizon.

statement: It’s now growing again in quarter 3; the growth in quarter 4 will step up.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real production GDP releases: true if the September 2025 quarter records positive growth AND the December 2025 quarter records growth greater than the September quarter; false if either quarter contracts or if December growth does not exceed September.
reasoning: Both quarters are now published. The September 2025 quarter grew 1.1% (later revised down to 0.9%), so the first half of the claim held — the economy was growing again. But the December 2025 quarter grew only 0.2%, a sharp step DOWN from September, not the step up Luxon predicted; it also undershot the RBNZ's 0.5% forecast and every major bank pick except ANZ's. Construction was the largest negative contributor to Q4 GDP (-1.4%). The criterion's stated failure condition — 'false if ... December growth does not exceed September' — is squarely met.

statement: I’m advised that around 4,300 fewer 18- and 19-year-olds will be eligible for the jobseeker support as a result of the parental assistance test, which has two parts: the parental income test and the parental support gap test.
criterion: MSD benefit statistics for 18- and 19-year-olds receiving Jobseeker Support, comparing the twelve months after the parental assistance test takes effect with the pre-implementation baseline: true if the reduction attributable to the test is approximately 4,300 (within about 20%), false if it is materially larger or smaller.
reasoning: The parental assistance test is not yet in force. Work and Income states it applies from 2 November 2026; the Budget 2025 MSD factsheet gave an implementation date of July 2027. Today is 15 August 2026, so on either date the twelve-month post-implementation window the criterion requires has not begun, and no MSD benefit statistics measuring the actual reduction exist. MSD's published forecast is that approximately 17,800 people aged 18 and 19 will be ineligible over the first two years of implementation, which is not inconsistent with a ~4,300 figure for a narrower cohort or period, but that is a projection rather than the outcome data the criterion specifies. No searching could resolve this yet.

statement: Yes, it is the case that, as the economy recovers, we expect that more jobs will be created in the construction sector.
criterion: Stats NZ construction sector employment (HLFS industry series or filled jobs, construction): true if construction employment by the December 2026 quarter is above the September 2025 quarter level; false if it is at or below that level.
reasoning: The criterion measures construction employment in the December 2026 quarter against the September 2025 quarter. As of 15 August 2026 the December 2026 quarter has not occurred, and Stats NZ will not release that data until early 2027. The most recent evidence runs against the prediction but cannot settle it: construction activity has declined for four consecutive quarters, total building work has fallen for nine consecutive quarters through Q1 2026, construction output was down 5.91% year-on-year in March 2026, and Westpac's read of the March 2026 employment indicators was that construction had stabilised but not returned to growth. Counter-signal exists too — construction job listings rose 35% in the twelve months to March 2026, and Infometrics forecasts construction employment to lift slowly — so the December 2026 outcome is genuinely open.

statement: It is interesting that the commentary to the bill notes that the Resource Management Act component of allowing these small, stand-alone dwellings to not have to go through a consenting process is going to be done through a proposed National Environment Standards for Granny Flats that is expected to take effect by the end of 2025.
criterion: The New Zealand Gazette / legislation.govt.nz record for the National Environmental Standards for Granny Flats (or equivalently named NES made under the Resource Management Act). True if the standard was made and in force on or before 31 December 2025; false if it had not commenced by that date.
reasoning: The Resource Management (National Environmental Standards for Detached Minor Residential Units) Regulations 2025 — the 'granny flats' NES referred to — were approved by the Governor-General on 15 December 2025 and gazetted 18 December 2025, but their stated commencement is 15 January 2026. The criterion's true arm required the standard to be both made AND in force on or before 31 December 2025; it was made in 2025 but had not commenced by that date, so it did not 'take effect by the end of 2025' as the bill commentary expected. The instrument itself exists and does what was described, and the slippage was about two weeks, hence partly rather than wholly wrong.

statement: As Professor John Turkey pointed out, without building consents, authorities almost certainly will lose that robust oversight of how many new dwellings are being added and the pressure on local infrastructure.
criterion: After the exemption comes into force, whether councils can report a count of exempt small stand-alone dwellings built in their district and use it for infrastructure planning — false if the Act's completion-notification requirement yields a usable national/local dataset comparable to consent records, true if councils report they cannot account for the dwellings built.
reasoning: The building consent exemption for small stand-alone dwellings commenced only on 15 January 2026 (Commencement Order gazetted 18 December 2025), roughly seven months before the check date, and the criterion's resolve date is 31 December 2027. The regime does require a PIM before work starts and a completion notification to the territorial authority, so a data path exists in principle, but no aggregate national or council-level count of exempt dwellings has been published, and no council has yet reported that it cannot account for dwellings built. Neither arm of the criterion — a usable consent-comparable dataset, or councils reporting they cannot account for the dwellings — is yet testable.

statement: There are several cases that have been heard that will have to be re-heard in light of this legislation if it passes.
criterion: Court records and Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti reporting on customary marine title applications after the amendment bill's enactment: true if one or more applications already determined under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 are re-heard or remitted for fresh determination under the amended threshold; false if no previously-determined application is re-heard, or if the bill does not pass.
reasoning: The bill passed — the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act 2025 received Royal assent on 24 October 2025. Its transitional schedule (clause 4) stripped legal effect from CMT decisions made in the interim period between the policy announcement and enactment, requiring seven cases to be reheard under the amended s58 threshold, four of which had already had customary marine title recognised; the Government allocated up to $15m toward affected applicants' rehearing costs. A concrete instance has since occurred: the Ruapuke Island Group's customary marine title over Te Ara a Kiwa/Foveaux Strait, determined by the High Court in August 2025, was reheard and re-determined by Justice Churchman in a judgment released 26 February 2026, which found the group met the revised tests. That satisfies the criterion's true arm — a previously determined application re-heard under the amended threshold.

statement: Well, as has previously been traversed in this House, it is the case throughout New Zealand’s history that, as economies recover, fewer New Zealanders leave, and we expect that to be the case.
criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for New Zealand citizen departures, and departures to Australia: true if annual citizen departures for the year to December 2026 are lower than for the year to September 2025; false if they are the same or higher.
reasoning: The criterion requires Stats NZ annual NZ-citizen departures for the year to December 2026, compared against the year to September 2025. As of 2026-08-15 that period is incomplete and the release will not appear until ~February 2027, after the resolve-by date. Baseline for comparison is 72,700 citizen departures in the September 2025 year (a record, net citizen loss 46,400). Latest available actual is the June 2026 year: 26,200 citizen arrivals and 63,900 departures (net citizen loss 37,700), departures down 3% on the June 2025 year and ~12% below the Sep-2025 baseline; total net migration rose to a 17,600 gain, driven mainly by falling departures. So the claim is currently trending toward 'true', but cannot be resolved against the criterion as written until the December 2026 year is published.

statement: After a period of consistent clarity about building, focusing on growth, focusing on investment, and giving confidence to the broader community, in our second and third terms the economy was growing well, and we managed to reverse the flow across the Tasman, and that’s going to happen again this time.
criterion: Stats NZ international migration series for NZ-citizen migration to/from Australia: true if the annual net loss to Australia falls to zero or becomes a net gain at any point before the resolve-by date; false if a net annual loss to Australia persists throughout.
reasoning: The criterion allows until 2027-06-30 for the annual net migration loss to Australia to reach zero or turn into a net gain. That has not happened and the window is still open, so no verdict can be returned yet. Evidence to date shows the loss narrowing but nowhere near reversal: Stats NZ recorded a net loss of 31,100 to Australia in calendar 2024 and 28,500 in the year to December 2025, and the narrowing came from more arrivals from Australia (16,800 to 19,000) rather than fewer departures (47,800 to 47,500, essentially flat). In the June 2026 year, 64% of the 63,900 NZ-citizen departures went to Australia (~41,000 people); in the March 2026 year it was 63%, close to 40,000. Closing a ~28,000 annual net gap within the remaining ~10 months would require an unprecedented swing, so the claim looks far off track, but per the criterion it is not yet due.

statement: There are at least four job seekers sitting on that front bench queuing up for that job, and Christopher Luxon’s days are numbered.
criterion: National Party leadership records and public reporting: true if Christopher Luxon ceases to be leader of the National Party before the 2026 general election; false if he leads the party into that election.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on whether Luxon ceases to be National Party leader before the 2026 general election, which Elections NZ confirms is Saturday 7 November 2026 - still nearly three months away as of 2026-08-15. Luxon remains leader and Prime Minister. He survived a caucus confidence vote on 12 August 2026 following a leadership challenge by Defence Minister Chris Penk, his second public leadership test of the year; he then sacked Penk from his portfolios and Penk announced he would leave Parliament. Reporting notes continued unrest and poor polling, so the claim is live but unresolved; it cannot be graded until the election or an earlier leadership change.

statement: Your bill will succeed.
criterion: The parliamentary progress record for the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill; true if the bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent, false if it is defeated at any reading or lapses at the end of the 54th Parliament.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill passed third reading and received Royal assent. It did. The parliamentary progress record shows first reading 19 Feb 2025 (passed), second reading 8 Oct 2025 (the day Court spoke, passed), third reading 12 Nov 2025 (passed), and Royal assent 17 Nov 2025. It is now on the statute book as the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Act 2025, Local Act 2025 No 2, in force the day after assent. Auckland Council's own OurAuckland announcement in November 2025 confirms enactment and notes cross-party support. Checked for the disconfirming case (defeat at a reading or lapse at the end of the 54th Parliament) and found none — the bill never lost a reading and was enacted a year before the Parliament's term ended.

statement: It might make $40 million, $50 million a year, that’s going to be a significant benefit, but it’s not going to pay for all of those things—and certainly not all the things that Simon Court was talking about—in a short period of time.
criterion: Auckland Council's annual report / Auckland Future Fund annual investment report for a full financial year of operation: true if reported annual investment income (or distributable return) falls in or near the $40–50 million range; false if materially outside it (e.g. below $25m or above $80m).
reasoning: The criterion requires an Auckland Future Fund annual report covering a FULL financial year of operation. The only annual report published so far covers the 9 months ended 30 June 2025 — a partial year, and an atypical one: proceeds of the $1.31bn Auckland Airport share sale (4 Dec 2024) sat in term deposits and on-call cash pending appointment of a global investment manager, so the fund earned only interest revenue and underperformed its return target. FY2026 (1 July 2025 – 30 June 2026) is the first full financial year; the fund and its trustee must report within three months of year end, i.e. by ~30 September 2026, and no FY2026 annual report was findable as of 15 August 2026 (latest quarterly report located is July–September 2025). The resolve-by date of 31 October 2026 has not passed. Note for whoever resolves this later: the criterion's two branches may diverge. Auckland Council material states the fund is expected to provide the council over $60 million per year from 2025/2026, but for the first three years (2024/25, 2025/26, 2026/27) distributions are set as a rate on net contributed capital rather than on the fund's actual earnings — so the 'distributable return' is a formula output, while reported investment income is a separate figure. Against the $60m+ distribution figure Foster's $40–50m would read as understated; against actual investment income it is untested until the report lands.

statement: In fact, Auckland could reach 2 million people by 2030, so that just gives you some indication of the challenges that lie ahead and the infrastructure need that is unrelenting.
criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimate for the Auckland region as at 30 June 2030; true if the estimate is 2,000,000 or more, false if below.
reasoning: The criterion names a specific source and date: the Stats NZ subnational population estimate for the Auckland region as at 30 June 2030. That estimate cannot exist until late 2030 at the earliest (the 30 June 2025 estimates were the most recent published as of August 2026), and the resolve-by date is 31 December 2030. So the claim is not yet resolvable against the criterion as written. Directional evidence, which does not substitute for the criterion: Auckland's estimated resident population was 1,816,000 at 30 June 2025, and Stats NZ's subnational population projections (2023-base–2053) have Auckland growing about 1.1 percent a year. A Stats NZ news release in April 2026 is headlined 'Auckland population projected to reach 2 million by 2033' (an earlier release framed it as 'may hit 2 million in early 2030s'), with Stats NZ noting the milestone could come earlier or later depending on migration. I checked for the disconfirming case — a projection or estimate putting Auckland at or above 2 million by 2030 — and did not find one; the median projection puts it roughly three years later than 2030. That leans against Brewer, but he said 'could reach', and only the 2030 estimate settles it.

statement: What we have is a set of reforms that are not going to make energy cheaper for New Zealand households and businesses.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI electricity subindex and MBIE retail electricity price series: true if average residential and commercial electricity prices have not fallen in real terms by the end of 2027; false if they have fallen in real terms over that period.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against Stats NZ CPI electricity subindex and MBIE retail price series at the end of 2027. Today is 15 August 2026, so the measurement window is still open and roughly a third of the way through — under rule 6 this is not_yet_due. Interim evidence runs strongly in the direction Woods predicted: Stats NZ reports electricity up 12.5 percent in the year to March 2026, with higher electricity prices accounting for more than a tenth of the 3.1 percent annual CPI increase, and this was the third consecutive quarter in which electricity was the largest single upwards contributor to annual inflation. Against 3.1 percent headline inflation, a 12.5 percent electricity increase is a large real-terms rise, not a fall. MBIE's Quarterly Survey of Domestic Electricity Prices put the national average residential price at roughly 39c/kWh at the February 2026 snapshot (about 34.6c in Wellington to nearly 49c in Balclutha). Two things could still move this before end-2027: the criterion also requires commercial prices, which I found no comparable published series for at 2026 levels, and prices can fall in real terms over 2026-27 even from a raised base. So the trend favours the claim but the verdict must wait for the December 2027 quarter CPI.

statement: In Hawke’s Bay alone, our region is set to add another thousand new jobs in agriculture and horticulture.
criterion: Stats NZ regional filled-jobs / employment data for the Hawke's Bay region in the agriculture and horticulture industries: true if the count rises by approximately 1,000 or more above its October 2025 level, false if growth is materially smaller or negative.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against Stats NZ regional filled-jobs / employment data for Hawke's Bay agriculture and horticulture, measured against the October 2025 baseline, by 30 June 2027. Today is 15 August 2026, so under rule 6 this is not_yet_due. I searched for published Stats NZ regional filled-jobs figures for Hawke's Bay ag/hort covering the period since October 2025 and did not find a released series at that industry-by-region granularity; what is available publicly is forecast rather than outturn. Infometrics' employment outlook for Hawke's Bay TLAs projects regional employment growth largely above 1.0 percent per annum over five years, with healthcare and horticulture expected to create the most jobs, while construction and sheep/beef farming are expected to shed jobs. That last point matters for how this eventually resolves: the criterion is about the combined agriculture-and-horticulture count, so horticulture gains could be partly offset by pastoral losses, and a headline horticulture figure alone would not satisfy it. Genuinely open at this date.

statement: It’s very serious in its implications and the actual tension and the time period is part of that, but so is, obviously, the invasiveness of searching and the humiliation that is involved in the control over people in that situation—but probably the most contentious part will be the issue over force used in that situation.
criterion: The Hansard record of the remaining committee-stage and third-reading debate on this omnibus bill, plus Amendment Papers tabled: true if the provisions on use of force attract more debate time and more contested amendments than the secure-care duration and search-on-entry provisions; false if either of those other parts draws more.
reasoning: The bill is the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill (omnibus: Children's Act, Crimes Act, Oranga Tamariki Act, Public Records Act). Committee stage finished on 8 Oct 2025; third reading 21 Oct 2025; assent as 2025 No 57. Criterion has two limbs. Limb 2 (contested amendments) supports White decisively: of ~11 amendments put to divisions in the Part 3 debate, ~6 concerned use of force — Kahurangi Carter's AP 366 (remove force provisions), AP 370 (de-escalation before force), AP 371 (bar contractors using force), and Willow-Jean Prime's amendments to cls 17, 24, 25 and 28 covering new ss 384I (force to prevent absconding), 384KB (force during searches) and 384KK (recording use of force) — all lost on party lines. Only ~3 divisions concerned searches (image-retention APs 368/369) and 1 concerned secure-care duration (AP 367, reducing it to 3 hours). Limb 1 (debate time) does not: search powers drew roughly twice the speeches and question blocks of force in the Part 3 committee debate (harmful-items definitions, scanners, pat-downs, vehicle searches, image retention/disposal, searches of people entering the residence), with secure-care duration a distant third. Force led modestly at the third reading (Prime and Marama Davidson both centred on s 384KB and de-escalation, Chhour replying on 'reasonable force'), but not enough to overturn the committee-stage balance. The criterion requires force to lead on both measures and is explicitly false if either other part draws more; searches drew more debate time. So the substance of the hedged call ('probably the most contentious part') holds on the amendment record but is overstated as a claim about the debate overall.

statement: Now the Minister is saying that it’s going to pass again, it will still pass before Christmas, a year after it was first introduced in this House.
criterion: The Parliament bill page and Hansard record for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill; true if the third reading is passed on or before 25 December 2025, false if the bill has not completed its third reading by that date.
reasoning: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill passed its third reading on 21 October 2025, supported by National, ACT and NZ First and opposed by Labour, the Greens and Te Pati Maori. It received Royal assent on 24 October 2025. That is well inside the criterion's cutoff of 25 December 2025, so the bill did 'pass before Christmas' as Henare said the Minister was claiming. Checked for the disconfirming possibility that the third reading slipped or the bill was recommitted after 8 October: no evidence of that — the bill went straight from third reading to assent. Henare's accompanying framing ('a year after it was first introduced') is approximately right rather than exact (introduction was in September 2024, so about 13 months), but the criterion tests only the passage date.

statement: This wretched bill will be the first bill on the repeal list of things that we will do to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi when there is a change of Government in one year’s time.
criterion: The result of the New Zealand general election due in 2026 and the government formed after it; true if a government excluding the current National-led coalition takes office within about a year of October 2025, false if the incumbent coalition is returned.
reasoning: Abel's prediction turns on there being 'a change of Government in one year's time' from October 2025. The 2026 New Zealand general election has been set by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon for Saturday 7 November 2026, with advance voting opening 26 October 2026 and enrolment closing 25 October 2026. As of today, 15 August 2026, the election has not been held, no results exist, and no government has been formed — so the criterion (whether a government excluding the current National-led coalition takes office) cannot yet be assessed. The criterion's own resolve-by date is 31 December 2026, after the election and the expected coalition-formation period. Note for the record that the election falls slightly outside Abel's literal 'one year's time' from October 2025, but the criterion's 'within about a year' wording and its December 2026 deadline plainly intend resolution against the post-election government, which does not yet exist.

statement: There is better legislation coming. The Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs has assured me that he’s working on his Companies Amendment Bill and that he anticipates having it in the House sometime soon.
criterion: The Parliament bills register / Order Paper: true if a Companies Amendment Bill in the name of the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs is introduced and read a first time by the resolve-by date; false if no such bill has reached the House by then.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether a Companies Amendment Bill in the name of the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs was introduced and read a first time by 2026-06-30. It was not — and still has not been as of 2026-08-15. The government-bill disclosure register (a disclosure statement is required of every government bill at introduction) lists all 2026 government bills, numbers 198-332, with no Companies or Corporate Governance Amendment Bill, and none in 2025 either. I also checked under the bill's expected actual title, the Corporate Governance Amendment Bill (Phase 1 of the Companies Act 1993 modernisation), so the verdict does not turn on Russell's informal naming. Cross-checks agree: Hansard shows no such first reading; the Companies Register news page announces no such bill; law-firm trackers (Bell Gully, MinterEllison) still describe it as forthcoming, with the expected introduction date slipping from 'early 2025' to 'second half of 2025' to 'early 2026'. Minister Simpson did introduce other commerce/consumer bills in this window (Commerce Commission Reform, Promoting Competition and Other Matters, Retail Payment System surcharges), which is disconfirming evidence in the other direction — his legislative programme was active, the companies bill simply was not part of it. Caveat on method: bills.parliament.nz is a JavaScript app I could not load directly, so this rests on the disclosure register plus Hansard, Companies Office and legal-press checks rather than on the Order Paper itself.

statement: I trust that the Minister's legislation that is promised will deal with that particular issue.
criterion: The text of the Government's promised companies/business law reform bill as introduced; true if it extends residential-address suppression or equivalent privacy protection beyond directors and their co-residents (e.g. to other household members or shareholders), false if the bill is introduced without such an extension.
reasoning: The criterion is judged against 'the text of the Government's promised companies/business law reform bill as introduced'. No such bill has been introduced: the government-bill disclosure register shows no Companies or Corporate Governance Amendment Bill among the 2025 or 2026 government bills, and Hansard shows no first reading. With no text in existence there is nothing to test the criterion against, and the resolve-by date of 2027-12-31 has not passed, so this is not yet due rather than failed. Directional note for whoever resolves it later: the announced policy would, if enacted as designed, satisfy the criterion. Cabinet agreed in August 2024 to a unique-identifier plus address-for-service model that MBIE and law-firm summaries describe as extending to shareholders as well as directors, which is broader than the harm-based, director-and-co-resident scheme in the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Act 2025 that Russell was speaking about. That is a policy intention, not enacted text, so it does not resolve the item.

statement: The Minister’s legislation will solve it properly.
criterion: The Government's Companies Act reform bill as introduced and enacted; true if it lets directors substitute a service address for their residential address without having to establish a risk of physical or mental harm, false if it retains a harm-based eligibility test or does not address director address disclosure at all.
reasoning: The criterion requires the Government's Companies Act reform bill 'as introduced and enacted'. No such bill has been introduced, let alone enacted: it is absent from the government-bill disclosure register's full 2026 list (and 2025), absent from Hansard, and absent from Companies Office notices, while legal commentators still write about it as pending. The resolve-by date of 2027-06-30 is still ahead, so the correct answer is not yet due. For later resolution: the announced Phase 1 design points toward the criterion's 'true' branch — a unique identifier for directors letting them display an address for service instead of their residential address, without an application establishing risk of physical or mental harm. Bell Gully explicitly contrasts this with the harm-based application route that became the Companies (Address Information) Amendment Act 2025. Phase 2 (Law Commission review of directors' duties) is running to a 2027 final report, which is a plausible reason the Phase 1 bill has slipped. None of this is enacted text, so it cannot resolve the item now.

statement: But they did it, and yet this Government is going to strip away conferred rights, rights that the court has actually already recognised.
criterion: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill as enacted, read against the register of customary marine title orders and agreements already made. True if the amended test is applied so as to remove, reopen or override recognitions granted before enactment; false if orders already made by the courts are expressly preserved and only pending or future applications are affected.
reasoning: The Amendment Act received Royal assent 24 Oct 2025 and applies retrospectively to 25 July 2024. Under clause 4 of the new Schedule 1AA, customary marine title decisions/orders granted between 25 July 2024 and enactment are taken to have no legal effect and must be reheard under the tightened s58/s59 test — i.e. recognitions granted by the courts before enactment are removed and reopened, which is the criterion's 'true' branch. The criterion's 'false' branch did not occur: existing orders were not expressly preserved across the board and the Act is not limited to pending or future applications. Disconfirming check: orders made before 25 July 2024 ARE preserved, and Ngā hapū o Ngāti Porou's bespoke regime is carved out, so the stripping is bounded rather than universal — but Webb's claim was specifically about rights the court had already recognised, and those (the post-July-2024 window, following the Re Edwards line) were voided. Application is already visible in the High Court's Ruapuke Island minute inviting rehearing of an affected application.

statement: With a covered centre court, we’ll be able to serve up more events year-round, and welcome even more fans, players, and international media.
criterion: The event schedule for the Manuka Doctor Arena centre court in the twelve months following completion of the roof, compared with a comparable pre-roof year: true if the number of ticketed events hosted on centre court rises; false if it is the same or lower.
reasoning: The criterion requires the centre-court event schedule for the twelve months following completion of the roof. The $15m roof was only fully funded in late 2025 (Government $5m in Oct 2025, Auckland Council $1.5m, Tātaki Auckland Unlimited's final $5m); construction is scheduled to begin in 2026 with installation targeted ahead of the January 2027 ASB Classic. As at August 2026 the roof is not complete, so no post-completion year exists to compare against a pre-roof year. The item's own resolve-by date is 2028-12-31.

statement: Our investments into tourism and hospitality will mean more international visitors, more full tables in our restaurants, more jobs being created across the country, and a stronger economy overall.
criterion: Stats NZ international visitor arrivals and Stats NZ accommodation and food services filled jobs / employment indicator, comparing the 12 months to October 2026 against the 12 months to October 2025. True if both international arrivals and hospitality employment are higher; false if either is flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion compares the 12 months to October 2026 against the 12 months to October 2025 on two Stats NZ series (international visitor arrivals, and accommodation & food services filled jobs). Today is 15 August 2026: the measurement window has not closed, and the October 2026 releases are not published until later in 2026. Partial evidence points one way on the arrivals leg only — Stats NZ recorded 3,674,600 overseas visitors in the year ended June 2026, up 299,300 (9%) on the year to June 2025, with June 2026 at 95% of June 2019 levels — but I found no hospitality filled-jobs figure for the period, and the criterion requires BOTH legs to be higher over the specified window. Judging now would substitute an easier question for the one written down.

statement: Growth is coming; jobs are coming.
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP and Household Labour Force Survey. True if GDP records positive growth in a majority of the quarters between Q4 2025 and Q4 2026 and total employment is higher at the end of that period than at 14 October 2025; false if the economy records no sustained return to growth or employment is flat or lower.
reasoning: The criterion requires a majority of the five quarters Q4 2025-Q4 2026 to show positive GDP growth plus employment higher at end-of-period than 14 Oct 2025. As of Aug 2026 only two of five quarters are published: Dec 2025 quarter +0.2% and Mar 2026 quarter +0.8%, both positive but not yet a majority. Jun 2026 quarter GDP is due Sept 2026 and the Dec 2026 quarter endpoint not until ~March 2027. Disconfirming context on the 'jobs' half: unemployment hit 5.6% in the June 2026 quarter (up from 5.4% in March, highest since 2014) with underutilisation at 13.8%, though employment levels rose 0.5% that quarter. Criterion's own resolve-by date is 2027-03-31, which has not passed.

statement: The new targets have New Zealand on track to meet its climate obligations by 2050.
criterion: New Zealand's net emissions accounts and Climate Change Commission budget assessments against the 2050 target in the Climate Change Response Act and NZ's NDC; true if the 2050 target is met, false if reported emissions exceed it.
reasoning: The criterion resolves against 2050 net emissions accounts versus the Climate Change Response Act 2050 target; resolve-by is 2050-12-31, so the outcome cannot be observed. Noting disconfirming context that does not itself satisfy the criterion: the Climate Change Commission's 2026 monitoring report finds NZ will meet the first emissions budget but the second (2026-2030) budget is 'at significant risk, and that risk has increased in the last year', and current plans and policies are insufficient to meet the third budget or the 2050 target, with the decarbonisation rate needing to more than double. That is evidence against 'on track' but is not the 2050 outcome the criterion names, so scoring it false would substitute an easier question than the one written.
