I checked for the disconfirming outcome (a select committee referral or submissions process) and found none.

statement: They’re going to need a new one tomorrow, because this one’s not going to make it through.
criterion: The division record for the bill's reading on or about 22 October 2025: true if the bill was voted down, false if it proceeded to the next stage.
reasoning: Same debate and same division as the Hamilton item: the Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Coal Mining) Amendment Bill was voted down at its first reading on 22 October 2025, Ayes 55 to Noes 68, 'Motion not agreed to.' It did not proceed to the next stage, satisfying the criterion for true. The 'need a new one tomorrow' phrasing is rhetorical framing around the checkable core ('this one's not going to make it through'), and that core is borne out exactly by the division record.

statement: I'm sorry, you're going to get voted out.
criterion: The official result of the 2026 New Zealand general election declared by the Electoral Commission, and the government formed afterwards: true if National, ACT and New Zealand First do not together form the incoming government; false if they return to government.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the official 2026 New Zealand general election result declared by the Electoral Commission and the government formed afterwards. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon announced the election for Saturday 7 November 2026 (advance voting from 26 October). As at today, 16 August 2026, the election has not been held, so there is no declared result and no post-election government to judge against. The criterion's own resolve-by date of 31 December 2026 falls after the election, so the item remains resolvable later rather than unresolvable.

statement: I think we will need to improve it when we take Government in 2026, but at least this gives us something to work on.
criterion: The composition of the government formed after the 2026 New Zealand general election, per the Governor-General's appointment of Ministers and any coalition or confidence-and-supply agreements. True if the Green Party is in government (in Cabinet or as a support party with ministerial portfolios); false if it sits on the opposition benches.
reasoning: The criterion turns on the composition of the government formed after the 2026 NZ general election. That election is scheduled for 7 November 2026 (announced by PM Luxon; confirmed by Elections NZ and Wikipedia) and has not been held as of 16 August 2026. No Governor-General appointment of Ministers and no coalition/confidence-and-supply agreements exist to check, so the prediction cannot yet be resolved. Resolve-by date is 2026-12-31, still in the future.

statement: In that regard, we do want to give policy certainty, and the policy certainty we do want to give, which is partly being granted through this bill, is for investors to come to New Zealand, invest in offshore renewable energy, and invest in renewable energy in general, and not to invest in the declining sunset fossil gas industry, because that’s not something that’s going to be continued and supported across the next Government.
criterion: The coalition/confidence agreements and first-year energy policy decisions of the government formed after the 2026 New Zealand general election; true if that government withdraws or does not maintain support for oil and gas exploration (e.g. does not fund or promote new exploration and does not retain the 2024 reinstatement of permitting), false if it continues or extends that support.
reasoning: The criterion is explicitly about the coalition/confidence agreements and first-year energy policy decisions of the government formed after the 2026 election. That election takes place 7 November 2026 and has not occurred as of 16 August 2026, so there is no post-election government, no agreements, and no first-year energy decisions on oil and gas exploration to assess. Resolve-by 2027-06-30 is roughly ten months away.

statement: The billions of dollars in private investment that this framework attracts will translate directly to demand for engineers, specialised marine technicians, and other high-value jobs.
criterion: Committed private capital in New Zealand offshore renewable energy projects under the feasibility/commercial permit regime, per MBIE permit records and developers' announced final investment decisions; true if cumulative committed private investment reaches NZ$1 billion or more with associated construction/operations hiring, false if it remains below that or no project reaches a final investment decision.
reasoning: The criterion requires cumulative committed private capital of NZ$1b+ in NZ offshore renewables under the feasibility/commercial permit regime, with associated hiring, judged by 2032-12-31. The Offshore Renewable Energy Act only became law in 2026 and the first feasibility permits were expected to be issued within months of passage; MBIE's regime is just standing up. The leading project, Taranaki Offshore Partnership (NZ Super Fund + Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners), has committed about NZ$15m to feasibility for a ~1GW, ~NZ$5b farm, with final investment decision signalled around the end of this decade and commissioning mid-2030s. So committed capital is currently far below the threshold and no FID has been taken, but the events that would decide the criterion fall inside the remaining window, so a false verdict now would be premature rather than evidenced.

statement: Whānau who don't have access to resources to build their dream home are going to see this as an opportunity to whack up what they will see as housing options, as permanent full-time housing.
criterion: MBIE and territorial authority reporting on small stand-alone dwellings built under the Act (consent/notification volumes and occupancy), together with Stats NZ dwelling and household statistics for Tairāwhiti and Ikaroa-Rāwhiti. True if such dwellings are documented as being occupied as households' primary permanent residences at a non-trivial rate; false if the records show them used overwhelmingly as ancillary dwellings on properties whose main house is separately occupied.
reasoning: The granny-flat (small stand-alone dwelling) building consent exemption only came into force on 15 January 2026 — about seven months before the date of checking, and the criterion's own resolve-by is 2028-10-31. MBIE has published early interest indicators (52,000+ downloads of the exemption guidance) but no PIM-application or completion-notification volumes, and no occupancy data at all. Stats NZ has published nothing on how dwellings built under the Act are occupied, and certainly nothing broken down for Tairāwhiti / Ikaroa-Rāwhiti. Neither the true branch (documented occupation as primary permanent residences at a non-trivial rate) nor the false branch (records showing overwhelmingly ancillary use) can be tested against evidence that does not exist yet. I checked specifically for disconfirming material — reporting that these units are being used mainly as ancillary/secondary flats — and found only commercial and council explainer pages noting the units may be rented out with no family connection required, which is a rule description, not usage evidence.

statement: It's estimated that up to 2,000 claims a year could benefit from this process.
criterion: Ministry of Justice Disputes Tribunal caseload statistics for the first full year after the raised jurisdiction takes effect; true if the number of claims filed with a value above $30,000 approaches ~2,000 a year, false if it is materially below (e.g. under half that).
reasoning: The criterion asks for Ministry of Justice Disputes Tribunal caseload statistics for the first full year after the raised jurisdiction takes effect. The increase from $30,000 to $60,000 commenced on 24 January 2026, so the first full year does not close until late January 2027, and MoJ caseload statistics for it are necessarily unpublished. No filing counts for claims valued above $30,000 are available from any source. What is confirmable is the provenance of the number Goldsmith quoted: MoJ's own modelling estimated about 2,000 claims per year would see improved access to justice from the change, so the figure is not invented — but that is the forecast, which is the thing being predicted, not the outcome that would verify it. I searched for early caseload or uptake reporting (including law-firm commentary published in April 2026, several months after commencement) and found only descriptions of the new rules and the $468 filing fee tier, no volume data.

statement: Let’s be very clear, because what we are going to hear from Opposition parties is the challenging of the Government’s position in this space.
criterion: The Hansard record of the second reading debate on the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill (22 October 2025 onward): true if Opposition party speeches challenged the Government's position in this area, false if Opposition parties instead spoke in support of the bill and the Government's approach to it.
reasoning: The Hansard record of the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill second reading, which Doocey moved on 22 October 2025 on behalf of the Minister for Energy (Hon Simon Watts), shows Opposition speeches did challenge the Government's position on offshore renewable and energy policy. Green MP Francisco Hernandez called the bill 'one step forward and 10 steps back in the context of the wider energy policy' and attacked the removal of clean energy subsidies; Green MP Scott Willis, while saying 'We will support this bill', added 'we do not feel as though all our concerns have been addressed' and criticised the Government for still not delivering the national policy statement for renewable electricity generation, plus fast-track processes limiting community consultation. Labour's Glen Bennett raised decommissioning liability ('we don't want another Tui oil field debacle...the Government and us taxpayers having to foot the bill') and criticised the House as 'often slow and often playing catch up'; Deborah Russell raised land-banking and the incompatibility of offshore wind with seabed mining off south Taranaki. Testing the criterion's false branch as written — that Opposition parties instead spoke in support of the bill AND the Government's approach to it — only the first half holds: every Opposition party did support the bill itself, and Russell noted it built on work begun under the previous Government. But support for the legislation was explicitly coupled with contestation of the Government's wider approach, so the false branch is not satisfied and the true branch is. Doocey's own speech also implicitly confirms the framing, since he pre-emptively disputed the Opposition's characterisation of the Government's position.

statement: It is now down to 3.7 percent in the year to June 2025, and further improvement is expected in the September quarter, driven by continuing strong growth in exports.
criterion: Stats NZ Balance of Payments and International Investment Position, September 2025 quarter release; true if the annual current account deficit is below 3.7% of GDP, false if it is 3.7% or wider.
reasoning: Stats NZ's Balance of Payments and International Investment Position: September 2025 quarter release reports the annual current account deficit for the year ended September 2025 at $15.4 billion, or 3.5% of GDP — below the 3.7% threshold the criterion set, and narrower than the 3.7% ($16.3b) recorded for the June 2025 year she cited. The predicted 'further improvement in the September quarter' therefore materialised on the annual measure the criterion names. (Note: on a seasonally adjusted quarterly basis the September quarter deficit of $3.8b was $153m wider than June's, but the criterion is explicitly written against the annual deficit as a share of GDP.)

statement: Civil works are expected to start in November 2025, with the full development of a hundred homes to be expected to be completed by mid-2027.
criterion: Far North District Council building consent and code-compliance certificate records for the Bisset Road, Kaikohe development, plus Ngāpuhi/MHUD project reporting. True if civil works commenced in November 2025 and all 100 homes were completed by 30 June 2027; false if completion slips past that date or fewer than 100 homes are delivered.
reasoning: The criterion resolves on 30 June 2027; the current date is 16 August 2026, so the completion half of the prediction cannot yet be judged. Public sources confirm the project exists and is funded ($34.1m Crown + $17.4m Te Hau Ora o Ngāpuhi, plus $4m Regional Infrastructure Fund for roads/stormwater/wastewater) and is fast-track consented, but I found no source confirming civil works actually commenced in November 2025 — coverage only says work was 'expected to begin'. A disconfirming signal worth checking at resolve time: the Bisset Road fast-track planning material describes dwelling construction from 2026 onwards at roughly 15 homes per year, a rate that would not deliver 100 homes by mid-2027. Far North District Council consent and CCC records should be checked directly when the date passes.

statement: This, if it becomes law and the House approves it, will become the Parliament Act 2025 and it will be the one place.
criterion: The short title of the Act as enacted, on legislation.govt.nz: true if it is enacted as the Parliament Act 2025, false if it is enacted under a different year in its title or is not enacted at all.
reasoning: The Parliament Bill passed its third reading and was enacted. legislation.govt.nz lists it as the 'Parliament Act 2025', Public Act No 62, as enacted 12 November 2025, administered by the Office of the Clerk of the House of Representatives and the Parliamentary Service. The short title carries the year 2025, exactly as the criterion requires; I found no evidence of it being enacted under a different year or failing to pass.

statement: In the future, 95 percent of electricity will come from cheap, clean renewables, but there is one major barrier that we must overcome.
criterion: MBIE annual electricity generation statistics, renewable share of total generation; true if the renewable share reaches 95 percent or above in a calendar year on or before 2030, false if it remains below 95 percent through 2030.
reasoning: The criterion allows any calendar year up to and including 2030 to reach a 95%+ renewable share of generation, so it cannot resolve until after 2030-12-31. Current MBIE data: 88.1% (2023), 85.5% (2024), ~88% across calendar 2025. Quarterly figures in 2025 were 94.5% (Mar), 89.4% (Sep) and a record 96.4% (Dec), driven by strong hydro inflows and new utility-scale solar — so 95% has been exceeded in a single quarter but never over a full year. Nothing yet falsifies or confirms the claim.

statement: They are already producing 26 megawatts, 9 megawatts, 24 megawatts, and currently, in work right now, 49 megawatts of geothermal power in the station that’s about to be commissioned in November.
criterion: Eastland Generation / Ngāti Tūwharetoa Geothermal Assets commissioning announcements for the new Kawerau geothermal station; true if a station of about 49 MW is commissioned and generating by 30 November 2025, false if commissioning falls after that date.
reasoning: The station is Eastland Generation's TOPP2 — a 49 MW Ormat binary plant on the Kawerau geothermal reservoir, developed with Ngāti Tūwharetoa Geothermal Assets, who supply the geothermal fluid. The capacity and the project identity in the quote are accurate. But commissioning missed the criterion's 30 November 2025 line: TOPP2 synchronised to the national grid on 3 December 2025 (lifting Eastland's operating capacity to 118 MW / ~898 GWh a year), reached full operation in early 2026, and was officially opened in March 2026. The criterion states commissioning after 30 Nov 2025 is a fail, so this fails — narrowly on grid synchronisation (three days), and by months on full operation. I looked for evidence of an earlier November first-power or commissioning milestone and found none reported.

statement: In closing, I think that next year's election will definitely be fought as the “electric” election.
criterion: Campaign coverage and voter-priority polling for the 2026 NZ general election; true if electricity/energy policy features as a top-tier issue in major-party campaigns and leaders' debates, false if it is a secondary issue behind cost of living, health and crime.
reasoning: The 2026 general election is on 7 November 2026 and the criterion turns partly on the leaders' debates, which have not occurred — as of August 2026 the PM's office was still weighing broadcaster bids to host the Luxon–Hipkins head-to-heads. Evidence to date leans toward the prediction: Newsroom headlined 'Power prices spark up an electric election' in February 2026, energy dominated the first major multi-party debate in May 2026, and energy is a headline campaign plank for NZ First (gentailer split, $1b offshore survey), the Greens (Kiwipower, $980m over four years) and Labour (affordability/gas terminal), with reporting that 55% say energy issues will affect their vote. Disconfirming evidence: Ipsos's May 2026 issues monitor has cost of living at 60% as the dominant single concern, with energy surfacing mainly inside it (petrol/fuel 26%, up from 9% in February) and unemployment rising to 19% — consistent with the criterion's 'secondary behind cost of living' failure condition. Both readings remain live until the campaign and debates run.

statement: It is a thing that is recognised in other colonised lands that don't have treaties, such as Australia, and it was recognised from even the earliest days of Government in this country.
criterion: For Australia: Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992) 175 CLR 1 and the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) — true if native title is recognised at common law/statute without any treaty. For New Zealand: early colonial authority such as R v Symonds (1847) and the Native Lands Act 1865 — true if customary title was legally recognised then. False if either limb is unsupported.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are supported. AUSTRALIA: Mabo v Queensland (No 2) [1992] HCA 23; (1992) 175 CLR 1 held by 6-1 that the common law of Australia recognises a form of native title surviving the Crown's acquisition of sovereignty, displacing terra nullius; the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) then set out the statutory process for determining it. Australia has no treaty with its Indigenous peoples (at the date of the speech, 21 Oct 2025, no national treaty existed; Victoria's statewide treaty legislation passed later, on 30 Oct 2025), so recognition there indeed operates without a treaty. Commonwealth v Yarmirr (2001) 208 CLR 1 (Croker Island) further recognised non-exclusive native title over sea and sea-bed, which is directly on point for a foreshore-and-seabed debate. NEW ZEALAND: R v Symonds (1847) incorporated aboriginal title into NZ law, Chapman J holding native title to be a recognised right of customary use and possession extinguishable only by the Crown with the free consent of the Native occupiers. Earlier still, the Land Claims Ordinance 1841 vested sole pre-emption in the Crown on the premise that Maori held a customary title requiring extinguishment, and the Native Lands Acts 1862/1865 established the Native Land Court expressly to investigate and convert customary title. Since NZ government began in 1840, 1841-1847 is fairly described as 'the earliest days of Government in this country'. Disconfirming check: Wi Parata v Bishop of Wellington (1877) repudiated this line and held sway for a century, but that is a later reversal and does not contradict Abel's claim about what was recognised in the earliest days. Neither limb is unsupported, so the criterion returns true.

statement: This bill fulfils a specific coalition agreement between New Zealand First and National.
criterion: The National–New Zealand First coalition agreement of November 2023 (published text). True if it contains a commitment to amend the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 to restore or clarify the customary marine title test; false if no such clause appears.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether the November 2023 National-New Zealand First coalition agreement contains a commitment to amend the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 to restore or clarify the customary marine title test. It does. A primary compilation of the published coalition agreement texts (Russell McVeagh's policy matrix, which sets the National-ACT and National-NZ First agreements in parallel columns) has a row headed 'Marine and coastal area' in which the National-NZ First column reads verbatim: 'Amend section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area Act to make clear Parliament's original intent, in light of the judgment of the Court of Appeal in Whakatohea Kotahitanga Waka (Edwards) & Ors v Te Kahui and Whakatohea Maori Trust Board & Ors [2023] NZCA 504.' Section 58 is the customary marine title test, and the clause is expressly about clarifying Parliament's original intent for it, matching the criterion. Attribution check: the National-ACT column for that row is blank, so Costello's description of it as a commitment 'between New Zealand First and National' is accurate rather than a general coalition-government commitment. The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill, which passed its third reading on 21 October 2025 (the date of the speech) and received royal assent on 24 October 2025, did exactly this, and contemporaneous reporting and the official documentation both trace the bill to that coalition clause.

statement: I think we go back to when the first claims were lodged under this Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, that every single centimetre of our coastline was subject to a claim.
criterion: The register of applications lodged under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 by the 3 April 2017 deadline (Te Arawhiti / Ministry of Justice records of High Court applications and Crown engagement applications), mapped against the New Zealand coastline. True if the applications collectively cover effectively the whole coastline; false if material stretches were never subject to any application.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether applications lodged by the 3 April 2017 deadline collectively cover effectively the whole coastline, and makes it false only if material stretches were never subject to any application. The application record: roughly 585-600 applications were lodged by the deadline, split between the two pathways (about 202-205 in the High Court and about 382-387 for Crown engagement/ministerial determination), covering over 10 million hectares of foreshore and seabed out to 12 nautical miles, plus all harbours and estuaries. Multiple sources characterise the geographic coverage as effectively total: 'practically all the marine and coastal area of New Zealand is claimed under the Act' (Gulf Users Group); 'every square inch of the coastline was being claimed, in some places many times over' and 'every inch of the marine and coastal area of New Zealand' (Democracy Action, an opponent of the claims, so directionally motivated but consistent with the rest); Horizons Regional Council's 2025 committee report records applications covering the entirety of its regional coastline; and Te Tari Whakatau's engagement strategy organises the work into 20 coastal areas 'which together, include all of the takutai moana and all applicant groups'. Overlapping applications are extensively documented (15 groups for Whangarei Harbour, 7 for the Northern Wairarapa Coast). Disconfirming check: I searched specifically for gaps - stretches of coastline with no application, including outlying areas such as Fiordland, Stewart Island and the Chathams - and found no source identifying any material stretch that was never subject to an application. CAVEAT ON EVIDENCE QUALITY: I was not able to obtain the register itself mapped against the coastline as the criterion literally specifies (the Ministry of Justice and LINZ pages give counts but no coverage analysis; Te Arawhiti's site has migrated and the Korero Takutai geospatial tool was not retrievable), so this rests on consistent secondary characterisation rather than a coverage map, and the most emphatic 'every inch' phrasings come from an advocacy group. The best-documented neutral characterisation is 'practically all', which still satisfies the criterion's 'effectively the whole coastline' standard. Costello's phrasing is rhetorical hyperbole ('every single centimetre') and hedged ('I think'), but the substance holds. Note the same claim was made by Paul Goldsmith in the same third-reading debate.

statement: The Prime Minister of the time, John Key, made it very clear that there would be very limited numbers of successful claims because of the need to prove uninterrupted title for the duration since 1840.
criterion: Hansard and contemporaneous press statements/interviews by John Key during the 2010–2011 passage of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill. True if he stated that successful claims would be very few owing to the test of exclusive use and occupation since 1840 without substantial interruption; false if no such statement is on record.
reasoning: Scoop's report of John Key's post-Cabinet press conference on 14 June 2010 — the day Cabinet agreed to repeal the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 and pursue replacement legislation — records that Key "said he did not believe many claims would be successful as they would still have to demonstrate exclusive use and occupation of the land since 1840." That meets the criterion directly: a statement by Key, during the 2010-2011 development/passage of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill, that successful claims would be few because of the 1840 test. The statutory test as enacted is exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption; Costello's paraphrase ("uninterrupted title for the duration since 1840") is loose but substantively faithful. Disconfirming check: the frequently cited "no more than 10 per cent of the coastline" assurance belongs to Attorney-General Chris Finlayson, not Key, and I looked for evidence that the "few claims" assurance was Finlayson's alone and misattributed to Key — but the June 2010 presser report places the substance in Key's own mouth, and secondary accounts (Don Brash; Democracy Action, quoting Key that only a "relatively small" amount would go into customary title) corroborate rather than contradict it. The only overstatement is one of degree: Key "did not believe many claims would be successful" is marginally softer than "made it very clear there would be very limited numbers," which is not material.

statement: Yet Māori did not ask for the marine and coastal area, takutai moana legislation, nor the foreshore and seabed legislation that was before it.
criterion: The legislative history of both Acts (Cabinet papers, the Crown's response to the Court of Appeal's Ngāti Apa decision, select committee records, the 2004 hīkoi and Waitangi Tribunal Wai 1071 report): true if both Acts were Crown-initiated rather than sought by Māori claimants or Māori organisations; false if the record shows Māori bodies requested either statute.
reasoning: The core holds. Both statutes were Crown-initiated Government bills, not instruments sought by Māori claimants. The Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 was the Crown's response overturning the Māori litigants' win in Attorney-General v Ngāti Apa (2003) — Māori had asked the Māori Land Court to determine customary status, not Parliament to legislate; it drew the ~15,000-strong hīkoi to Parliament in May 2004, and the Waitangi Tribunal in Wai 1071 found the underlying policy in breach of the Treaty and contrary to the rule of law and non-discrimination. The 2011 Act was likewise a Government bill, and Māori bodies overwhelmingly rejected it: of 72 submissions from iwi, hapū and Māori organisations at select committee, only one supported passage without significant amendment, and a hīkoi marched from Te Rerenga Wairua to Parliament on 22 March 2011 against it. But the claim is materially overstated as to the 2011 Act. The review that produced it existed because the Māori Party demanded it in its November 2008 confidence-and-supply agreement with National; the resulting Ministerial Review Panel was Māori-led (Sir Eddie Durie, Richard Boast, Hana O'Regan) and reported that 85% of submitters who addressed the question favoured repeal, feeding a replacement regime; and the Māori Party then supported and voted for the 2011 Act, with Tariana Turia opening its third reading. So a Māori political party did seek repeal-and-replacement legislation and backed the resulting statute — even though the terms iwi actually received were near-universally opposed. True of the 2004 Act without qualification; true of the 2011 Act only under a reading ("iwi/hapū claimants did not ask for this statute's terms") that the blanket phrasing does not signal.

statement: But what we have is a counterfeit kāwanatanga, changing the rules again; an illegitimate use of kāwanatanga as per what the Waitangi Tribunal has already declared, and this massive hara that ripples through to te ao Māori.
criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's reports on the takutai moana amendment (the urgent inquiry into the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment proposal, Wai 3400): true if the Tribunal found the Crown's proposed amendment to be an unjustified or illegitimate exercise of kāwanatanga in breach of Treaty principles; false if the Tribunal made no such finding.
reasoning: The Waitangi Tribunal's Takutai Moana Act 2011 Urgent Inquiry Stage 1 Report (Wai 3400), released 13 September 2024, found in terms that "the Crown's actions are such a gross breach of the Treaty that it is an illegitimate exercise of kāwanatanga." Lyndon's phrase "an illegitimate use of kāwanatanga as per what the Waitangi Tribunal has already declared" is essentially a direct rendering of that finding, and her reference to "changing the rules again" matches the report's subject: the Crown's proposed amendment to the customary marine title test and the policy process behind it. The Tribunal (Judge Miharo Armstrong presiding, with Ron Crosby, Professor Rawinia Higgins and Tā Pou Temara) also found the Crown dismissed official advice, failed to consult Māori, breached the principles of active protection and good government, and sought to amend the Act before the Supreme Court could rule; it recommended the Crown halt the amendment, engage meaningfully with Māori, and warned that proceeding would significantly endanger the Māori-Crown relationship. Disconfirming check: I looked for a narrower or contrary characterisation of the finding — e.g. that the Tribunal criticised only process, or that the "illegitimate kāwanatanga" language came from a different inquiry (Wai 2660, the earlier kaupapa inquiry, or the later Financial Assistance Scheme report) — but the Tribunal's own news release confirms the wording and attaches it to Wai 3400. The remaining evaluative language in the quote ("counterfeit kāwanatanga", "massive hara") is the speaker's own characterisation, not a Tribunal finding, but the attributed claim itself is accurate.

statement: Right now, people are burning the bill on the coastline, affirming that they are there now and they will be there tomorrow because we are not going anywhere.
criterion: Contemporaneous news reports and organiser/social media records from October 2025 for the Northland and Bay of Plenty locations named later in the speech: true if bill-burning protests on the coastline are documented around 21 October 2025; false if no such protests occurred.
reasoning: Contemporaneous reporting confirms the protests were happening as Lyndon spoke. NZ Herald published on 21 October 2025 under the headline 'Protesters begin burning copies of Marine and Coastal Area Bill on beaches across New Zealand', reporting that 'Protesters have begun to gather on beaches' with social media users livestreaming people feeding wood and paper into large fire pits, crowds listening to speeches and singing. The #BurnTheBill action was organised out of Te Tai Tokerau (Northland) by kaumatua Reuben Taipari, who said the initiative 'came from a Te Tai Tokerau kuia' and was deliberately local rather than a national hikoi; gatherings were timed to Parliament's 6pm third reading on 21 October 2025. Te Ao Maori News' same-day report describes '#BurnTheBill demonstrations' with whanau gathering on beaches to light fires, share waiata and karakia and throw copies of the Bill into the flames, and quotes Lyndon directly. Greenpeace Aotearoa's independent resistance timeline logs 'protestors across the country take to the beaches and burn copies of the bill in protest' on 20 October 2025, days after a 20,000-signature petition was delivered on 16 October. Disconfirming check: I looked for reporting that the beach protests failed to materialise or were confined to Parliament grounds (Te Pati Maori MPs also burnt a copy outside Parliament on 21-22 October) and found none - the beach actions are separately and repeatedly documented. Caveat on the criterion as written: Northland involvement is well documented (organiser, origin, Ngatiwai's related Poor Knights action on 30 October), but I did not find sources naming specific Bay of Plenty beach locations; coverage describes the action generically as 'beaches around the country'. The criterion's decisive test - bill-burning protests on the coastline documented around 21 October 2025 - is satisfied.

statement: It delivers on a coalition agreement commitment with New Zealand First, and I commend it to the House.
criterion: The published National–New Zealand First coalition agreement (November 2023): true if it contains a commitment to amend the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 to restore Parliament's original intent on the customary marine title test; false if no such commitment appears there.
reasoning: The National-New Zealand First coalition agreement signed 24 November 2023 contains the commitment: 'Amend section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area Act to make clear Parliament's original intent, in light of the judgment of the Court of Appeal in Whakatohea Kotahitanga Waka (Edwards) & Ors v Te Kahui and Whakatohea Maori Trust Board & Ors [2023] NZCA 504.' The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill, which passed its third reading on 21 October 2025 (royal assent 24 October 2025), does exactly that: it inserts a declaratory statement overturning the Court of Appeal and High Court reasoning in Re Edwards, defines 'exclusive use and occupation' and 'substantial interruption' in s58, and amends the s106 burden of proof to require proof from 1840 to the present. Disconfirming check: I specifically tested whether the clause belongs to the National-ACT agreement rather than the NZ First one, since misattribution between the two deals is the obvious way this claim could fail. It does not - NZ Herald's coverage is headlined 'Tighter rules for customary marine title return under NZ First coalition deal', and NZCPR, Democracy Action and RNZ all attribute the s58 promise to the National-NZ First agreement. Sourcing limitation: the signed agreement PDF returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch and local PDF text extraction was unavailable, so the clause wording rests on multiple independent sources quoting it verbatim rather than on my own read of the primary document. Note that the bill as enacted was a modified version after an earlier government retreat, but the criterion asks only whether the coalition agreement contains such a commitment, and it does.

statement: The reality is that Casey Costello was a spokesperson for Hobson’s Pledge, a group that is on the record, clear for being fundamentally opposed to indigenous rights.
criterion: Hobson's Pledge media releases, campaign material and news interviews naming its spokespeople, plus its published position statements: true if Costello is documented as a Hobson's Pledge spokesperson and the group's own published material opposes Māori-specific rights and Treaty-based provisions; false if she never held that role or the group's stated positions do not bear that characterisation.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are met from Hobson's Pledge's own published material. First limb - the spokesperson role: Costello's own post on hobsonspledge.nz, 'Why I am stepping down as spokesperson of Hobson's Pledge' (26 July 2023), reads 'It has been an honour (and sometimes a challenge!) to be a spokesperson for Hobson's Pledge for the past seven years' and 'Since Hobson's Pledge is mission-driven and not party aligned, this means I must stand down as a spokesperson and trustee.' She was a founding trustee from 2016 alongside Don Brash, and the group's own archived releases quote her as 'Hobson's Pledge spokesperson Casey Costello' on Maori wards and Ihumatao. She stepped down to stand for NZ First at the 2023 election, so Andersen's past tense ('was a spokesperson') is accurate. Second limb - the group's published positions: its own 'Hobson's Pledge' page states there is 'no longer any need for special Maori representation in government, whether it be Maori electorates in Parliament', 'no longer any need for the Waitangi Tribunal', that the Treaty 'did not create a partnership' and 'did not establish any principles', and proposes repealing the Marine and Coastal Area Act 2011 - the very statute under debate. Disconfirming check: I looked for evidence she never held the title (e.g. that she was only a trustee, or that the group disputes the label) and found the opposite - the claim is documented in her own words on the organisation's own website. The one qualification is characterisation rather than fact: 'fundamentally opposed to indigenous rights' is Andersen's framing, which Hobson's Pledge itself would reject, framing the same positions as equality before the law and need-not-ethnicity. But the criterion's own test is whether the group's published material opposes Maori-specific rights and Treaty-based provisions, and on its own words it plainly does.

statement: In 2004, the Foreshore and Seabed Act caused huge upheaval within New Zealand. Tens of thousands of people protested, political parties fractured, and trust between Māori and the Crown was broken.
criterion: Contemporaneous reporting and police/organiser estimates for the May 2004 foreshore and seabed hīkoi to Parliament, plus the record of Tariana Turia's resignation from Labour and the founding of the Māori Party: true if the hīkoi is credibly estimated at 10,000+ and a party split is documented; false if attendance estimates are an order of magnitude lower or no party fractured.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are satisfied. Hikoi size: criterion bar was 10,000+; The Spinoff's 20-year retrospective says 'at least 15,000 people' reached Parliament, one of the largest protests ever to reach Parliament's gates; Re:News reports estimates of 20,000 up to activists' 50,000; comparison reporting during the 2024 Treaty Principles hikoi (35,000+ police estimate) described 2004 as roughly half that. Party fracture: documented — Tariana Turia resigned from Labour in May 2004 over the Act, won the Te Tai Hauauru by-election and was sworn in 27 July 2004 as co-leader of the newly founded Maori Party, which took four of seven Maori seats from Labour in 2005. Minor overstatements that do not move the verdict: 'political parties' is plural but only Labour fractured, and 'tens of thousands' sits at the upper end of the credible range rather than its centre.

statement: Former Attorney-General Chris Finlayson—again, hardly a left-wing radical—warned that this legislation would be extremely harmful to race relations and it will rip away the good work that was done.
criterion: Chris Finlayson's public statements, media interviews or select committee submission on this Bill: true if he described the amendments as extremely harmful to race relations; false if no such statement exists or his stated position is materially different.
reasoning: The criterion asked whether Finlayson described the amendments as extremely harmful to race relations; he used that exact phrase. Speaking to RNZ (reported 6 Aug 2025 by RNZ and Newsroom, repeated by Te Ao Maori News 16 Oct 2025), the former Attorney-General said there was no justification for the change and that it was 'extremely harmful' to race relations in New Zealand, adding 'I think it's a very bad day for race relations in New Zealand', and rejecting the government's framing: 'These amendments do not restore the original intention of Parliament. They undermine them.' Andersen's second clause ('rip away the good work that was done') fairly paraphrases his 'Tangata whenua have a few wins in court, and it's ripped away from them by the government, which changes goal posts 15 years later.' Disconfirming check: Paul Goldsmith published an NZ Herald rebuttal of Finlayson, corroborating rather than contradicting that he said it.

statement: Hoi anō rā, I think the best way for me to address this bill is as a wīwī Nāti, as Ngāti Porou being the first and only iwi to have our own takutai moana bill.
criterion: The New Zealand statute book: true if Nga Rohe Moana o Nga Hapu o Ngati Porou Act 2019 is the sole iwi-specific foreshore/takutai moana Act; false if any other iwi has an equivalent standalone Act.
reasoning: Nga Rohe Moana o Nga Hapu o Ngati Porou Act 2019 is the sole iwi-specific takutai moana statute. Ngati Porou were the only iwi to conclude an agreement with the Crown under the repealed Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004; the Crown honoured that commitment after repeal, updated the deed to the MACA 2011 framework, and gave it effect in the 2019 Act. The Act disapplies Parts 3 and 4 of MACA 2011 to nga hapu o Ngati Porou while leaving them in force for everyone else — a bespoke regime no other group has; third-reading reporting called it 'the first and only one of its kind'. Counter-candidates checked and excluded: Te Whanau-a-Apanui negotiated under the 2004 Act but has no standalone Act (its marine claim sits inside a wider package); Nga Pahauwera's 2008 AIP covered foreshore/seabed interests but what passed was the Ngati Pahauwera Treaty Claims Settlement Act 2012, a historical-claims settlement, and they later pursued customary marine title through the High Court; Te Whakatohea's CMT came via the Edwards litigation, not its 2024 settlement Act. Precision note not affecting the verdict: the Act is framed around nga hapu o Ngati Porou rather than the iwi as such.

statement: No, I did not, and I would just like to highlight that the regulatory impact statement to this bill refers to the coalition agreement, which includes this legislation to take away customary rights, so that was mentioned as one of the key reasons that this decision was taken by the Government.
criterion: The published Regulatory Impact Statement for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill: true if it references the coalition agreement commitment among the drivers of the proposal; false if the RIS makes no such reference.
reasoning: The RIA-framework document for this Bill — the Supplementary Analysis Report 'Takutai Moana: Clarifying section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011' (Te Arawhiti, finalised 18 Sept 2024, quality-assured by the Ministry of Justice's Regulatory Impact Assessment panel) — references the coalition agreement as a driver in multiple places. Its Problem Definition opens: 'The government's coalition agreement commits to amend section 58 of the Takutai Moana Act to restore Parliament's intent in light of the Court of Appeal's decision in Re Edwards.' It has a dedicated section headed 'Coalition agreement commitment' quoting the National–NZ First Coalition Agreement commitment to 'Amend section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area Act to make clear Parliament's original intent, in light of the judgment of the Court of Appeal in Whakatohea Kotahitanga Waka (Edwards)'. It further states 'Te Arawhiti identified a range of policy options for implementing the coalition agreement commitment' and, under 'Limitations and Constraints on Analysis / Narrow scope', 'The Minister directed officials to prepare options for implementation of the coalition agreement commitment. The coalition agreement has meant that all options considered needed to be legislative in nature.' Disconfirming check: the only wrinkle is nomenclature — para 56 of the September 2024 Cabinet paper records that 'A regulatory impact statement was not prepared for the original policy Cabinet paper. A supplementary analysis report has now been prepared and is attached to this paper.' So the document Andersen calls the 'regulatory impact statement' is formally a Supplementary Analysis Report, but it is the RIS-family impact analysis for this Bill and it does reference the coalition agreement among the key drivers, satisfying the criterion. Her gloss that the agreement 'includes this legislation to take away customary rights' is characterisation, which the criterion does not test.

statement: Cabinet was explicitly warned by officials not to proceed in this way. That advice was ignored and, as a result, up to seven cases may now need to be reheard, affecting more than 280 kilometres of coastline and consuming millions of dollars in costs.
criterion: Ministry of Justice advice to Cabinet and the Regulatory Impact Statement for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill: true if officials recommended against retrospective application and the advice estimates roughly seven affected cases and >280 km of coastline; false if the advice contains no such recommendation or materially smaller figures.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are met. (1) Officials recommended against retrospective application. The Supplementary Analysis Report states: 'Te Arawhiti advised the Minister that the section 58 amendments should not be applied retrospectively i.e. option (a) above. Specifically, Te Arawhiti considered there was not reasonable justification for retrospective application of any new CMT test and that this was based on well-established norms and conventions around retrospectivity, and the specific Treaty-related context of the Takutai Moana Act.' Treasury's ministerial consultation briefing for the 21 May 2025 Cabinet Social Outcomes Committee paper says in bold: 'We do not support option 2 as the costs and risks to the Crown likely outweigh any potential benefits', noting the retrospectivity clauses 'are unlikely to make the amendments equitable, as it only covers a small subset of judgements', and recommends Ministers 'request that the paper includes a further option to amend the Bill to exclude retrospective application of the CMT test to manage fiscal costs.' Cabinet nonetheless retained retrospectivity to the July 2024 announcement date. (2) Figures. Treasury's 22 July 2025 email records: 'The estimated cost of $14.211 million noted above is based on the re-hearing of seven applications' and that if the effective date were moved to 4 August 2025 'the cost is likely to reduce to $8.332 million... because only four applications would need to go through the re-hearing process.' The earlier estimate was 'up to $20 million'. So seven cases and millions of dollars are directly documented, and officials did offer a later cut-off that Cabinet declined. 1News, reporting the Office of Treaty Settlements and Takutai Moana advice to Minister Goldsmith, gives the coastline figure: seven court cases would 'likely need to be re-heard', overturning rights across '280km of coastline', with officials warning of costs 'around $20 million'. Disconfirming check: the September 2025 Cabinet paper says 'As at 18 September, this would mean that four judgments awarding customary marine title delivered after that date will be overturned and will need to be reheard' — i.e. the realised count at that point was four, not seven. Andersen's hedge 'up to seven' matches the officials' upper estimate rather than the September snapshot, so it is not an overstatement. Her 'more than 280 kilometres' is marginally above the 280 km reported in the advice, a trivial difference well short of 'materially smaller figures'.

statement: It applies the new test back to 24 July 2024, meaning that any case heard before the New Zealand courts can be reopened.
criterion: The Bill's application/transitional provisions as reported back from the Justice Committee: true if the new test applies to applications determined on or after 24 July 2024 and the reopening extends to all previously heard cases; false if the date differs, or if reopening is confined to a narrower class (e.g. only determinations made on or after that date), which would make "any case heard" an overstatement.
reasoning: The date is right; the reach is materially overstated. The Bill's transitional schedule (Schedule 1AA) is described in the Cabinet paper as: 'cl 3 - applicants who have proved the existence of CMT in the High Court by the date of the policy announcement (i.e., on or before 24 July 2024) will have their CMT orders, any appeals, and any necessary re-hearings progressed under the current law; cl 2 - any other applicants will be subject to the amendments from this Bill, including those who have had their applications heard but not decided; and cl 4 - any new High Court findings on applications in the interim period (between the date of announcement and the amendment Bill coming into force) will have no legal effect once the Bill comes into force and will need to be reheard.' The Cabinet paper elsewhere records 'some provisions will have retrospective effect dating back to 25 July 2024', and the September 2025 paper confirms that date survived into the version reported back from the Justice Committee and the October 2025 Amendment Paper. Simpson Grierson's analysis of the enacted Act agrees: the new test reaches all undetermined applications and all MACA Act court decisions made after 25 July 2024, while 'any CMT orders granted between that date and the Bill's enactment will have no legal effect and must be reheard' — orders granted before that date stand. So the first half of Andersen's claim ('applies the new test back to 24 July 2024') is accurate, but the second half is not: reopening is confined to determinations delivered on or after the announcement date, and CMT proved in the High Court on or before 24 July 2024 is expressly preserved. Disconfirming check for a reading that would rescue 'any case heard': cl 2 does capture applicants 'who have had their applications heard but not decided', so a case argued before July 2024 but undecided is subject to the new test. That is a strained reading of 'any case heard before the New Zealand courts can be reopened', which naturally implies all previously determined cases. Note on grading: the criterion as written assigns 'false' to precisely this branch, but it also labels the defect an 'overstatement', and the first limb (the 24 July 2024 date) holds exactly — which is the definition of partly_true. I have graded partly_true and flagged the tension rather than silently resolving it either way.

statement: This is also very much in alignment with the Infrastructure Commission, which has encouraged us to price things so that it spreads peak demand.
criterion: Te Waihanga / NZ Infrastructure Commission published advice, its 30-year National Infrastructure Plan and its congestion-pricing work; true if the Commission has recommended demand pricing (including congestion charging) as a means of spreading peak demand, false if no such recommendation exists in its published output.
reasoning: Te Waihanga's published output does recommend demand/congestion pricing to spread peak demand. Its 2023 research report 'Buying time: Toll roads, congestion charges, and transport investment' argues for pricing road use to manage congestion, and the National Infrastructure Plan recommends time-of-use charging explicitly on peak-spreading grounds — drivers 'pay a bit more to use busy roads at peak times', which 'shifts less-urgent trips to off-peak times and encourages public transport use', with modelling of ~35% less excess delay and ~20% less new capital needed. Te Waihanga also made a submission to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee supporting Auckland congestion pricing, and its CE publicly urged removing barriers to congestion charging. No published Commission output contradicts the characterisation.

statement: I can recall, in introducing the second reading, the Hon Chris Bishop’s comments on the New York scheme, which he’d just been to see, which has just started, and saying, “This is working really, really well and people are actually going, ‘We didn’t like the idea, but now we like it—we see what it’s doing’ ”.
criterion: NYC MTA congestion relief zone reporting on traffic volumes and travel times since January 2025, plus published polling on New Yorkers' support; true if traffic entering the zone fell materially and polling shows support rising from a minority to a majority, false if traffic/travel-time measures are unchanged or polling shows sustained opposition.
reasoning: The traffic limb of the criterion is met: MTA data shows vehicle entries to the congestion relief zone down ~12% overall (about 87,000 fewer vehicles per day; 14% in August 2025 vs baseline), AM-peak crossing speeds 4-36% faster, collisions down 14%, and transit ridership up 9% (subway) to 13% (bus) Jan-Aug 2025. The polling limb as written is not met. Siena found NYC voter opinion flipped from 32% keep / 56% eliminate (Dec 2024) to 42% / 35% (March 2025) - a plurality, not a majority - and statewide opinion stayed net negative (33-40 in March, 39-41 in May 2025). Majority support appears only in subgroups: Manhattan residents 57%, frequent CBD drivers 66%. A Morning Consult finding that ~60% wanted Trump to let the program continue is a different question from supporting the toll (that same poll had 27% support / 47% oppose statewide). So the shift Bishop described is real and in the direction he claimed, but 'now we like it' overstates it against the majority threshold the criterion set.

statement: This Government has made that cost of living crisis worse by halving the walking and cycling budget and increasing the public transport farebox recovery, which directly translates into higher bus and train fares.
criterion: The Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024 (and Budget 2024 NLTF allocations) walking and cycling activity class funding compared with GPS 2021: true if the allocated range is roughly half the previous one; plus the GPS/NZTA farebox recovery ratio target: true if the required ratio was raised above the previous setting. False if either the cycling allocation was not materially reduced or the farebox recovery requirement was unchanged or lowered.
reasoning: Both factual limbs hold. Walking and cycling: the 2024-27 NLTP allocates about $460m against roughly $910m actually programmed in 2021-24, which Greater Auckland describes as 'slashed in half'; GPS 2024's activity class range is $135m-$230m for 2024/25 falling to $70m-$110m per year thereafter, and the class now also has to absorb ~$63m of footpath/cycleway maintenance previously funded elsewhere (Newsroom puts the drop at 40% against 2021-24 actual funding, so 'halving' is at the upper end but within the criterion's 'roughly half'). Farebox recovery: GPS 2024 states funding should be supplemented by increased farebox recovery and third-party revenue, and NZTA's ministerial expectations require approved organisations to actively increase public transport 'private share' (the renamed farebox recovery ratio) with annual targets by 30 June 2027 - a raised requirement relative to the prior setting. The fare consequence is real: Auckland sits near 27-34% against an expectation around 40%, and Auckland Transport's 5.2% Feb 2025 fare rise lifted recovery only from 33.64% to 34.79%, implying large further fare increases or service cuts. The 'made the cost of living crisis worse' framing is causal rhetoric rather than a checkable fact, but the two specific claims are accurate.

statement: You see, their former mentor, Chris Finlayson, has said: “These amendments do not restore the original intention of Parliament. They undermine them.”—they undermine them.
criterion: Public record of Chris Finlayson's statements on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill — his select committee submission, published opinion pieces, or media interviews up to 21 October 2025. True if he made a statement in these or materially equivalent terms; false if no such statement exists or if his stated position is that the amendments do restore Parliament's original intention.
reasoning: Finlayson made the statement in materially identical — in fact verbatim — terms. Interviewed by RNZ in early August 2025 (article 'Former Attorney-General criticises marine and coastal rights law changes', ~6 Aug 2025, also covered by Newsroom on 6 Aug 2025), the former Attorney-General who piloted the 2011 Act said: 'These amendments do not restore the original intention of Parliament. They undermine them. Let there be no doubt about that at all [...] What they are doing by these foolish amendments is destroying the settlement that the National Party and the Māori Party reached in 2010.' The statement is on the public record well before 21 October 2025, and Jackson's quotation reproduces it word for word including the emphatic repetition. Disconfirming check: I searched for any Finlayson statement supporting the government's 'restoring Parliament's intent' framing and found the opposite — he disputes that framing directly, arguing the Supreme Court had already stated Parliament's 2010 intention correctly, and separately warned the changes would harm race relations. No source shows him endorsing the amendments.

statement: We've never stopped access to the foreshore.
criterion: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 public-access provisions (which preserve free public access to the common marine and coastal area) together with the register of customary marine title orders and recognition agreements to October 2025. True if no CMT order or agreement has operated to exclude general public access to a foreshore area; false if any documented instance of public access being stopped under the Act can be identified.
reasoning: Against the criterion as written, I could identify no CMT order or recognition agreement that has operated to exclude general public access to a foreshore area up to October 2025. Section 26 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 guarantees free public access to the common marine and coastal area even where customary rights are recognised, and CMT is expressly non-exclusionary — it cannot prevent access, navigation, fishing or existing uses, and cannot be sold. The only statutory route to restricting access is a wāhi tapu protection right, which requires a High Court order or Crown recognition agreement and a demonstration that the prohibition is necessary. Disconfirming check: I specifically searched for instances of that mechanism being used. The Crown's recognition process for Ngāti Pāhauwera found the tests for protected customary rights and wāhi tapu protection were not met; in the Ngāi Tūmapūhia-a-Rangi proceedings the court rejected Ngāti Hinewaka's wāhi tapu claims over Matakitaki-a-Kupe and Ōhinerua as not satisfying the statutory requirements, and that group's final orders were not issued until 2026 (Re Ngāi Tūmapūhia-a-Rangi Hapū Inc (No 3) [2026] NZHC 1365). The organisations campaigning hardest against the regime (Hobson's Pledge, NZCPR, Democracy Action) describe the wāhi tapu power in the abstract but cite no case of access actually being stopped. Officials in the committee-stage debate likewise stated that public access, fishing and recreation in a CMT area are unaffected apart from the limited wāhi tapu exception. Caveat: the claim is true as a statement about outcomes to date, not about legal impossibility — the Act does permit wāhi tapu conditions that would restrict access, and public access has never extended to crossing private land (including Māori land) to reach the coast.

statement: As the last speaker on this third reading of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill, I don’t want to drag it out, but I do want to just put on record that Ngāti Porou has got a carve-out from this Act and their takutai moana is not going to be affected by this bill.
criterion: Nga Rohe Moana o Nga Hapu o Ngati Porou Act 2019 and the text of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill as passed. True if the Ngāti Porou arrangement sits outside the amended Act and the bill contains no provision applying to it; false if the amendment bill's customary marine title provisions extend to the Ngāti Porou rohe moana.
reasoning: The Ngāti Porou arrangement does sit outside the amended regime, and the amendment bill's tightened customary marine title tests do not extend to ngā rohe moana o ngā hapū o Ngāti Porou. Two independent strands confirm this. First, the pre-existing statute: under the Ngā Rohe Moana o Ngā Hapū o Ngāti Porou Act 2019, Parts 3 and 4 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 — which contain the CMT test in ss 58–59 that the 2025 bill amends — cease to apply to ngā hapū o Ngāti Porou in respect of ngā rohe moana; their customary marine title is recognised through their own bespoke regime and Crown recognition documents (recorded separately on the LINZ Marine and Coastal Area Register). Second, the bill itself: a Committee-stage Amendment Paper made the bill not apply to Ngā Rohe Moana o Ngā Hapū o Ngāti Porou, on the stated rationale that the changes to the CMT tests do not apply to ngā hapū o Ngāti Porou because their bespoke legislation rests on prior agreements with the Crown. The Minister confirmed this in the Committee debate, referring to the existing legislative arrangement with Ngāti Porou and how the Act is intended to interact with it. Two minor imprecisions that do not disturb the substance: the carve-out is properly from the amending bill (their rohe moana was already outside Parts 3–4), while Part 2 of the 2011 Act still applies to ngā rohe moana with modifications; and MACA continues to apply within that area to other hapū or persons and to any non-ratifying hapū, so the exclusion is not absolute as to every claimant in the geographic rohe.

statement: Because congestion is only one negative impact of our car dependency, the health costs from air pollution actually exceeds the cost of congestion itself, and yet this bill ignores that evidence entirely, presumably because it’s an inconvenient truth that air pollution from motor vehicles—and this is the 53rd Parliament, so no doubt the costs have increased, like everything else—causes approximately $10 billion in social costs every year, including 13,000 cases of childhood asthma prevalence.
criterion: The Health and Air Pollution in New Zealand (HAPINZ 3.0) study, checking the social cost and childhood asthma figures attributed specifically to motor vehicles rather than to all air pollution sources; and NZTA/Ministry of Transport congestion cost estimates for comparison. True if the motor-vehicle share of social costs is ~$10bn with ~13,000 childhood asthma cases and exceeds published congestion cost estimates; false if those figures are the all-sources totals rather than the vehicle share, or if congestion costs are higher.
reasoning: HAPINZ 3.0 attributes $10.5bn in annual social costs and 13,229 childhood asthma cases specifically to motor vehicles (2016 base year), not to all air pollution sources — motor vehicles were 67.3% of the $15.6bn all-sources human-made total. Published congestion cost estimates are far lower: ~$1.3bn/yr for Auckland (2017), rising to a projected $2.6bn/yr by 2026, and roughly $1–1.25bn nationally (NZIER: 0.5–0.9% of GDP). So both the vehicle-share figures and the 'exceeds congestion' comparison hold as the criterion specifies. Caveat not required by the criterion: the two costs are not like-for-like (VOSL-based health valuation vs lost-productivity congestion cost), and the $10.5bn is 2016 data, so her aside that costs have since increased is unverified.

statement: The city raises $50,000—or $50 million I should say—each month from the scheme that it can then plough back into public transport, and buses travel faster in Manhattan as a result.
criterion: MTA published monthly Congestion Relief Zone revenue reports for 2025: true if gross monthly revenue is approximately $50 million, false if materially different (e.g. under $35m or over $70m). Plus MTA bus speed data for Manhattan crosstown/CBD routes before and after 5 January 2025: true if average speeds rose.
reasoning: MTA monthly Congestion Relief Zone reports for 2025: January (5–31) $48.66m gross / $37.5m net; February $51.9m gross / $40.4m net; April $56.7m; May $61m, with a first-year average of roughly $55m gross per month and $518m net collected through November 2025 (~$46m/month net). That sits inside the criterion's $35m–$70m band and 'approximately $50 million' is a fair characterisation, whether read as gross or net. On buses, MTA data show CRZ bus speeds up 2.3% over Jan–Sep 2025, reversing declines in 2023–24, and 11 of 13 crosstown local/SBS routes inside the zone 1–5% faster in January 2025 versus January 2024. Disconfirming check: the NYC Comptroller found Manhattan local bus speeds unchanged at 6.5 mph, so the speed gain is real per the MTA source the criterion names, but modest and contested.

statement: The noise complaints in the city of Manhattan have fallen by 70 percent.
criterion: NYC 311 complaint data for the Congestion Relief Zone comparing 2025 with the equivalent 2024 period, for the noise/honking complaint categories: true if the fall is approximately 70 percent, false if materially smaller, or if the reduction is not attributable to the charging zone (e.g. a citywide trend of the same size).
reasoning: A ~70% figure exists but is narrower than the unqualified claim. NYC 311 data for ZIP codes south of 60th St show honking complaints fell 69% between 5 January and 6 March 2025 versus the same 2024 period (219 → 67 complaints; also 0 vs 27 horn-honking camera summonses). That is the honking subcategory only, not 'noise complaints' generally, over a two-month window, on very small raw counts. Over longer periods the effect shrinks materially: the state reported honking/vehicle-noise complaints down 45% in the CRZ at six months, and 17% in the CRZ for the full first year. Disconfirming check on attribution: citywide vehicle-noise complaints fell about 23% over 2025 — larger than the CRZ's 17% full-year fall — so much of the sustained reduction tracks a broader trend rather than the charging zone. Substance holds for the early honking window; the blanket 'noise complaints have fallen by 70 percent' is overstated.

statement: We can say with certainty that it has the potential to reduce 10 percent or more of drivers at a particular time of day when the charging is in place.
criterion: Published evaluations of the schemes he names (Transport for London congestion charge impact monitoring reports; Stockholm congestion tax evaluations; Singapore ERP studies; Milan Area C; NYC congestion pricing data). True if peak-period vehicle volumes in charged zones fell by 10% or more in multiple schemes; false if the documented reductions are materially below 10%.
reasoning: Published evaluations of the named schemes show peak/charged-period reductions of 10% or more in multiple cases: London (15% traffic reduction in year one; 21% fewer vehicles entering the zone by year four; ~26% average congestion reduction during charging hours per TfL monitoring), Stockholm (~20-22% fewer cordon crossings during charged hours, sustained since 2006), Singapore ERP (~15% inbound reduction within two months of the 1998 launch, ~16% in the Restricted Zone), Milan Area C (~30% fewer entries). NYC is the weakest example but still reached 11% fewer vehicles entering the Congestion Relief Zone over its first year (MTA figure published Jan 2026; early-2025 weekly data was only ~5-8%). Twyford's claim is hedged as 'potential to reduce 10 percent or more' during charged hours, which the multi-scheme record supports. Checked the disconfirming side: the only scheme materially below 10% at the time he spoke was NYC's partial-year data, which does not overturn the pattern across London, Stockholm, Singapore and Milan.

statement: Good things often take time, and I'm very pleased to see that policy work that I started as transport Minister, probably seven or eight years ago, has finally found its way, through a succession of other Ministers, to this House in the form of this bill.
criterion: Ministry of Transport and Auckland Council records for "The Congestion Question" work programme and any related ministerial announcements. True if that congestion-pricing work programme was initiated under Twyford as Minister of Transport in 2017-18 and is the lineage of the current bill; false if the work began under a different Minister or materially later.
reasoning: The lineage and the timing are right, but the authorship is overstated. The congestion-pricing work programme that leads to this bill is the Smarter Transport Pricing Project, later renamed The Congestion Question — a joint MoT / Auckland Council / AT / NZTA / Treasury / SSC investigation. Its terms of reference were agreed in April 2017 and it was publicly launched in June 2017 by then-Transport Minister Simon Bridges with Finance Minister Steven Joyce and Auckland Council. Twyford did not become Minister of Transport until 26 October 2017, i.e. after the programme was established. What he did do is continue and fund it as Minister, overseeing the Phase I report (March 2018) and subsequent phases, which fed the select committee inquiry and ultimately the Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Bill. So 'seven or eight years ago' (2017-18) is accurate and his stewardship is real, but 'policy work that I started as transport Minister' misattributes the origin — it began under a different Minister, months before he held the portfolio.

statement: That’s a viable solution along State Highway 16 now that a busway is at last being retrofitted into State Highway 16.
criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi project records and funding decisions for the Northwestern Busway / SH16 bus improvements. True if dedicated busway infrastructure on SH16 was under construction as at October 2025; false if only bus shoulder lanes or interim improvements existed and the busway itself remained unfunded or unstarted.
reasoning: As at 21 October 2025 no dedicated busway was under construction on SH16. NZTA's own position was that construction 'could begin from 2027' (enabling works for Brigham Creek Station in early 2027, completion early 2029), and applications for statutory approvals under the Fast-track Approvals Act were not lodged until December 2025 — after Russell spoke. The separated bi-directional busway itself (Stage 2, Brigham Creek to Te Atatu plus the city-centre connection, costed at roughly $4.1-4.6 billion) remained unfunded. What did exist on SH16 in October 2025 was bus shoulder lanes used by the WX1 express. Against that, the programme is not vapour: ~$116m was approved by the NZTA Board in late 2024 for early consenting and strategic property purchase, Stage 1 (Brigham Creek and Lincoln Road stations, $330-380m) was progressing, and Westgate Station — branded the first step of the Northwest Busway — was physically under construction, opening 16 August 2026. So the substance (a busway is finally being delivered on SH16) holds, but 'is at last being retrofitted' materially overstates the status: the busway itself was unstarted and its main stage unfunded.

statement: London and Stokholm are both great examples of congestion charging working where traffic reduced by 15 percent to 30 percent in London; 20 to 25 percent in Stokholm.
criterion: Transport for London's Congestion Charging Impacts Monitoring reports and the published evaluations of the Stockholm congestion tax. True if measured traffic-volume reductions in the charged zones fall within the stated bands; false if the documented reductions are materially outside 15–30% for London or 20–25% for Stockholm.
reasoning: Both stated bands are supported by the sources the criterion names. London: TfL's impacts monitoring found traffic consistently down at least 15% in the first month, an initial drop of ~21% in vehicles entering the zone, over 18% sustained reduction during weekday charging hours, and a 30% fall in chargeable vehicles entering the zone (congestion also ~30% lower) — measured reductions therefore sit inside 15-30%. Stockholm: the Swedish Road Administration recorded traffic passing in and out of the cordon down 20-25% during the 2006 trial, with reductions stabilising around 20-22% once permanent — inside 20-25%. Minor imprecision: the top of the London band (30%) corresponds to chargeable vehicles/congestion rather than all-vehicle volume, which fell nearer 15-21%; but nothing documented is materially outside the bands she gave. Checked for disconfirming evidence: some analyses note congestion later crept back up in London (traffic volumes still lower) and rose ~5% in Stockholm 2006-2012, but neither contradicts the traffic-volume reductions claimed.

statement: We did have these half-price fares; the Government has removed them, so I’m keen to know what this Government is going to do to make sure the other side of the ledger of the congestion charge is about enabling people to get other forms of transport.
criterion: Ministry of Transport / NZTA records and Budget documents on the half-price public transport fares scheme introduced under the previous Government: true if half-price fares existed and were discontinued under the current Government; false if they were never in place, or if they remain in force.
reasoning: Half-price fares did exist and half-price fares were removed by the current Government — but not the ones the unqualified phrasing implies, and not all of them. Timeline: universal half-price public transport fares ran from 1 July 2022 as part of Labour's cost-of-living transport relief package, and were ended on 30 June 2023 by the Labour Government itself, replaced from 1 July 2023 with targeted Community Connect concessions (free travel under 13, half-price 13-24, half-price for Community Services Card holders and Total Mobility users). The current National-led Government then withdrew funding for the under-13 free and 13-24 half-price concessions, which ended 30 April / 1 May 2024, saving ~$327m over four years. So the substance holds for youth half-price fares, but it is materially overstated: the universal half-price scheme she is most naturally heard as describing was discontinued under the previous Government, and half-price fares remain in force today for Community Services Card holders and Total Mobility users.

statement: The other thing, I suppose, is just really noting that former Minister of Transport Simeon Brown has said we want to make sure we’re not adding further cost to people using roads during a cost of living crisis.
criterion: Hansard, Beehive press releases and media reports of Simeon Brown's statements while Minister of Transport: true if he made a statement to this effect about not adding further road-user costs during the cost of living crisis; false if no such statement is on record.
reasoning: A statement to this effect is on record, which is the test the criterion sets. RNZ reports of the August 2024 congestion-charging announcement state that Brown had opposed congestion charging, 'saying he did not want to add further cost to people using the roads during a cost-of-living crisis'. The underlying direct quote is from RNZ/NZ Herald, 3 July 2023: 'The National Party has always been very clear that congestion charging can't be an additional charge on motorists, it needs to be part of wider transport funding reform.' Qualification worth noting: the sourced statements were made while Brown was National's transport spokesperson in Opposition, not during his term as Minister of Transport (Nov 2023 - Jan 2025); I searched for a ministerial-era statement in that form and did not find one — as Minister he took the opposite direction, legislating for time-of-use charging while framing it as 'not about raising revenue'. Leary's descriptor 'former Minister of Transport' identifies the person rather than dating the remark, and the substance she attributes to him is accurately on the record.

statement: When I looked at the numbers a few months ago—and don’t hold me to account—the 38 percent increase in the size of the gaming sector, I think it actually hit something like $780 million in the last year, which is fantastic.
criterion: The New Zealand Game Developers Association annual industry survey for 2024 and 2025 (total industry revenue and year-on-year growth rate); true if revenue is within rounding of $780 million with growth near 38 percent, false if either figure is materially different.
reasoning: The NZGDA 2025 survey reports FY2024/25 industry pre-tax revenue of NZD 759.57 million, up 38.6% on the prior year's $548m. Luxon's growth figure (38 percent) is exactly right — NZGDA's own chair uses "38% revenue growth". His revenue figure is not: $759.57m is about $20m (2.7%) below the "something like $780 million" he cited, and does not round to $780m as the criterion requires. Checked for a competing figure that would support $780m (e.g. a revised or later NZGDA release); the only larger number is the $1b milestone reported well after October 2025, so no source available on 2025-10-22 gives $780m. Substance holds — record year, 38% growth — with the dollar total overstated, and he hedged it explicitly ("don't hold me to account", "I think", "something like").

statement: Why isn’t he aware that the gaming sector has grown 86 percent in the last 2½ years since the gaming rebate was introduced by the previous Labour Government and that his Government, despite repeated requests from the sector, has not been willing to expand eligibility so that the budget that was set aside for it actually gets spent?
criterion: New Zealand Game Developers Association annual survey revenue figures for 2023 through 2025, measured from the introduction of the rebate (Budget 2023); true if cumulative growth over that period is near 86 percent, false if materially different.
reasoning: NZGDA survey revenue: FY2021/22 $407m; FY2022/23 $434.4m (+7%); FY2023/24 $548m (+26%); FY2024/25 $759.57m (+38.6%). The Game Development Sector Rebate was introduced in Budget 2023 (May 2023), so the last pre-rebate survey year is FY2022/23 at $434.4m. Growth from there to $759.57m is 74.9%, not 86%. The 86% figure reproduces exactly only if measured from the FY2021/22 base of $407m (759.57/407 = 86.6%) — a three-year window starting a full year before the rebate existed. Labour's own press release uses the same 86% without stating the period, confirming that is the arithmetic.
