So the claim is real data, but the growth is attributed to a period the baseline predates, and 86% overstates post-rebate growth (~75%). Checked the disconfirming direction too: no NZGDA publication attributes 86% growth to the rebate period. The rest of the quote, outside the criterion, does check out — the scheme has $40m/year allocated but paid roughly $22.4m to 40 studios in 2025.

statement: It’s also why we’re backing farmers because, actually, dairy’s up 14 percent, red meat’s up about 9 percent, and horticulture’s up 19 percent.
criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for the Primary Industries (June/September 2025 edition) export revenue figures by sector; true if each sector's growth is within rounding of the stated figure, false if any is materially different.
reasoning: MPI publishes SOPI in June and December; the current edition on 2025-10-22 was SOPI June 2025 (there is no September edition). Its forecasts for the year to 30 June 2025: dairy +16% to $27.0b, meat and wool +8% to $12.3b, horticulture +19% to $8.5b, forestry +9% to $6.3b, seafood +2% to $2.2b, total food and fibre +12% to $59.9b. Horticulture at 19 percent matches exactly. Red meat "about 9 percent" is close: SOPI's meat-and-wool aggregate is +8%, and red meat excluding weak wool sits slightly above that, so the hedged figure is defensible. Dairy is wrong: 16%, not 14% — a 2-point error, and notably in the direction of understating his own case. Checked whether another MPI figure gives dairy 14%: the +14% figure belongs to meat and wool in the later SOPI June 2026 release, not to dairy in any 2025 edition. Two of three figures hold; one is materially off.

statement: He said that, ultimately, we need to balance the right to strike and actually make sure we protect the interests of other New Zealanders.
criterion: The public record of Simeon Brown's remarks on doctors' right to strike (media interviews and transcripts, October 2025); true if he framed it as balancing the right to strike against the interests of other New Zealanders, false if his remarks were materially different or if he went further than Luxon's characterisation.
reasoning: Brown's public remarks (ASMS conference 16 Oct 2025 and follow-up 17 Oct) do contain the balancing substance Luxon describes: he explicitly acknowledged that strike action was doctors' "legal right", said "No one disputes that doctors need to be recognised for the job you do, but New Zealanders also deserve a health system that works for them", and "Patients should never be collateral damage in disputes between management and unions". So the rights-versus-other-New-Zealanders framing is genuinely his. However, the criterion also fails the claim if Brown went further than Luxon's characterisation, and he did: he accused doctors of having "crossed an ethical line", and said that if strikes continued, changes to the law for life-preserving services "may well have to be considered" — i.e. restricting or removing the right to strike, which patient advocate Malcolm Mulholland attacked as bargaining in bad faith and the PSA called an attack on fundamental workplace rights. I found no instance of Brown using a 'balance' formulation verbatim. Luxon's rendering is directionally faithful but materially softer than what Brown actually said.

statement: But, again, there are offers that have been extended to the unions that haven’t been taken out to members.
criterion: Public Service Commission, PPTA, NZEI and PSA statements on the status of the pay offers live as at 22 October 2025; true if at least one extended offer had not been taken to a member ballot by that date, false if every extended offer had been put to members.
reasoning: At least one extended offer had not been put to a member ballot as at 22 October 2025. PPTA Te Wehengarua's own statement records that the Government presented an offer for settlement of the Secondary Teachers' Collective Agreement on 10 October 2025 'with a condition it would lapse if strike action was notified'; PPTA proceeded to strike and never balloted it — 'despite the offer now lapsing, we have provided it to members and this week they will have the opportunity to provide feedback on it'. Feedback is not a ratification vote. Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche confirmed the offer was put in writing at the president's request ('we acted at the President's request to put our significantly improved offer to him in writing', 11 Oct 2025). Luxon had made the same point on 12 October, saying the strike was 'preordained' because the union refused to take the offer to members. ASMS had likewise declined to put a Health NZ offer back to its members in April 2025. Disconfirming check: several other offers WERE balloted and rejected by members (NZEI primary teachers in Sept 2025, NZNO nurses, earlier PPTA offers), so the broader implication that unions were generally withholding offers is contestable — but the criterion as written asks only whether at least one extended offer had not gone to a member ballot, and that holds.

statement: Why didn’t the Government increase eligibility for the game development rebate given the current $40 million budget for the rebate isn’t being fully utilised?
criterion: MBIE / CODE (Centre of Digital Excellence) reporting on the Game Development Sector Rebate: appropriated budget versus rebate actually paid out for the most recent year; true if payments fell materially short of the $40 million appropriation, false if the fund was fully or near-fully subscribed.
reasoning: The Game Development Sector Rebate is appropriated at $40 million per annum (NZ On Air scheme page: 'NZD $40m-per-year'), but actual payouts fall well short. NZ On Air's own announcement of the second-year results states 40 studios received a share of $22.44m — roughly 56% of the appropriation — up from 33 studios the previous year. Registrations that year totalled an estimated rebate request of just over $24m, still well under the cap. Labour's own fact sheet accompanying its 23 October 2025 policy said expanding the scheme (threshold $250k->$200k, rate 20%->25%, cap $3m->$4.5m) would cost an extra ~$11 million on top of roughly $22 million and would still not exceed the $40m limit, and NZGDA director Lance Burgess said the increases could be accommodated within the annual $40m cap 'because of the current underspend'. Disconfirming check: I looked for evidence the fund was fully or near-fully subscribed and found none — the reported shortfall is ~$17-18m a year. Hipkins' premise that the $40m is not being fully utilised is accurate.

statement: This morning, the New Zealand Superannuation Fund published its latest annual report. It shows that the super fund's total size was $85 billion at 30 June 2025, with average return since its inception of 10.1 percent per annum.
criterion: The New Zealand Superannuation Fund Annual Report for the year ended 30 June 2025: net fund size and since-inception annualised return; true if both figures match within rounding, false if either is materially different.
reasoning: The Guardians of NZ Superannuation released the 2025 Annual Report on 22 October 2025, the morning Bishop spoke. The report gives Fund size at 30 June 2025 as $85.1 billion (up $8.4b on the year) and the return since inception in September 2003 as 10.09% p.a. pre-tax after costs. Bishop's '$85 billion' and '10.1 percent per annum' both match within rounding. Checked for a competing figure: the 9.92% sometimes quoted is the 20-year annualised return, a different measure, not since-inception.

statement: The other 70 percent have been divested or liquidated as Temasek invested, divested, and grew their portfolio to $434 billion Singaporean.
criterion: The Temasek Review 2025 net portfolio value, and Temasek's own published account of how many of its 35 initial 1974 portfolio companies remain held; true if the portfolio value is within rounding of S$434 billion and around 10 of the 35 original companies remain, false if either is materially different.
reasoning: Temasek Review 2025 reports net portfolio value of S$434 billion as at 31 March 2025, a record and up S$45b year on year - matching the quoted figure exactly. On the 1974 portfolio, Temasek's own published account states that of the 35 companies in its inception portfolio, 10 still remain directly or indirectly, and 'the other 25 have been divested or liquidated as Temasek invested, divested, and grew their portfolio' - 25/35 = 71.4%, so 'the other 70 percent' is Temasek's own framing with the portfolio value updated to the 2025 figure. Both halves of the criterion are met.

statement: How can she stand by her statement that “Costs are under control, and inflation is under control” when there have been four consecutive increases in inflation?
criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index annual rate for the four quarters to September 2025; true if the annual rate rose in each successive quarter, false if it fell or was flat in any of them.
reasoning: Stats NZ annual CPI rates: September 2024 2.2%, December 2024 2.2%, March 2025 2.5%, June 2025 2.7%, September 2025 3.0%. Over the four quarters to September 2025 the annual rate rose in three of them; the December 2024 quarter was flat on September 2024 at 2.2%, which the criterion explicitly makes disqualifying. So the substance - inflation rising quarter on quarter through 2025, from within-band to the top of the RBNZ band - holds, but the streak is three consecutive increases, not four.

statement: Three years ago, it was 7.3 percent. It is now 3 percent.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual rate for the September 2022 quarter and the September 2025 quarter; true if the figures are within rounding of 7.3 percent and 3.0 percent respectively, false if either is materially different (note the 7.3 percent peak print falls in the June 2022 quarter, so the 'three years ago' anchor is part of what must be checked).
reasoning: The current figure is exactly right: Stats NZ reported annual CPI inflation of 3.0% for the September 2025 quarter (released 20 Oct 2025). The anchor is slightly overstated. Three years before the 22 Oct 2025 statement, the prevailing print was the September 2022 quarter at 7.2%, not 7.3%. The 7.3% figure is the June 2022 quarter 32-year peak, roughly three years and four months earlier. The 0.1pp gap is not material and the substance (inflation fell from a ~7.3% peak to 3.0%) holds, but the 'three years ago' framing attaches the peak print to a quarter it does not belong to, so this is partly_true rather than true under the criterion as written (which required both figures to be within rounding).

statement: The Government has come to the table and put a record investment in Budget 2025 of over $700 million.
criterion: Budget 2025 education vote documents for the learning support package: total appropriation and whether it exceeds any prior learning support allocation; true if the figure exceeds $700 million and is the largest such allocation, false if the appropriation is materially smaller or a previous Budget allocated more.
reasoning: The Ministry of Education's Budget 2025 learning support page states the package is $645.8 million of operating funding plus $100.9 million of capital funding, totalling $746.7 million, which exceeds $700 million. On the 'record' element: the largest prior learning support allocations found were Budget 2018 ($283.8m over four years) and Budget 2019 ($335.8m over four years), roughly $619.7m combined across both. No earlier Budget with a larger single learning support allocation was found, and the Government's own framing is 'largest boost to Learning Support in a generation'. Both limbs of the criterion are satisfied. Minor caveat, not enough to downgrade: the total is spread over four years and includes capital, and the official claim is 'in a generation' rather than all-time.

statement: As I outlined to the House yesterday, the Government’s spending $1.2 billion to move the next tranche of the roads of national significance to the next phase of development following the board’s approval of the investment cases.
criterion: NZTA board minutes and the Minister of Transport's October 2025 announcement on the roads of national significance investment cases; true if the sum committed to move that tranche to the next development phase is $1.2 billion, false if the announced figure is materially different or no such board approval occurred.
reasoning: On 20 October 2025 Bishop, as Transport Minister, announced that the NZTA Board had endorsed investment cases for all Roads of National Significance and committed nearly $1.2 billion combined to move them to the next phase of development: more than $675 million approved for consenting, design, route protection, site investigations and early works, plus more than $515 million of approved RoNS property funding for property acquisition. The tranche covers Northland Expressway Sections 2 and 3, East West Link, Hamilton Southern Links, Petone to Grenada and Cross Valley Link, SH1 Wellington Improvements including a new Mt Victoria tunnel, and the Hope Bypass. Both limbs of the criterion hold: the board approval of investment cases occurred, and the announced sum is not materially different from $1.2 billion ($675m + $515m = ~$1.19b, officially described as 'nearly $1.2 billion').

statement: Tomorrow, I will be in Wellington, and I do understand that all rallies, planned events, and sign-waving events have been called off due to severe weather in Wellington.
criterion: NZEI/PPTA public notices and contemporaneous news reports for 22–23 October 2025, plus MetService severe weather warnings for Wellington; true if the Wellington rallies and sign-waving events were called off on weather grounds, false if they proceeded or were only partly cancelled.
reasoning: NZEI Te Riu Roa's own 23 October strike-rally page carries the notice for the Wellington region (and Levin/Wairarapa): 'ALL PLANNED EVENTS, RALLIES AND SIGNWAVES HAVE NOW BEEN CANCELLED'. The grounds were weather: MetService issued a rare red severe wind warning for Wellington and Wairarapa south of Carterton for 23 October 2025, with gusts forecast to 130-150 km/h and 142 km/h recorded at Mt Kaukau. Contemporaneous reporting (RNZ, Kaitiaki, Wellington.Scoop) confirms NZEI, the PSA and doctors' unions all cancelled their Wellington outdoor rallies while rallies elsewhere (e.g. Auckland) went ahead. Disconfirming check: the strike itself was not cancelled (formal notices had already been served) and some events moved indoors nationally, but Stanford's claim was specifically about rallies/planned events/sign-waving in Wellington, and those were called off in full, not partly.

statement: I would like to just say that we have been listening to them, which is why we have delivered the biggest investment in learning support in a generation, more than they did in the last six years combined; which is why we have invested in paying for their teacher registration fees; which is why we’ve invested in an aspiring principal programme; which is why we’ve invested in a teacher bonding scheme, among many, many things we’ve done to back the sector.
criterion: Budget appropriations for learning support (Vote Education) under Budgets 2024–2025 compared with the equivalent learning support appropriations across Budgets 2018–2023; true if the current Government's new learning support funding exceeds the six-year total of the previous Government, false if the earlier total is equal or greater.
reasoning: The investment is real and the individual policies check out, but the specific comparison fails the criterion. Current Government: Budget 2025 provided $645.8m operating + $100.9m capital (~$747m) for learning support (LSCs $192.5m, Early Intervention Service $266m, ORS $122.5m, behaviour/communications $41.5m); the Ministry's Budget 2024 material contains no comparable learning-support package. Previous Government: the Beehive's own Budget 2019 release states that Budgets 2018 and 2019 combined provided $619.7m of NEW learning support funding ($335.8m over four years in Budget 2019, including $217m for ~600 Learning Support Coordinators, on top of Budget 2018's ~$284m). Budget 2020 added a $128m four-year baseline increase for ORS teacher-aide hours (plus a $31m COVID teacher-aide response fund), and Budget 2021 added $67.3m for learning support, with further behaviour/attendance funding in Budget 2022. That puts the 2018-2023 six-year total above $800m, and above $687m even on the most conservative tally (2018+2019+2021 only) - i.e. greater than Budget 2025's $646m operating and greater than the $747m operating-plus-capital figure. So the earlier six-year total is larger, which the criterion resolves against the claim. The defensible part is that Budget 2025 is the largest single-Budget learning support boost in decades, and the other limbs of the statement are all true: $53.3m to cover Teaching Council registration/practising-certificate fees from July 2025 to 2028; an aspiring/beginning principals programme (200 aspiring, up to 450 early-career principals); and a new Teacher Bonding Scheme from October 2025 ($7.5m annually by 2030, up to $40,000 over five years). Hence materially overstated rather than wholly false.

statement: Why have over 40,000 educators been forced to take to the streets just to get their Minister to listen to their concerns?
criterion: NZEI Te Riu Roa and PPTA membership/participation figures for the 23 October 2025 education sector strike, and contemporaneous reporting of turnout; true if participants number over 40,000, false if materially fewer.
reasoning: NZEI Te Riu Roa's own media release states that adding ~1,300 area school teachers took the number of NZEI educators striking on 23 October 2025 to 'more than 40,000' (primary teachers, principals, support staff and Ministry of Education specialist staff). PPTA Te Wehengarua's ~21,000 secondary and area school teachers struck the same day, so the educator total was roughly 60,000+, within a wider multi-union action reported at more than 100,000 workers - the largest strike in New Zealand since 1979. Contemporaneous reporting put teacher participation at 40,000-50,000 or higher, so the figure is not materially fewer than 40,000 on any reading. Disconfirming check: 'took to the streets' is looser than the participation figure, since red-warning weather forced cancellation of the Wellington, Wairarapa and Canterbury marches, so not all 40,000+ physically rallied; the strike participation itself, which is what the criterion tests, is comfortably above 40,000.

statement: Does he stand by his statement, in response to our questions yesterday, that nurses have safe staffing conditions, when Te Whatu Ora’s own data showed that 50 percent of day shifts were understaffed in 16 districts over 10 months last year in our hospitals?
criterion: Te Whatu Ora care capacity demand management / shift-level staffing data released for 2024 (including via OIA); true if roughly 50 percent of day shifts in 16 districts over a 10-month period were recorded as below target staffing, false if the recorded proportion or district count is materially different.
reasoning: Te Whatu Ora 'shifts below target' data obtained by NZNO under the OIA covers January–November 2024 across 16 health districts and records ~51% of all day shifts understaffed (35% of evening shifts; 56% of day shifts in surgical wards). Both quantities the criterion tests — a roughly 50% day-shift proportion and a count of 16 districts — match the record. The only discrepancy is the period: Jan–Nov is 11 months, not the 10 stated, a peripheral detail the criterion does not test and one that understates rather than inflates the claim. The Ombudsman separately found Health NZ 'unreasonably' delayed and obstructed release of this dataset. Health NZ disputes the interpretation, arguing SBT 'is not a proxy for understaffing' but a 'moment in time' measure — a caveat about meaning, not about whether the data showed what was described, which is what the claim asserts.

statement: Does he stand by his statement that nurses have safe working conditions, when nurses report that emergency departments are currently, under his Government’s hiring freeze, so short-staffed that some patients who soil themselves are left lying for hours in their own excrement because staff do not have time to help?
criterion: Health New Zealand recruitment directives, vacancy control policies and Ministerial instructions in force in October 2025; true if a freeze or blanket pause on hiring applied to clinical roles including emergency department nursing, false if recruitment for those roles continued under normal or merely tightened approval processes.
reasoning: Neither branch of the criterion fits cleanly. Against 'true': the formally declared Health NZ freeze (June 2024) applied to non-frontline, non-patient-facing roles, and Health NZ has explicitly and repeatedly denied any hiring freeze ('For the avoidance of doubt, there is no hiring freeze at Health New Zealand'), citing nursing FTE growth of over 3,000 in the two years to March 2025. I found no formal blanket pause covering ED nursing in force in October 2025. Against 'false': recruitment did not continue under 'normal or merely tightened approval processes' — just over 3% of nurse vacancies were approved for recruitment in 2025, ~1,445 nursing vacancies sat unfilled (~1,300 for two years), appointments ran through regional quota committees, graduate hiring stayed below half each round, and RNZ/NZ Herald/Crux documented frontline clinical roles going unfilled while Health NZ said otherwise. The substance (recruitment effectively choked for clinical nursing roles) holds; 'hiring freeze' overstates the formal policy position. Separately and not decisive for this criterion, the underlying anecdote checks out: a Waikato Hospital ED nurse reported in mid-2025 that patients who soil themselves can lie for hours in their own filth because staff lack time to help.

statement: Is he concerned that neonatal wards across Auckland, Whangārei, Christchurch, Palmerston North, and Tauranga hospitals were understaffed for more than a third of the shifts in the first half of this year, and, if so, what impacts does he think that these unsafe working conditions have on parents and newborns?
criterion: Health New Zealand neonatal unit shift staffing records for January–June 2025 for Auckland, Whangārei, Christchurch, Palmerston North and Tauranga; true if more than 33 percent of shifts were recorded below target staffing at those units, false if the recorded rate is materially lower.
reasoning: The criterion names a specific source — Health NZ neonatal unit shift staffing records for January–June 2025 at Auckland, Whangārei, Christchurch, Palmerston North and Tauranga. That dataset exists (RNZ obtained Jan–June 2025 shifts-below-target data by OIA and published the Wellington maternity extract of it), but no neonatal breakdown for those five named units has been published. I searched by hospital name, by unit type, via RNZ/NZ Herald/Kaitiaki coverage, and via the Green Party's own October 2025 releases, and could not locate it. The nearest available evidence is adjacent rather than matching and is directionally consistent with the claim: Waipapa Christchurch Hospital's NICU was below target for ~80% of shifts (865 shifts) in 2023; Palmerston North's neonatal ward triggered unsafe staffing ratios more than 25% of the time; NICUs nationally report ~20% below CCDM-calculated staffing; 45% of children's-ward shifts were understaffed in the 2022–2024 Infometrics analysis. None covers the stated units in the stated window, so the criterion as written cannot be resolved either way. Per rule 6, absence of published data is not evidence of falsity.

statement: Well, in answer to the first part of the question, there is no hiring freeze.
criterion: Health New Zealand recruitment policy documents and vacancy control settings in force in October 2025; true if no freeze or pause on recruitment applied, false if a hiring freeze or equivalent recruitment pause was in effect for any substantial part of the workforce.
reasoning: A recruitment freeze or its equivalent was in force over substantial parts of the Health NZ workforce in October 2025. Health NZ ordered an immediate hiring freeze on ALL non-frontline roles (hospital roles not dealing directly with patients, public health roles not dealing directly with the community) in 2024, and there is no evidence it was lifted — the PSA was still publicly demanding the new Health Minister 'lift the hiring freeze on the health workforce' in January 2025, saying it had 'impacted many urgently needed frontline roles'. For clinical roles Health NZ denied a 'freeze' but moved recruitment from open hiring to an approval gate (regional recruitment forum -> national recruitment team -> cost-saving programme team). The practical effect during calendar 2025: just over 3 per cent of nurse vacancies were approved for recruitment; 1,445 nursing vacancies sat unfilled across Health NZ with ~1,300 unfilled over two years (saving over $200m by not replacing leavers); and fewer than 45-47 per cent of graduate nurses were placed through ACE, leaving ~800 graduate nurses unemployed. RNZ reported frontline hospital roles going unfilled 'amid hiring freeze, despite Health NZ saying otherwise'. Disconfirming check: Health NZ and ministers did formally deny a 'hiring freeze', particularly for graduate nurses, and pointed to continued recruitment for frontline clinical roles — so the statement is defensible only as a narrow point about labelling, not about substance. The criterion asks whether a freeze or equivalent recruitment pause applied to any substantial part of the workforce, and it plainly did.

statement: The fact that, in less than two years, we’ve added 2,100 extra nurses into Health New Zealand is a really good thing, and the fact that we’ve made consistent efforts and investments in the healthcare system—$17 billion in our first Budget; up another 7 percent in our second Budget—is all good stuff.
criterion: Health New Zealand nursing workforce (FTE or headcount) figures for late 2023 compared with late 2025, and Vote Health appropriations in Budgets 2024 and 2025; true if the net nurse increase is about 2,100 and the Budget figures match, false if the workforce growth or funding figures are materially different.
reasoning: The Budget figures broadly match the Government's own published material; the nurse figure is materially overstated. BUDGETS: at Budget 2024 a multi-year arrangement funded health cost pressures with $16.68 billion over three Budgets (Health NZ baseline +$1.430b in 2024/25, +$1.370b in 2025/26, +$1.370b in 2026/27) — 'about $17 billion' is a fair round of the Government's headline, though it is a three-year total presented as a single Budget number. At Budget 2025 the Government announced a $7 billion increase in Vote Health operating funding over the forecast period including $1.37b p.a. to Health NZ's baseline, taking total health spending to $32.7b in 2025/26, and its own release states this is 'an increase of 7.4 per cent in total funding and 6.2 per cent per capita' — so 'up another 7 percent' matches the official figure (independent analysis computed the Vote Health appropriation increase at 4.8 per cent). NURSES: the 2,100 figure is gross hires/headcount, not a net workforce increase. Health NZ FTE data show 29,404 FTE nurses in March 2024 and 29,458 FTE in March 2026 — a net increase of 54 FTE over two years. The large rise the Government points to (~2,496-2,900 FTE) occurred between December 2022/June 2023 and March 2024, i.e. largely before and immediately after the coalition took office in November 2023, and stalled thereafter. NZNO called the framing 'creative accounting'; the claim does not net off attrition and counts part-time hires as whole nurses. Disconfirming check: the Government did genuinely hire on the order of 2,100 nurses, so the claim is true as a gross-hires statement — it is the 'added ... into Health New Zealand' framing (implying net workforce growth attributable to this Government) that fails.

statement: I could point to the progress made on our ambitious target to see 20,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime by 2029, and the most recent data released for the 12 months to May shows there were 29,000 fewer victims than when we came into Government; 9,000 ahead of our target.
criterion: The NZ Crime and Victims Survey series used for the Government's victims-of-assault target, and the Government Targets quarterly report for the 12 months to May 2025: true if the published estimate is a reduction of about 29,000 victims against the stated baseline and the target is 20,000 by 2029; false if the published reduction is materially smaller, or measured against a different baseline than the one implied.
reasoning: Every element matches the published Government Targets data for the period Goldsmith cited. The target (Government Target 4) is to reduce victims of violent crime — defined as sexual assault, non-sexual physical assault and robbery — by 20,000 by 2029, measured against a New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey baseline of 185,000 for the 12 months to October 2023 (just before the Government took office). The DPMC target factsheet published for the quarter (baseline October 2023, current May 2025) and NZCVS reporting show 156,000 victims in the 12 months to May 2025 — 29,000 fewer than the baseline, i.e. 9,000 beyond the 20,000 target. That is precisely what he said, including the correct baseline and the correct target year. Disconfirming check: I looked for a different baseline or a smaller published reduction, and for whether 'serious violent crime' overstates the measure — the target is officially described as covering assault, robbery and sexual assault, which the Government routinely labels serious violent crime, and a later NZCVS release (year to October 2025) shows the reduction widening to 49,000, consistent rather than contradictory. Caveats worth noting but not affecting the verdict: NZCVS is a sample survey with margins of error, and the reduction is a survey estimate not a causal attribution. Method note: beehive.govt.nz and rnz.co.nz blocked direct fetching and the DPMC PDF did not parse cleanly, so the figures come from the DPMC factsheet metadata/snippets plus NZ Herald reporting of the same release.

statement: In a three-month period, bailiffs scanned more than 70,000 number plates and identified 982 with overdue court fines and reparations.
criterion: Ministry of Justice fines-enforcement reporting on the July–October 2025 number-plate scanning trial: true if the official figures record more than 70,000 plates scanned and 982 vehicles identified; false if the recorded totals differ materially.
reasoning: Official Ministry of Justice trial figures for 9 July – 6 October 2025 (the three-month period) record 67,536 number plates scanned and 982 people identified with overdue fines or reparations (of whom 278 paid on the spot, 127 arranged repayment, 115 had cars seized, 45 clamped; $225,399 recovered). The 982 figure matches exactly and the three-month framing is right, but 'more than 70,000' overstates the scanned total of 67,536 by about 2,500 (~3.7%) — the recorded total is below, not above, 70,000. No later official figure covering the period to 22 October was found that would exceed 70,000 while still pairing with 982.

statement: Well, alongside our target to reduce the number of victims of serious crime, we’ve also got a target led by Minister Chhour to reduce the number of children and young people with serious and persistent offending by 15 percent, which, the good news is, we have achieved as a Government already.
criterion: The Government Targets quarterly reporting for the youth serious and persistent offending target: true if the most recent published measurement before October 2025 shows a reduction of 15 percent or more against the stated baseline; false if the published reduction is under 15 percent.
reasoning: Government Targets reporting supports the claim as at 22 October 2025. Minister for Children Karen Chhour announced on 21 October 2025 — the day before this statement — that Target 3 (15% fewer children and young people with serious and persistent offending behaviour) had been achieved and surpassed, citing a 16% reduction, four years ahead of the deadline. The DPMC Target 3 factsheet for the quarter ending September 2025 confirms this: baseline (June 2023) 1,100, current (September 2025) 892 — an 18.9% reduction and below the target threshold of <900. Disconfirming check: the most recent factsheet published before October 2025 (quarter ending June 2025) showed 938 as at May 2025, a 14.7% reduction, i.e. just short of 15%. So on a strict reading of the criterion's 'before October 2025' wording the last quarterly factsheet was marginally under; but the measurement published immediately before Goldsmith spoke, and the next quarterly report, both show 15%+ and the target level met. The claim was accurate when made.

statement: The ads clarified the information about the offers on the table and were a perfectly valid way of drawing attention to the enormous disruption being caused to families, to children, and to patients by the ongoing strikes.
criterion: The published text and imagery of the Public Service Commission's October 2025 advertisements: true if they principally set out the details of the offers made; false if their principal content characterises or criticises the unions' bargaining stance.
reasoning: The Jane Meares independent review reproduces the actual tiles. There were two sets. The first (17–19 October 2025, two tiles) contained no offer details at all: 'Strike action on 23 October will disrupt medical and education services' with copy citing 845,000 students and 6,000 patients, and a second tile whose copy reads 'Despite best efforts, unions have chosen industrial action over continuing to talk at the table… Resolution can only be achieved through constructive dialogue—not disruption. Unions need to return to the table.' That set's principal content is disruption plus a characterisation of the unions' bargaining stance — the criterion's falsifying category. The second set (21–22 October, six tiles, running the day before and the day of Meager's statement) is entirely offer detail: graduate nurses 11%/$8,377, nurse practitioners up to $6,000 professional development allowance, senior nurses $3,224 on a $106,739 salary, 66% of trained primary teachers on ≥$100,000, 70% of secondary teachers to $107,886, and a 4.7% increase for top-scale teachers. So six of eight tiles do set out the offers, supporting Meager; but the claim omits that the earlier set carried no offer information and instead advocated the employer's bargaining position. Meares found the messaging was 'not targeted solely at informing the public about what they might expect on the Day of Action, advocating also for the Commission's position in the bargaining', while stopping short of a political-neutrality breach.

statement: In the last financial year, more than nine tonnes of illicit drugs were stopped from entering New Zealand.
criterion: NZ Customs Service annual report / joint Customs-Police border seizure statistics for the 2024/25 financial year: true if the total weight of illicit drugs intercepted exceeds nine tonnes; false if the published total is below that.
reasoning: The NZ Customs Service Annual Report 2025, covering the 2024/25 financial year (1 July 2024 – 30 June 2025), reports 9.3 tonnes of illicit drugs prevented from reaching communities through seizures at New Zealand's border and by overseas partners. That exceeds the nine-tonne threshold the criterion set. Minor unsignalled nuance: the total combines NZ border seizures with offshore partner seizures of NZ-bound consignments, but those were still stopped from entering New Zealand, so the claim's substance stands. No source was found putting the 2024/25 total below nine tonnes.

statement: Since the merger of the voluntary and professional fire services in 2017, there has been a long period of time where the rate of replacement of fire engines has not kept up in such a way that it’s kept the average age down.
criterion: FENZ fleet asset data / annual reports on appliance numbers, replacement rates and average fleet age from 2017 to 2023: true if the average age of the appliance fleet rose over that period; false if it held steady or fell.
reasoning: No published FENZ series gives average fleet age year-by-year from 2017 to 2023, so the criterion cannot be met by a direct measurement. All available evidence supports the claim's direction and none contradicts it: FENZ's fleet was reported at an average age of about 25 years against a 20-25 year design life; internal documents obtained by RNZ show FENZ failed to run regular fleet reviews and used appliance life to govern project life; FENZ received $25m/yr for three years specifically to address an 'ageing' fleet and concedes 'the age of our fleet needs to be reduced'; a parliamentary inquiry into fleet management was opened over fleet age and reliability. FENZ's own figure of 317 new appliances since the 2017 merger across a ~1,300-truck fleet implies roughly a 37-year replacement cycle, well below the rate needed to hold average age steady — arithmetic that disconfirms the alternative that age held steady or fell. Seymour's claim is qualitative and hedged, and the evidence supports it.

statement: Bargaining is available. It’s simply a question of the firefighters turning up.
criterion: The FENZ / NZ Professional Firefighters Union bargaining record for the period to October 2025 — dates offered, sessions scheduled and which party attended: true if FENZ made dates available that the union did not attend; false if FENZ cancelled, declined or failed to attend scheduled bargaining.
reasoning: The bargaining record to 22 October 2025 shows the opposite of what Seymour described. Bargaining sessions were scheduled for 9-10 October 2025. On 3 October FENZ notified the NZPFU it would not bargain, and would file for facilitation in the Employment Relations Authority, unless the union withdrew its notice of a one-hour stoppage on 17 October; FENZ filed that urgent facilitation application on 7 October and did not attend the scheduled sessions. The ERA adjourned the application, saying it was best served by letting bargaining continue as planned. FENZ subsequently repeated the same precondition in relation to the union's 31 October strike notice, and had used the same approach in March 2025 (refusing to table a new offer unless industrial action was withdrawn). The union stated it would attend the agreed dates. This matches the criterion's 'false' branch — FENZ declined scheduled bargaining — rather than the 'true' branch of FENZ offering dates the union did not attend. Caveat on sourcing: the session-level detail comes largely from NZPFU releases, a party to the dispute, but FENZ's precondition is corroborated by RNZ's independent reporting of FENZ publicly demanding the strike notice be withdrawn, and by the existence of FENZ's own facilitation application.

statement: Why should firefighters accept a pay offer that is a pay cut in real terms?
criterion: The percentage increases in FENZ's 2025 offer to the NZ Professional Firefighters Union, compared with Stats NZ CPI annual inflation over the term of the offer: true if the offered increases fall below CPI over that period; false if they match or exceed it.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether FENZ's 2025 offer to the NZPFU falls below Stats NZ CPI over the term of the offer. The only offer on the table as at 22 October 2025 was FENZ's July 2025 offer: 2% from 1 July 2025, 1.5% from July 2026 and 1.5% from July 2027 — 5.1% over three years, about 1.7% a year, with explicitly no compensation for the 2024-25 period and no pay increase since July 2023. Stats NZ annual CPI was 3.0% in the 12 months to the September 2025 quarter (released 20 October 2025, two days before the statement), and subsequent readings were 3.1% (March 2026) and 4.1% (June 2026). Every offered annual increase is roughly half the prevailing CPI rate, and the two-year gap since the last rise compounds the erosion. Checking the disconfirming side: FENZ later lifted the offer to a 6.2% average over three years (late 2025/2026, after the statement), which is still ~2% a year and below CPI, so the conclusion does not flip. The offer is a pay cut in real terms.

statement: Since coming into office, this Government has added around 2,000 more nurses to the public health system compared to 2023, alongside hundreds of additional doctors.
criterion: Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora published workforce headcount (or FTE) data for nursing and medical staff, 2023 baseline versus the latest 2025 reporting period. True if the nursing increase is around 2,000 and the medical increase is in the hundreds; false if materially lower, or if the increase depends on a headcount-versus-FTE switch or a change in who is counted.
reasoning: Health NZ workforce data released under OIA shows +2,100 nurses and more than 600 doctors (481 RMOs, 168 SMOs) on a headcount basis between September 2023 and March 2025 — so the magnitudes in the claim (~2,000 nurses, hundreds of doctors) match the published data against a 2023 baseline, and the criterion's headcount-vs-FTE trap is not what drives it: nursing FTE also rose about 2,496, from 26,908 in June 2023 to 29,404 in March 2024. Where the claim overstates is the attribution 'since coming into office'. Essentially all the growth occurred in the June 2023–March 2024 recruitment drive begun under the previous government: Health NZ added 1,883 net nurses between September 2023 and March 2024 but only 278 between March 2024 and March 2025, and nursing FTE moved from 29,404 (March 2024) to 29,458 (March 2026) — a net 54 FTE across the coalition's own tenure, with roughly 1,445 nursing vacancies unfilled. Looking for disconfirming evidence, I found no Health NZ series showing continued growth of that scale post-March 2024; NZNO characterised the framing as 'creative accounting'. The numbers are real; crediting them to this Government's time in office is not supported.

statement: That's backed by a record additional $16.68 billion investment in health over three Budgets, including initiatives focused on improving workplace safety and reducing wait-lists for patients.
criterion: Treasury Budget documents and Vote Health appropriations for the three Budgets referenced. True if the additional (not baseline) health funding across those Budgets sums to approximately $16.68 billion and exceeds the additional funding in any prior three-Budget span in nominal terms; false if the total is materially different, or if a previous three-Budget period delivered a larger nominal increase.
reasoning: The $16.68b is a genuine Budget 2024 figure and sums as stated: a multi-year cost-pressure arrangement of $5.720b (Budget 2024) + $5.480b (Budget 2025) + $5.480b (Budget 2026), so the criterion's arithmetic limb is met. But each component is a four-year forecast-period total, not a single-year uplift — Budget 2024's $5.720b is '$1.430b a year' and the pre-commitments are '$1.370b a year' each — so the three totals overlap and the money is spread across roughly six years of spending. New Zealand Doctor fact-checked exactly this framing ('$16.68 billion over six years, not three'). It is also cost-pressure funding for inflation and demographic growth rather than new initiatives: the ASMS/NZNO joint analysis found the 2024/25 Budget lifted operational health funding by about 0.4%, not enough to expand the workforce, which sits awkwardly with 'including initiatives focused on improving workplace safety and reducing wait-lists'. On the criterion's 'record' limb I could not confirm the claim: counted on the same cumulative forecast-period convention, the prior three-Budget span is at least comparable — Budget 2021's $4.7b over the forecast period, Budget 2022's $11.1b operating over four years (billed at the time as the 'largest investment ever in our health system'), plus Budget 2023's $1.3b of cost pressures and $707m for prescriptions. I found no evidence establishing the prior span was smaller, so the 'record' descriptor is unverified rather than disproven. Also, when Brown spoke in October 2025 the Budget 2026 tranche was still a pre-commitment, not appropriated.

statement: Our economy has been shrinking. Jobs have been disappearing. Unemployment is increasing.
criterion: Stats NZ national accounts (real production GDP, quarterly) and the Household Labour Force Survey for the quarters to September 2025. True if real GDP contracted in recent quarters, employment/filled jobs fell, and the unemployment rate rose over 2024-25; false if GDP grew, employment rose and unemployment fell over that period.
reasoning: Judged on data published before 22 Oct 2025. Real production GDP fell 0.9% in the June 2025 quarter (Stats NZ, released 18 Sep 2025) and was down 1.1% over the year to June 2025, following a 1.0% contraction in the Sept 2024 quarter — the economy had contracted in recent quarters. Filled jobs (business employment data) were 2.23m in the Sept 2025 quarter, down 1.0% (22,221 jobs) on a year earlier, so jobs were falling. The unemployment rate rose over 2024-25, from the low-4s to 5.2% (June 2025) and 5.3% (Sept 2025), an eight-year high, with unemployed people up 8.2% year-on-year and participation falling. All three limbs of the criterion are satisfied. Disconfirming check: GDP rebounded +1.1% in the Sept 2025 quarter, but that release came in December 2025, after the statement, so it does not bear on the claim as made; HLFS employment was flat quarter-on-quarter in Sept 2025 even as filled jobs fell over the year.

statement: New Zealanders are voting with their feet; record numbers of New Zealanders are simply giving up and leaving the country.
criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics: annual NZ-citizen departures and net NZ-citizen migration loss for the year to the statement date. True if either series reached a record high in the published series; false if it sat below earlier peaks.
reasoning: Stats NZ international migration statistics. In the August 2025 year — the most recent release available on 22 Oct 2025 — NZ-citizen migrant departures reached a record 73,900, exceeding the previous record of 73,300 set in the July 2025 year, and the net migration loss of NZ citizens was a record 47,900. The subsequent September 2025 year release confirmed the pattern, with 72,700 citizen departures described by Stats NZ as an annual record and a net citizen loss of 46,400 (versus 44,800 a year earlier), mostly to Australia. Both series named in the criterion reached record highs in the published series, so the criterion's 'true' condition is met on either. Disconfirming check: the record is in departures and net citizen loss, not total net migration, which remained a gain (12,400 in the September 2025 year); the causal framing ('giving up') is the speaker's interpretation and is not part of the criterion.

statement: Instead of giving those young New Zealanders hope, we have a Government that describes New Zealand as “wet, whiny and miserable”; that calls New Zealanders “bottom-feeders”; and that says that our emerging businesses, those who are creating the jobs of the future, are “C-listers” and unworthy of Government support.
criterion: The public record (Hansard, transcripts, contemporaneous media reports) of statements by members of the current Government. True if each of the three quoted phrases is attributable to a Government member in the sense described; false if any of the three is not so attributable or is materially misquoted.
reasoning: All three phrases trace to Christopher Luxon, now PM, but each is reworded and the third's target is materially recharacterised. (1) 'wet, whiny': Luxon said in June 2023 that NZ 'has become a very negative, wet, whiny, inward-looking country and we have lost the plot' (and earlier, to Crux, 'very wet, whiny and negative'). The word 'miserable' is not attested in any version; he also later said he meant the then-Labour Government. He was Leader of the Opposition, not a Government member, at the time. (2) 'bottom-feeders': Luxon's actual words on Newstalk ZB in March 2022 were 'we don't just do bottom feeding and just focus on the bottom' — a criticism of welfare policy focus, later narrowed by him to misbehaving state housing tenants. Widely reported as calling people 'bottom feeders', but he did not apply that noun to New Zealanders, and again he was in Opposition. (3) 'C-listers': genuine and made as PM (June 2024, Japan trip), where Luxon said past trade delegations 'got very watered down; just sort of the C list really' and were 'tag-alongs' who 'weren't able to convert well enough'. But he was describing business delegates on Ardern/Hipkins-era trade missions, not emerging businesses, and did not say they were 'unworthy of Government support' — that gloss is Hipkins's. Substance holds (the phrases are Luxon's), but the framing is overstated on all three counts, so this falls short of 'attributable in the sense described'.

statement: Quality safety measures are stable or improving over the past five years.
criterion: Health Quality & Safety Commission quality and safety markers and adverse events reporting, plus Health NZ quality indicators, for the five years to 2025. True if the indicator set as a whole is flat or improving over that span; false if a material share of the published measures show deterioration.
reasoning: The criterion's own named sources contradict the claim. Health NZ's Clinical quality and safety review: longitudinal data (Nov 2024, published Mar 2025), which explicitly draws on Te Tāhū Hauora HQSC Quality and Safety Markers, Quality Alerts, and adverse-event/harms data, sorts indicators in Table 1 as: 7 improved, 3 stayed the same, and 8 DETERIORATED. The deteriorated column includes healthcare-associated Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia (2016-2024), hospital- and non-hospital-acquired pressure injuries (2021-2024), postoperative DVT/PE (2021-2024), HDC nationwide complaint rate, self-discharge ED mortality (2016-2023), patient experience of access to primary and secondary care (2020-2024), and both waiting-time measures. Quantified: a 42.5% rise in hospital-acquired pressure injury rate and 27.6% rise in non-hospital-acquired PI (2017-2023/24); a 30% increase in the observed-vs-expected ratio of postoperative DVT/PE (2012/13-2023/24), with more episodes than expected in every reporting period since Jan 2021; HA-SAB median rate roughly doubled from 0.11 (Q1 2012) to 0.15 (Q2 2019) and has risen since. The report's own executive summary calls outcomes 'a mixed picture' and states access 'is getting worse'. Nearly all of these deteriorations fall inside Brown's five-year window, and they continued past the report: an HQSC quality alert in June 2025 again flagged rising pressure injuries, and HQSC HA-SAB surveillance recorded 966 events in the two years to June 2024. Disconfirming check: real sustained improvements do exist over the same span (falls resulting in fractured neck of femur down 46%, orthopaedic SSI down 10%, cardiac SSI down 44%, inpatient cardiac arrests down, perioperative mortality down, seclusion down, hospital standardised mortality broadly stable), and NZ ranked 4th of 10 countries in the 2024 Commonwealth Fund Mirror Mirror report — so the claim is not baseless. But the criterion sets the bar as 'the indicator set as a whole is flat or improving', with 'a material share showing deterioration' making it false, and 8 of 18 indicators in the authoritative published set deteriorated. That is a material share, so the blanket statement fails as written.

statement: Recently, I announced the introduction of peer support workers in the North Shore emergency department, completing the roll-out of the service across all three major Auckland hospitals alongside Dunedin, Christchurch, Wellington, and Waikato hospitals.
criterion: Health New Zealand service records and ministerial announcements for peer support workers in emergency departments at each named hospital. True if the service is operating at all sites listed as at October 2025; false if any named ED has no peer support worker in place, or if the Auckland roll-out covers fewer than all three major hospitals.
reasoning: Every element checks out against ministerial announcements and Health NZ service records. The North Shore announcement is real and recent relative to the 22 Oct 2025 speech: the Beehive release 'Peer support workers join North Shore Hospital' is dated 10 October 2025 and states the introduction completes 'the rollout of the service across all three major Auckland hospitals'. The three major Auckland hospitals are Middlemore (Counties Manukau), Auckland City, and North Shore (Waitematā) — Middlemore was the launch site in September 2024, and Auckland City is confirmed operational in the May 2025 Waikato release. Each other named site is confirmed operating before 22 October 2025: Wellington Hospital ED and Christchurch Hospital both have dedicated Beehive releases marking their service starts; Waikato Hospital ED in Hamilton started in May 2025 and was explicitly described as 'the fifth major hospital' to implement the service, with the release naming Middlemore, Auckland City, Wellington and Christchurch as the preceding four; Dunedin was the sixth, run by Life Matters Suicide Trust, phased in from November and fully implemented by September 2025, announced in early October 2025. Disconfirming check: I looked for any named ED lacking the service and found none — the reverse, the roll-out is broader than Doocey's list, with Tauranga also in place, and Health NZ/ministerial reporting in 2026 confirms peer support specialists working in eight EDs across Counties Manukau, Auckland, Waitematā, Christchurch, Hamilton, Dunedin, Tauranga and Wellington, i.e. a superset of the seven sites named. Doocey named only the sites relevant to his point and did not overstate the Auckland coverage.

statement: Since coming into Government, the peer support lived experience workforce has grown by almost 100 percent.
criterion: Health New Zealand peer support and lived experience workforce headcount (or FTE) for late 2023 versus 2025, or the equivalent figure in the Ministry of Health mental health workforce reporting. True if growth over that period is close to 100 percent; false if materially lower, or if the doubling depends on a change in which roles are counted as peer support.
reasoning: The criterion asks for Health NZ peer support / lived experience workforce headcount or FTE for late 2023 versus 2025, or the equivalent in Ministry of Health mental health workforce reporting. That series does not appear to be published. Health NZ's mental health workforce reporting (July 2025) breaks out growth by occupation — mental health nurses +21%, nursing support workers +20%, clinical psychologists and AOD counsellors +6% each, total MHA FTE +9% year-on-year between Q3 2023 and Q1 2025 — but does not report peer support or lived experience workers as a separate employment category with its own growth metric. Te Pou's workforce estimate series (2023, 2024 and 2025 Health NZ adult workforce estimates), which is the standard source for MHA workforce sizing, likewise publishes no peer-support-specific 2023-to-2025 comparison in its public summaries; its narrative says only that support and lived experience roles are 'growing strongly' and growing faster than clinical roles. Te Pou's CPSLE pages give no headcount past the 2022 survey. Disconfirming check: the nearest published quantification runs the other way — Te Hiringa Mahara's 2023 peer support workforce paper found an increase of 64 FTE, or 18%, across 2018-2022, with peer support still only 3.4% of the wider MHA workforce. Against a base of that order, a genuine near-doubling since late 2023 would be a very large absolute jump, and Doocey may instead be counting a narrower or newly-defined set of roles (the eight ED services, crisis recovery cafés, eating disorder services, the $1m peer workforce fund intakes) — which is exactly the counting-change caveat the criterion flags. But I found no published figure either supporting or refuting the claim, and no source disclosing which roles the minister counted, so I cannot return true or false. The underlying number likely exists only in Health NZ payroll/contract data not released publicly; an OIA or a written parliamentary question would be needed to resolve it.

statement: The game development rebate that's created jobs, that’s seen the gaming development sector grow by nearly 80 percent during the 2½ years that that rebate has been in place—they want it expanded.
criterion: NZ Game Developers Association annual industry survey figures for sector revenue/employment across the years spanning the rebate's introduction (2023) to 2025. True if growth over that period is close to 80% on the headline measure; false if materially lower.
reasoning: NZGDA annual industry survey: revenue NZ$434.4m for the year to 31 March 2023 (the rebate applied from 1 April 2023), NZ$548m in 2024 (+26%), NZ$759.57m in 2025 (+38.6%). Growth across the rebate window is +74.9%; measured from the pre-rebate FY22 base (~NZ$407m) it is 86%, the figure Labour's own release cites. 'Nearly 80 percent' falls between the two and is close to the headline measure, so it is not materially overstated. Employment also rose on the headline survey (1,097 to 1,418 FTEs, +29.2%, in the latest year alone), supporting the 'created jobs' clause, though jobs growth is well below 80% and the causal attribution to the rebate is not established by the survey itself.

statement: Eleven pages; no detail. I think there was one figure.
criterion: The Labour future fund policy document released in the week to 22 October 2025. True if it runs to about eleven pages and contains roughly one numerical figure; false if materially longer or if it contains multiple substantive figures.
reasoning: The document Labour released with the 20 October 2025 Future Fund announcement ('A Future Made in New Zealand', linked from labour.org.nz) is 12 pages, not eleven — a cover, a photo page, numbered content pages 3-10, a full-page photo and a back cover, so 8 pages of actual text. It contains about eight numerical figures, not one: S$354 million and S$434 billion (Temasek), A$4.2 trillion, $85 billion Super Fund with 11 percent invested domestically, 36,000 fewer jobs, more than 200 people leaving daily, and GDP down 'nearly a full percent'. Her underlying charge holds — every figure is context or attack material, and the document contains no costing, seed-capital number or size for the fund itself (the $200m seed figure came from the announcement, not the document) — but both specifics as stated are wrong.

statement: If we look at inflation: inflation has stayed within the band of 1 percent to 3 percent. From a high of 7.3 percent—eight official cash rate drops.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for each quarter since late 2023 and the RBNZ record of OCR decisions. True if every quarterly annual CPI print in the period referred to fell between 1% and 3%, the series peak was 7.3%, and exactly eight OCR cuts had been made by 22 October 2025; false if any quarter in scope printed above 3% or the count of cuts differs.
reasoning: Two of the three elements check out. The series peak was 7.3% (June 2022 quarter, a 32-year high), and exactly eight OCR cuts had been made by 22 October 2025: 5.50% to 2.50%, 300bp across August, October and November 2024, February, April and May 2025 (six consecutive), a hold in July 2025, then cuts in August (3.00%) and October 2025 (2.50%). But inflation did not 'stay' within the 1-3% band over the period since the government took office in late 2023: the December 2023 quarter printed 4.7%, March 2024 4.0% and June 2024 3.3% — all above the band. It re-entered only in the September 2024 quarter (2.2%) and has been in-band since: 2.2% (Dec 2024), 2.5% (Mar 2025), 2.7% (Jun 2025), 3.0% (Sep 2025, at the ceiling). True only for roughly the last year, which the phrasing does not signal.

statement: The Government has put its money where its mouth is: New Zealand First and National and a coalition agreement to put wool back into Government buildings.
criterion: The published National–New Zealand First coalition agreement (November 2023); true if it contains a commitment requiring or preferring woollen fibre in government building fit-outs, false if no such clause appears.
reasoning: The National–NZ First 2023 coalition agreement contains the commitment to 'direct government agencies where practical and appropriate to preference the use of woollen fibres rather than artificial fibres in government buildings'. NZ Government Procurement quotes that clause verbatim as the basis for amended Government Procurement Rule 69, effective 1 July 2025, applying to new government buildings costing $9m+ and refurbishments $100k+, with agencies required to report to MBIE when they do not use wool. The criterion is satisfied ('requiring or preferring'); the clause is a preference with a practicality caveat rather than an absolute mandate, but that is within the criterion as written.

statement: Two hundred people every day—a plane load every day—are now going offshore because they can no longer find the opportunities for them, for their children, and for their families.
criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for the most recent 12 months to October 2025; true if departures of New Zealand residents/citizens average close to 200 per day, false if the figure is materially below (e.g. under 150/day) or the claim only holds for gross departures of all travellers.
reasoning: Stats NZ international migration: in the August 2025 year (the most recent release available on 22 October 2025) there were 73,900 migrant departures of New Zealand citizens — 202 per day. In the September 2025 year the figure was 72,700 — 199 per day. Both are 'close to 200 per day'. Crucially these are long-term migrant departures of NZ citizens specifically (against 26,000 NZ-citizen arrivals), not gross departures of all travellers, so the criterion's failure condition does not apply. The causal framing ('can no longer find the opportunities') is rhetorical and outside the criterion.

statement: The fact that we have lost almost the size of Napier City in the last year should be concerning every single one of those Government backbenchers, because Kiwis vote with their feet.
criterion: Stats NZ migration estimates for the year to mid/late 2025 compared with Napier city's usually-resident population (approx. 67,000); true if the relevant loss figure is within roughly 10% of that population, false if it is materially smaller or only reaches that size on a gross-departures rather than net basis.
reasoning: Napier City's usually-resident population was 64,695 at the 2023 census, ~66,400 estimated June 2025. On a net basis — the natural reading of 'we have lost' — the net loss of New Zealand citizens was 47,900 in the August 2025 year (73,900 departures less 26,000 arrivals) and 46,400 in the September 2025 year: roughly 28% short of Napier, materially smaller than the criterion's ~10% tolerance. Overall net migration was still a gain (+12,400 in the September 2025 year), so New Zealand did not lose population at all. The figure only approaches Napier's size on a gross-departures basis (73,900), which the criterion explicitly excludes — and even then it exceeds Napier rather than falling 'almost' short of it. Checked the opposite direction: no published Stats NZ net measure for a 12-month period to late 2025 reaches ~60,000+.

statement: Our main issue is it’s one of our policies, one that the Rt Hon Winston Peters announced some 14 months ago at our 2024 convention.
criterion: New Zealand First's 2024 convention materials and contemporaneous news reports (approx. August-September 2024); true if Peters announced a sovereign wealth fund policy at that convention, false if no such announcement was made then or it was made by someone else at a materially different time.
reasoning: Context confirmed: Labour announced its 'NZ Future Fund' on 20 October 2025, two days before this speech, and Peters publicly accused Labour of a 'Temu-style mail-order imitation of a plan New Zealand First detailed last year'. NZ First's members passed a remit to investigate a $100 billion 'New Zealand Future Fund' at the party's 31st annual convention in Hamilton (12-13 October 2024), and Peters himself made it the centrepiece of his closing address, calling it 'brilliant' and saying it would be 'ring-fenced from politicians and ring-fenced from political interference'. The criterion's falsification conditions (no such announcement at that convention, or made by someone else at a materially different time) are not met: the announcement was made by Peters, at that convention. The only inaccuracy is arithmetic — 13 October 2024 to 22 October 2025 is about 12 months, not 'some 14 months'. The claim is anchored explicitly to 'our 2024 convention', which is correct, so the two-month overstatement is not a materially different time. Note the criterion guessed the convention was August-September 2024; it was actually October 2024.

statement: The turn around is on: strong wool—I should have told the Prime Minister this; he could have quoted it earlier—up 32 percent this year; fine wool: up 34 percent; and mid-micron wool up 41 percent.
criterion: New Zealand wool auction price indices (e.g. PGG Wrightson / NZ Wool Services International market reports, or Beef+Lamb NZ wool price series) for calendar 2025 to October; true if each of the three categories shows a rise within a few points of 32%, 34% and 41% respectively, false if any is materially different.
reasoning: The direction and rough magnitude are real — NZ wool prices rose sharply through 2025, with a large surge in September-October — but two elements are looser than stated. (1) Period: Patterson said 'this year', but when he repeated the identical three figures to media on 31 October 2025 he framed them as 'over the last 12 months, the strong wool indicator is up 32%, mid micron up 41%, and fine wool up 35%'. So the basis is a rolling 12-month change back to October 2024, not calendar 2025 to date, and the criterion's stated basis (calendar 2025 to October) is not what the numbers measure. (2) Strong wool: the most directly comparable contemporaneous independent measure, PGG Wrightson's market report of 30 October 2025, states 'the average of all strong wool types has increased 25% compared to the same time last year' — seven points below the claimed 32%. A 32% rise is plausible for the narrower Fusca/Wool Impact strong wool indicator (which was around 330c/kg clean in early 2025 and 430c/kg by 18 December 2025), so the figure is not fabricated, but it is index-dependent and sits at the top of the range. The mid-micron and fine wool figures hold up well: mid-micron wool saw a documented surge (22-28 micron lifting 14-27% at the opening 2025-26 Christchurch sales alone), and 16-20 micron fine wool was reported trading 35-40% higher year-on-year, consistent with 41% and 34-35%. Substance holds; the strong wool figure is materially overstated against the broadest published basket and the period is not the one signalled.

statement: It’s biodegradable, it’s flame retardant, it’s moisture absorbent, it’s anti-allergenic, it’s carbon negative.
criterion: Peer-reviewed life-cycle assessments of New Zealand wool (e.g. AgResearch / IWTO LCA work) covering on-farm emissions through processing; true if the net carbon balance of wool is negative on a full LCA basis and wool is naturally flame-retardant and biodegradable, false if full-LCA studies show a net positive carbon footprint.
reasoning: Four of the five properties check out. Wool is biodegradable (100% natural protein fibre, breaks down on land and in water without microplastic residue); it is naturally flame-retardant, not by treatment — high nitrogen (15-16%) and sulfur (3-4%) content, high moisture regain and low heat of combustion give it a limiting oxygen index of about 25%, above cotton and rayon, so it smoulders and self-extinguishes when the flame is removed; and it is highly moisture absorbent. But the criterion made the carbon claim decisive, and it fails. Full life-cycle assessments of greasy wool put the footprint at roughly 8.6-26 kg CO2e per kg (New Zealand, Australian and US studies), i.e. substantially net POSITIVE, with over 75% coming from enteric methane and manure nitrous oxide. The most industry-favourable reframing — an IWTO-backed peer-reviewed study applying ISO 14067:2018 biogenic carbon accounting, published in Agricultural Systems in January 2026, three months AFTER this speech — reduces wool's carbon intensity by 35% to 102% depending on herd demographics, climate and manure retention. Only the extreme upper end of that range crosses into net-negative, in a single drought-affected case-study farm with soil sequestration, and it was not published at the time of speaking. Disconfirming check: I looked specifically for LCA work supporting a net-negative result and found only this biogenic reframe and industry marketing material, no full-LCA study showing wool as net carbon negative as a general property. The criterion's falsification condition — 'false if full-LCA studies show a net positive carbon footprint' — is squarely met.

statement: In the last two years, this Government has reduced inflation, got it down from record levels to one now that businesses have confidence to invest.
criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series: compare the annual rate for the September 2023 quarter (start of the two-year window) with the most recent quarter before 22 October 2025. True if the rate has materially fallen AND the 2023 level was a record high in the CPI series; false if the rate has not fallen, or if 'record levels' is wrong because higher annual rates appear earlier in the series (e.g. the 1970s-80s).
reasoning: The fall is real but 'record levels' is wrong. Annual CPI inflation was 5.6% in the Sept 2023 quarter (start of the two-year window) and 3.0% in the Sept 2025 quarter, released 20 Oct 2025 — a material fall. But the cycle peak of 7.3% (June 2022 quarter) was headlined by Stats NZ itself as a '32-year high', not a record: NZ inflation reached 18.9% in mid-1987 and exceeded 10% for more than half the years 1969-1990. The 7.3% peak also predates the two-year window McClay claims credit for. Additionally, inflation had just risen from 2.7% (June 2025) to 3.0%, the highest in a year and at the top of the RBNZ band, so the trend had reversed at the moment he spoke.

statement: And we have seen a trade negotiation start with India when that Government, Labour, said it was not a priority for them: $12 billion of extra exports.
criterion: (a) MFAT trade agreement pages / official announcements on whether NZ-India FTA negotiations formally launched before 22 October 2025; (b) statements by Labour trade ministers 2017-2023 on India's priority in the FTA programme; (c) the source of the $12 billion figure — official MFAT/NZIER modelling. True if negotiations launched, Labour is on record deprioritising India, and $12bn traces to a published estimate; false if any of the three is contradicted.
reasoning: Legs (a) and (b) of the criterion hold; leg (c) fails. (a) NZ-India FTA negotiations formally launched 16-17 March 2025, announced by McClay and India's Piyush Goyal — before 22 Oct 2025 (MFAT timeline of negotiations). (b) Labour Foreign Minister Nanaia Mahuta is on record in 2022, sharing a stage with S. Jaishankar, saying an FTA 'is not a priority of the Labour Government' — though this is dated, since by the 2023 campaign Hipkins was promising a prime-ministerial delegation to India within 100 days, so Labour's stated position had already shifted. (c) The $12 billion does not trace to any published MFAT/NZIER estimate. MFAT's National Interest Analysis (modelling by Motu) puts additional exports at $340m by 2027 rising to $1.271bn by 2050, and GDP gains of ~0.07% ($401m) by 2037 — roughly an order of magnitude below $12bn; reported export-boost figures around conclusion were ~$1bn. The criterion's strict conjunctive rule ('false if any of the three is contradicted') would return false; I graded partly_true because the $12bn's referent is ambiguous in the sentence and may attach to total export growth rather than to India, making a flat 'false' an overreach. The headline substance (negotiations started with a country Labour had publicly deprioritised) is true; the quantification is unsupported.

statement: We have reduced ram raids from records high all over the country, when New Zealanders were just expecting when they got out of bed there would be another ram raid in their community to now a level so low that we hardly hear about them.
criterion: NZ Police retail crime / ram raid offence counts by month, 2022 through 2025. True if monthly ram raid counts peaked in the 2022-23 period and the most recent 2025 figures are down substantially (e.g. a majority reduction); false if counts are flat, rising, or the reduction is marginal.
reasoning: The criterion as written is met. NZ Police data show monthly ram raids peaked in August 2022 (86/month in the individually-reviewed dataset, 116/month in the text-search dataset) — the highest since the series began around 2017. Annual totals fell from 433 (2022) to 288 (2023); April 2023 was 64 versus 12 in April 2024; and by 2025 the rate was about 9 per month, back to pre-pandemic levels — roughly a 90% reduction from peak. That is a peak in the 2022-23 period and a large majority reduction by 2025. Two caveats that do not change the verdict under this criterion but qualify the 'we reduced' framing: much of the decline began before the November 2023 change of government, and analysts attribute it substantially to the fading social-media trend and physical barriers (bollards, fog cannons) rather than to policy; and 'record high' is only true against a series starting around 2017.

statement: Anybody who doesn't know that really just has to understand that 80 percent of all our goods exports that go overseas come from the primary sector.
criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries / Stats NZ merchandise trade data for the year to 2025: primary sector share of total goods exports by value. True if approximately 80% (say 75-85%), false if materially outside that band.
reasoning: MPI's Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries reports food and fibre at 81.1% of New Zealand's goods exports in the 2024 year, and McClay's own December 2025 ministerial release states the food and fibre sectors account for 83 per cent of all NZ goods exports. Both fall inside the criterion's 75-85% band, so '80 percent of all our goods exports' is accurate. The lower figures that circulate (e.g. 57%) use a goods-plus-services denominator, which is not the claim he made. Caveat: the MPI PDF would not fetch directly, so the 81.1% figure comes from search extraction of the MPI report, cross-checked against the Beehive release.

statement: In fact, what we want to do is acknowledge the fact that people in Aotearoa are leaving in droves.
criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates: annual departures of New Zealand citizens, and net migration loss of NZ citizens, for the years to 2024 and 2025 compared with the pre-2020 historical range. True if citizen departures or net citizen outflow are at or near series records; false if they sit within the ordinary historical range.
reasoning: Stats NZ records a net migration loss of 52,500 New Zealand citizens in the year to March 2024 - the first time the annual net loss exceeded 50,000, against a previous record of 44,400 more than a decade earlier - and a net loss of 47,100 NZ citizens for calendar 2024, the largest calendar-year loss on record. In the most recent data available when she spoke (year to August 2025), 73,900 NZ-citizen migrant departures exceeded the previous record of 73,300 set in the July 2025 year, with a net citizen loss of 47,900 versus 44,900 a year earlier. Both limbs of the criterion (gross citizen departures, net citizen outflow) are at or near series records rather than within the ordinary pre-2020 range. Checked for the disconfirming case: net outflow had eased slightly from the 2024 peak, but gross departures were simultaneously setting a new record, so the claim does not fail on that reading.

statement: We have $629.4 billion fraud that goes on in this country, and this country does nothing about it.
criterion: IRD tax gap estimates and any Treasury or academic estimate of total fraud/tax evasion in New Zealand, compared against NZ nominal GDP (~$430bn). True if a credible published estimate puts the figure at approximately $629.4 billion; false if published estimates are orders of magnitude lower, or if the figure is internally inconsistent with the accompanying claim that $80 million is 1 percent of it (which would imply $8 billion).
reasoning: No credible published estimate puts New Zealand fraud anywhere near $629.4 billion. The largest NZ figure found is a draft Serious Fraud Office report costing ALL economic crime at up to $9.4 billion a year; NZ Police estimate $700m-$1.4bn of government funds lost to fraud annually; Netsafe puts digital scam losses at $2.3bn (2024); the Tax Justice Network estimates tax evasion at ~$7bn; IRD's unpaid tax stock was ~$9.3bn at 30 June 2025. $629.4 billion is roughly 1.5 times New Zealand's entire nominal GDP (~NZ$430bn, ~US$250bn), which is not a possible magnitude for domestic fraud. It also fails the criterion's internal-consistency test: the accompanying '$80 million is 1 percent' implies ~$8 billion, consistent with the tax-evasion order of magnitude, indicating the stated figure is a scale error of roughly 80-fold. Searched neutrally on the subject (total cost of fraud in New Zealand, IRD tax gap, SFO estimates) rather than on the claim's direction, and looked specifically for any source that would support a figure this large - including global fraud estimates - and found none. Note: the NZ Hansard transcript for 22 October 2025 returned a server error and the daily PDF would not extract, so the surrounding context could not be recovered; the verdict does not depend on it, as the figure as quoted is checkable on its own.

statement: This resulted in the worst massacre in Israel’s history.
criterion: Compare the documented civilian and military death toll of the 7 October 2023 attacks (Israeli government / IDF figures, ~1,200) against the death tolls of prior single attacks or massacres on Israeli soil since 1948. True if 7 October is the deadliest; false if any earlier single attack recorded a higher toll.
reasoning: Israeli government/IDF figures put the 7 October 2023 toll at ~1,200 killed. The deadliest prior single attack on Israeli soil since 1948 was the 1978 Coastal Road massacre at 38 killed; CSIS states the October 7 toll is 'more than 31 times as large as the number of people killed in the next most fatal attack'. Checked for disconfirming cases: earlier candidate massacres (Ma'alot 1974, ~27; Kfar Etzion 1948, ~127; Hadassah convoy 1948, ~78) are all an order of magnitude below.
