Two reasons this is not sufficient to return 'false': (1) the specific document most likely to contain it — a Kāinga Ora OIA response dated 1 October 2025, 'Number of construction workers on Kāinga Ora new builds', six days before the question was asked — is listed on their OIA index but I could not retrieve the PDF, and kaingaora.govt.nz blocked automated fetching; parliament.nz/hansard.parliament.nz are behind a Radware bot challenge, so the Hansard exchange where the Minister answered was also unreachable. (2) The figure is not implausible on its face: the NZ Infrastructure Commission's published benchmark, cited in Budget 2026 material, is that every $1 billion of annual infrastructure investment supports about 4,500 jobs, and a residential-building-specific estimate would reasonably sit somewhat higher because housing construction is more labour-intensive than civil infrastructure. So the underlying advice may well exist and simply not be publicly indexed. Absence of a public trace here is not evidence the advice does not exist.

statement: Let me step you through the numbers: in the last 23 months under this Government, we have delivered over 7,000 new-build social homes. By comparison, under the entire past three years under the last Labour Government, only 6,000 homes were delivered, so I’ll take our record over your record any day.
criterion: Kāinga Ora and HUD public housing supply reporting on new-build social home completions, for the 23 months to October 2025 and for the three years to October 2023. True if both totals match on a like-for-like definition of new builds; false if either total is materially overstated or understated, or if the two figures use different counting definitions.
reasoning: The government-side number is roughly defensible; the Labour comparison is materially understated and not like-for-like, which the criterion explicitly makes disqualifying. Own side: the Beehive's September 2025 release claimed 'more than 6,800 net new social homes delivered since November 2023 by Kainga Ora and CHPs', so 'over 7,000' by 7 October 2025 is broadly consistent; AAP's fact-check counts 8,017 new builds over Nov 2023 - May 2026 (net increase 5,115 after 975 sales and 1,633 demolitions). Note the official wording is 'net new', while Willis says 'new-build' - different definitions with materially different values (6,800 net vs the gross build count). Labour side: HUD reported 8,121 public housing places added Nov 2017 - 30 Jun 2021; the Beehive reported a net increase of 12,017 public homes since Oct 2017 of which 9,917 were new builds (as at April 2023); 3,192 additional public homes were delivered in 2022/23 alone and Kainga Ora delivered 2,400+ new builds in 2020/21. Reconstructing the three years to October 2023 from these gives roughly 7,000+ net and substantially more on a gross new-build basis - not 6,000. A further mismatch: much of the 2023-25 delivery came out of the build pipeline commissioned and funded under the previous government (Kainga Ora completed 4,864 new homes in the 12 months to June 2024, the bulk of Willis's 23-month window). I could not locate a single authoritative published figure for Labour's last three years on the same new-build definition, which is why this is partly_true rather than false: the 7,000 holds approximately, the 6,000 does not.

statement: Crayfish and scallops have become functionally extinct.
criterion: Hauraki Gulf Forum 'State of Our Gulf' reporting and Fisheries NZ stock assessments for CRA 2 rock lobster and Coromandel/Hauraki scallops; true if those assessments describe gulf crayfish and scallop populations as functionally extinct or at a comparably collapsed level, false if they report populations at or near sustainable biomass targets.
reasoning: The criterion's named sources use this exact characterisation. Crayfish: Fisheries New Zealand deemed the Hauraki Gulf crayfish population 'functionally extinct' in 2016 (numbers too low to fulfil their ecological role controlling kina), and the Hauraki Gulf Forum's State of our Gulf reporting has repeated it - the 2023 report describes koura as depleted and warns of proliferating kina barrens; the 2026 report still describes them as depleted. A 2024 peer-reviewed study (Frontiers in Marine Science) using fisheries-independent surveys in the Gulf found lobster biomass on fished reefs at less than 10% of unfished levels and spawning stock biomass around 5% in statistical area 905, and expressly notes J. edwardsii 'have been described as functionally extinct in the Hauraki Gulf and northeastern New Zealand'. Scallops: the Coromandel/Hauraki fishery was closed to commercial and recreational fishing from March 2022, with an emergency closure of the last two open areas (Little Barrier, Colville Channel) in December 2022 after surveys showed further serious decline; State of our Gulf 2023 refers to the 'near loss of our last scallop beds' and the fishery remains closed. Disconfirming evidence checked: the fishery-wide Fisheries NZ CRA 2 stock assessment (2023, and the 2024 rapid update) estimates the stock above sustainable levels - around 40% of unfished SSB - which would be the criterion's falsifying branch. But that assessment covers the whole CRA 2 QMA and is CPUE-based; the Frontiers authors argue increased CPUE reflects changed fisher behaviour rather than recovery, and EDS's 2025 submissions to Fisheries NZ state rock lobster in the inner Gulf are 'close to being functionally extinct'. Court's claim was about the Gulf specifically, where the evidence is one-directional. Recent NIWA/Fisheries NZ surveys show some localised scallop recovery around Mercury Bay but little elsewhere - a minor qualification, not a refutation.

statement: There are around 2 million - odd people who live in the area around where the Hauraki Gulf marine protected areas are going to be established, in Auckland, Waikato, and the Bay of Plenty.
criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Auckland, Waikato and Bay of Plenty regions as at the date of the statement; true if the combined gulf-adjacent population is in the region of 2 million, false if materially different (e.g. below 1.5 million or above 3.5 million).
reasoning: Stats NZ subnational population estimates at 30 June 2025 (the most recent release before the 7 October 2025 statement) put Auckland at about 1,816,000, Waikato at 532,100 and Bay of Plenty at 351,500 - a combined ~2.70 million for the three regions in full. Court's claim was narrower than that: people living 'in the area around where the Hauraki Gulf marine protected areas are going to be established', i.e. the gulf-adjacent parts of those three regions. On that reading the figure is closer to 2.0 million (Auckland alone is ~1.82m, plus the Hauraki/Thames-Coromandel districts and the western Bay of Plenty fringe). Either construction sits inside the criterion's band - well above 1.5 million and well below 3.5 million - and 'around 2 million-odd' is a fair description of the gulf-adjacent population specifically. Disconfirming check: I looked for a reading that would push the total outside the band and found none; taking the three regions whole overstates to ~2.7m, still comfortably within tolerance.

statement: All they have done is to also remove all reference to whānau and hapū in this bill, although both play a significant role in the restoration work of the gulf, and, again, they have been sidelined, although they have led much of that restoration as well.
criterion: Compare the bill as reported back by the Environment Committee with the version as passed (and the Amendment Paper): true if every occurrence of 'whānau' and 'hapū' was struck out, false if either word survives anywhere in the enacted text.
reasoning: The Minister of Conservation's Cabinet paper 'Report back on the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill' states at para 22: 'Following consultation with colleagues, I propose to amend language in the Bill from "whānau, hapū, and iwi" to "iwi" to ensure that requirements in the Bill are not overly broad', and Recommendation 3 asks Cabinet to 'agree that references to "whānau, hapū and iwi" be replaced with "iwi"', affecting clauses 8, 19, 21(aaa), 29, 30, 30A, 32, 66, 67(3), 68(3). Independent commentary confirms this carried through to the enacted law: Assoc Prof Fiona McCormack (Science Media Centre, 7 Oct 2025) says the amendments 'remove reference to "hapū" and "whānau", weakening the role of mana whenua in marine governance and shifting decision-making to iwi-level structures'; Greenpeace and Waatea News report the same. Caveat: legislation.govt.nz returns 403 to automated fetching, so I could not run a word search over the enacted text to confirm no stray occurrence survives (e.g. in a definition or schedule); the 'every occurrence' half of the criterion rests on the Cabinet recommendation plus corroborating commentary. Also note the mechanism was the government's report-back amendments rather than the late Amendment Paper 2025/260, whose disclosure statement covers only the customary-fishing and ring-net changes.

statement: His own Cabinet paper stated, quite clearly, that that fishing could occur elsewhere in the gulf, but he chose to ignore that, sadly.
criterion: The proactively released Cabinet paper on the amendments to the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana marine protection bill: true if it states that the ring-net fishing in question could take place elsewhere in the gulf, false if it contains no such statement or says the opposite.
reasoning: The proactively released Cabinet paper 'Report back on the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill' (Minister of Conservation, DOC 'rtg-release-2024') states verbatim: 'Based on the nature and current distribution of ring-net fishing activities in the Gulf, it is likely that ring-net fishing activity that usually occurs within these HPAs could be relocated elsewhere in the Gulf with minimal impact to the fishers.' The same paper notes 'Providing for ring-net fishing in the two HPAs would benefit six ring-net fishers who collectively catch approximately 16 tonnes of fish per year in these areas.' The ring-net exemption for the Kawau Bay and Rangitoto/Motutapu high protection areas nonetheless proceeded and is in the enacted law plus the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection (Ring Net Fishing) Regulations 2025 — and reporting on the released documents shows DOC policy advisers had recommended against it on 24 September 2024 before the Minister sided with Seafood NZ. That matches the claim both in substance and in the 'he chose to ignore that' characterisation.

statement: Here, I would just make the comparison that we have seen, when we have seen threats to our livestock, and we have seen Governments pour in close to a billion dollars to try and prevent the spread of Mycoplasma bovis but nowhere near the equivalent when it comes to eradicating the threat that is Caulerpa brachypus.
criterion: MPI / Treasury reporting on the total cost of the Mycoplasma bovis eradication programme, and MPI/Biosecurity NZ budgets for the Caulerpa brachypus response: true if M. bovis spend approaches $1 billion and the Caulerpa response is an order of magnitude smaller, false if the figures are materially different.
reasoning: M. bovis: the eradication programme was costed at $886 million over ten years at launch in May 2018 (MPI/Treasury figure, widely reported; MPI's current pest management plan pages cite $870 million), funded 68% Crown / 32% DairyNZ and Beef+Lamb. That 'approaches $1 billion' as the criterion requires. Caulerpa: Biosecurity NZ states 'over $31 million has been spent or allocated' on the exotic caulerpa (C. brachypus / C. parvifolia) response — research, surveillance, removal-technique development and legal controls — built up from a $5m boost and a $10m injection in 2024 and $6.2m + $3.8m technology contracts in 2025; Biosecurity Minister Hoggard cited 'more than $20 million' in May 2025. The ratio is roughly 28:1, i.e. more than an order of magnitude. One nuance the criterion does not penalise: the $886m is the total programme cost shared with industry, so the government's own share is nearer $600m, making 'Governments pour in close to a billion' lean on the headline total; the comparison and the order-of-magnitude gap hold either way.

statement: We did not need New Zealand First’s support to pass this legislation. We could have passed it in its original format with members of the Opposition.
criterion: Party seat counts in the 54th Parliament and the division record for the bill: true if the combined votes of National, ACT and the Opposition parties reach a majority (61) without New Zealand First's members, false if New Zealand First's votes were arithmetically necessary.
reasoning: Seat counts in the 54th Parliament at October 2025: National 49, ACT 11, NZ First 8, Labour 34, Green 15, Te Pāti Māori 4-6, total 122-123, majority 62. National + ACT alone is 60, short of a majority, but National + ACT + Labour is 94, and adding the Greens and Te Pāti Māori gives ~113-115 — far above 62 without any of New Zealand First's 8 votes. So NZ First's votes were not arithmetically necessary. The substantive premise also holds: at the third reading every party in the House supported the bill, and Labour (which introduced the original bill in government) explicitly criticised the late ring-net amendment and said it would reverse it, i.e. it backed the unamended version. No division was recorded — the motion was agreed to — so the seat arithmetic plus the stated party positions is the available evidence.

statement: When you have an ocean, any part of ocean that is 99 percent exploited, compromise does not look like protecting 6 percent and still allowing commercial fishing in the high-protection areas.
criterion: Two separable factual claims. (a) Extent of protection: the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill as passed, plus DOC's published figures for the total area of the high-protection areas against the total area of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park — true if the high-protection areas amount to roughly 6 percent of the gulf, false if materially higher or lower. (b) Whether commercial fishing is permitted in high-protection areas: the text of the Act as enacted, including the late-stage Supplementary Order Paper — true if any commercial fishing method is authorised to continue within a high-protection area, false if all commercial fishing is excluded. The '99 percent exploited' figure resolves against the pre-Act share of the gulf open to fishing.
reasoning: (a) Extent: DOC's published figures put marine protection in the gulf at 0.3% before the Act and 5.9% after (excluding the Cable Protection Zone), delivered by the 12 high protection areas plus two marine reserve extensions; Greenpeace's analysis gives 'nearly 6%'. Another breakdown puts HPAs alone at 5.6% of the gulf. 'Protecting 6 percent' is accurate. (b) Commercial fishing in HPAs: confirmed. A late-stage Supplementary Order Paper authorises commercial ring-net operators with prior fishing history to continue in 2 of the 12 HPAs (Kawau Bay, and Rangitoto and Motutapu), 31 March-31 August, targeting kahawai, grey mullet and trevally. DOC and Fisheries NZ officials advised against it. So a commercial fishing method is authorised inside high-protection areas. (c) The '99 percent exploited' framing: pre-Act only 0.3% of the gulf had marine protection, so 99.7% lacked it — accurate on DOC's own accounting. Disconfirming check: the Cable Protection Zone covers a further 6.3% and does prohibit fishing and anchoring (for infrastructure, not conservation, reasons), so the strictly-open-to-fishing share was ~93.4% rather than 99%. That is the one figure that softens under a different denominator; both of the criterion's separable claims resolve true.

statement: Everyone can be proud of the huge environmental achievement where we see this bill delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf, nearly tripling the protected area in the Hauraki Gulf, establishing high-protection areas for 800 square kilometres of the gulf.
criterion: The Act as enacted plus DOC's published marine protection figures for the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park. (a) 'Nearly tripling' — true if the total protected area after commencement is between roughly 2.5 and 3 times the pre-Act protected area, false if materially outside that. (b) '800 square kilometres' — true if the combined area of the high-protection areas created by the Act is approximately 800 km², false if materially different. (c) 'Highest ever level of protection' — true if the post-Act protected proportion of the gulf exceeds every previous level recorded by DOC, false if any earlier regime protected more.
reasoning: (a) 'Nearly tripling': the Act lifts the area of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park under some form of protection from 6.6% (including the existing Cable Protection Zone) to 17.6% — a factor of 2.67, inside the 2.5-3x band. DOC's own media release uses the phrase 'nearly tripling marine protection', and The Conversation's independent write-up is headlined 'Protected areas in the Hauraki Gulf nearly triple'. (b) '800 square kilometres': DOC's media release states the government is establishing High Protection Areas covering 800 km², consistent with HPAs being ~5.6-5.9% of a park of roughly 1.2 million hectares. (c) 'Highest ever level of protection': post-Act protection (17.6%, or 5.9% at high-protection level against 0.3% before) exceeds every previous level; DOC describes it as the 'greatest ever protection' for the gulf and the most significant increase in marine protection in over a decade, and I found no earlier regime protecting more. Caveat that does not change the verdict against this criterion: the HPAs are not fully no-take, since the late Supplementary Order Paper permits commercial ring-net fishing in 2 of the 12 (about 3% of the total protected area), which is why opponents called it a 'hollow victory' — but the area figures Wedd cited are correct as stated.

statement: You actually can’t even kill Caulerpa or treat pests and other invasive species in a marine reserve.
criterion: The Marine Reserves Act 1971 and DOC's permitting practice for marine reserves; true if the Act and DOC policy bar pest or invasive-species control (including Caulerpa treatment) within a marine reserve, false if DOC can and does authorise such control inside reserves.
reasoning: The substance of the contrast is correct and is DOC's own framing: marine reserves under the Marine Reserves Act 1971 are strictly 'no take' and hands-off (s 3: reserves 'preserved as far as possible in their natural state'; marine life 'protected and preserved'), and DOC's permit regime under the Marine Reserves Regulations 1993 provides for scientific research and monitoring, not restoration or pest control. DOC states that High Protection Areas — unlike marine reserves — 'aim to protect and restore marine habitats while being flexible to provide for active habitat restoration,' with 'active habitat restoration activities, such as removing urchins from urchin barrens ... allowed, following a permitting process,' and its Conservation Blog says HPAs allow 'removing kina from kina barrens or reseeding shellfish beds.' However, the absolute claim that you 'can't even kill Caulerpa' inside a reserve is not established. Exotic caulerpa (C. brachypus, C. parvifolia) is an Unwanted Organism under the Biosecurity Act 1993 and is managed by Biosecurity New Zealand under that Act, which is not disapplied inside marine reserves; DOC is an active partner in marine biosecurity responses, including the joint MPI/DOC/Environment Southland eradication of invasive Undaria at Sunday Cove in Fiordland and the long-running Fiordland Marine Biosecurity Programme. Section 3 also lets the Director-General 'take such steps as may be necessary to ensure the continued welfare of any reserve.' I found no statutory prohibition on biosecurity treatment inside a reserve and no documented case of treatment being refused on that ground — but equally no documented case of caulerpa being treated inside a marine reserve (the Goat Island incident was in Omaha Cove, near but not inside the reserve). So: true that marine reserves do not provide for active management/restoration the way HPAs do; overstated as a flat legal bar on killing caulerpa or treating pests.

statement: Overfishing, habitat loss, pollution, sedimentation, and the effects of poorly planned urban development have led to what we see today in the gulf: a 57 percent decline in key fish stocks in the Hauraki Gulf, a 67 percent decline in seabirds, and a 97 percent decline in whales and dolphins.
criterion: The Hauraki Gulf Forum 'State of our Gulf' report series (and the underlying Sea Change / NIWA baseline work): true if those reports give declines of approximately 57% in key fish stocks, 67% in seabirds and 97% in whales and dolphins for the gulf; false if the reported declines differ materially from those figures.
reasoning: All three figures trace to Hauraki Gulf Forum 'State of our Gulf' material and match to within a couple of points. Whales/dolphins: State of our Gulf 2020 coverage reports dolphins down 97 per cent — exact match. Seabirds: the Forum's own 'The State of our Seabirds' (Gulf Journal, Nov 2021) states 'from the first settlement of the region in approximately 1350, seabird numbers in the Gulf ecosystem have declined by around 69%' — 67% is within rounding of the Forum's own figure and is the number the Forum-derived campaign material uses. Fish: State of our Gulf reporting puts the Gulf at under 45% of its 1925 fish biomass (i.e. a ~55% loss), with snapper down 83%, trevally 86% and sharks 86% on historic levels; a '57 percent decline in key fish stocks' is consistent with that and is the figure carried by WWF-NZ and Greenpeace Aotearoa citing the Gulf Journal 'State of the Gulf' reports. None of the three differs materially from the reports named in the criterion, so the criterion resolves true. Caveat worth recording though it is outside the criterion: the baselines are deep-historical (c.1350 Polynesian settlement for seabirds, 1925 for fish, pre-whaling for cetaceans), so attributing the whole of these declines to 'overfishing, habitat loss, pollution, sedimentation, and ... poorly planned urban development' overstates the causal story — the seabird decline was initially driven by introduced predators and harvest, and the cetacean decline largely by historical whaling. The 57% fish figure is also the weakest-sourced of the three: I could not retrieve a primary Forum document stating '57%' verbatim, only Forum data consistent with it plus advocacy repetition attributed to the Forum reports.

statement: In fact, crayfish and scallop populations are now functionally extinct in parts of the gulf.
criterion: Peer-reviewed surveys of Hauraki Gulf rock lobster (e.g. the University of Auckland/Leigh surveys) and Fisheries New Zealand scallop (SCA CS) stock assessments and closure notices: true if published assessments describe these populations as functionally extinct in parts of the gulf; false if surveys show populations at ecologically functional levels throughout.
reasoning: Crayfish: the Hauraki Gulf Forum's State of our Gulf 2020 explicitly describes kōura/rock lobster as 'functionally extinct' in many parts of the marine park, with numbers at roughly 20% of 1945 levels. The PM's Chief Science Advisor case study confirms this characterisation and cites the New Zealand Marine Sciences Society's fishery-independent analysis: legal-sized lobster biomass outside the Leigh and Tāwharanui marine reserves was 2-3% of that inside the reserves (~7% at Hahei), leading researchers to conclude the CRA2 stock in the Hauraki Gulf and Coromandel 'may be well below the hard limit.' Scallops: the Coromandel/Hauraki Gulf fishery (SCA CS) was progressively closed on survey evidence — a March 2022 closure across most of the Gulf following an alarming 2021 biomass survey, then an emergency closure of the two remaining fishable beds to commercial, recreational and customary fishing from 16 December 2022, with the Minister describing the population as collapsed. The claim is properly hedged ('in parts of the gulf'), which matches the sources. Two qualifications, neither material to the criterion: 'functionally extinct' is the Hauraki Gulf Forum's and independent scientists' characterisation rather than a formal Fisheries New Zealand stock-status category, and the official 2017 FNZ CRA2 assessment was less severe (likely below the soft limit, very unlikely below the hard limit). No survey shows either population at ecologically functional levels throughout the gulf.

statement: It’ll expand the protected area from currently 6.7 percent to over 18 percent of the gulf.
criterion: The bill's regulatory impact statement / DOC's published figures for marine protection in the Hauraki Gulf before and after the Act; true if the pre-Act figure is ~6.7% and the post-Act figure exceeds 18%, false if either figure is materially different.
reasoning: Both figures match the government's published numbers. DOC/official material states the Bill creates marine protection over 11.5% of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park on top of an existing 6.7% baseline (which counts the Submarine Cable Protection Zone), giving a total of ~18.2% — hence 'over 18 percent'. Most secondary coverage rounds this to '6% to 18%'. Disconfirming check: critics (Newsroom, LiveOcean, Greenpeace) argue the 6.7% baseline is inflated because the cable zone is not meaningful protection, and that truly no-take reserve area was under 0.5% before (rising to ~6% highly protected). That is a dispute about what counts as 'protected', not about whether the figures Marcroft quoted are DOC's published ones. Against the criterion as written — the pre-Act figure is ~6.7% and the post-Act figure exceeds 18% — the claim holds.

statement: The Government has already noted, and I note Matua Shane, Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, the Hon Shane Jones, has already taken steps to help protect the Hauraki Gulf and restore its mauri by having special permits available to go and smash up the kina.
criterion: Fisheries New Zealand / ministerial announcements and the special permit register under the Fisheries Act; true if special permits for kina removal in the Hauraki Gulf were issued or made available under Shane Jones as Minister, false if no such permit regime exists.
reasoning: The special permit regime exists and was created under Shane Jones as Minister for Oceans and Fisheries. Fisheries New Zealand consulted in 2024 on a new special permit purpose for targeted culling, harvest or translocation of kina and long-spined sea urchins from existing or at-risk kina barrens; Jones stated 'I introduced a new special permit purpose this year'. The first such permit was approved in November 2024 to the Te Kohuroa Rewilding Initiative for Te Kohuroa/Mathesons Bay in the Hauraki Gulf, with the first volunteer removal event on 16 November 2024. So permits were both available and actually issued in the Gulf before the 7 October 2025 statement. Disconfirming check: no evidence the regime was withdrawn or that the permits were confined outside the Gulf — the first approval was specifically a Hauraki Gulf site.

statement: So that has been done, and $15 million has already been put forward to deal with Caulerpa, which is that exotic invasive species which is causing a great concern right around the gulf and also up into Northland and down into the top of the Coromandel as well.
criterion: Budget documents and Biosecurity New Zealand / ministerial announcements on exotic Caulerpa funding; true if cumulative committed funding as at October 2025 is ~$15m, false if materially different.
reasoning: A $15m figure is real and traceable: $5m announced February 2024 plus $10m announced August 2024 under the Accelerated Programme, which MPI describes as 'more than $15m of government funding' for caulerpa surveillance, management and research (including the $6.2m to Northland Regional Council for suction dredging, announced February 2025). However, the criterion asks about cumulative committed funding as at October 2025, and MPI's own figure for the total caulerpa response is 'over $31 million' spent or allocated across research, surveillance, removal technique development, communications and legal controls. So $15m is an accurate name for one tranche but materially understates total committed funding — the error runs against the speaker's own interest rather than inflating the government's record. Substance (significant funding committed, exotic caulerpa affecting the Gulf, Northland and the Coromandel) holds; the specific total does not match cumulative spend.

statement: That flows out into the ocean, into the harbour, the Mahurangi Harbour, and so far just this year alone, the Mahurangi oyster farmers have had closures for 158 days due to sewage contamination being spilled by Watercare—a total of 4 million litres of sewage contamination being spilled into the Mahurangi River.
criterion: MPI/NZ Food Safety shellfish harvest closure notices for Mahurangi in 2025 and Watercare's reported overflow volumes for the Mahurangi River; true if closures total ~158 days and spill volume ~4 million litres, false if materially lower or higher.
reasoning: The closure-days figure holds; the volume figure is materially overstated. Aquaculture NZ's own data table (published 24 Oct 2025) records 2025-to-October as 32 spills, 180 closed days and 3,585 cubic metres, against 2023 (18 spills / 79 days / 1,055 m3) and 2024 (15 / 81 / 885). 158 closed days as at 7 October is consistent with 180 by 24 October. But 4 million litres = 4,000 m3, which exceeds the industry's full 1 Jan-24 Oct total of 3,585 m3; RNZ in September 2025 was reporting 'more than three million litres' for the year to date. The 1,200 m3 Lucy Moore Memorial Park pump-station spill that would have taken the annual total past 4,000 m3 did not occur until 29 October, three weeks after she spoke. Attribution to Watercare and to the Mahurangi River/Harbour is correct.

statement: The most recent spill was 50 cubic metres on 24 September.
criterion: Watercare / Auckland Council overflow incident reports for September 2025; true if a spill of ~50 m³ is recorded on 24 September 2025 at the Mahurangi site, false if no such incident or a materially different volume.
reasoning: The criterion points to Watercare / Auckland Council overflow incident reports for September 2025, but no itemised public overflow register for the Mahurangi/Warkworth network is published online, and the Auckland Council Mahurangi Harbour water-quality page returns HTTP 406 to automated retrieval. Media coverage documents only the large incidents by date and volume: ~1,200 m3 at Lucy Moore Memorial Park on 29 October 2025 and ~86 m3 at Elizabeth Street on 18 November 2025. No source found either confirms or excludes a ~50 m3 overflow on 24 September 2025. A spill of that size in late September is fully consistent with the 32 spills recorded for 2025, and small overflows of that magnitude are not individually reported in news coverage, so the absence of a public record is not evidence the spill did not happen.

statement: It was in 1975 that Cape Rodney-Okakari Point was set up as a marine reserve, so this year we celebrate 50 years of this marine reserve, and I would be very pleased to receive an invitation from Ngāti Manuhiri as they conduct the celebrations in November.
criterion: The New Zealand Gazette notice and DOC records for the Cape Rodney-Okakari Point Marine Reserve; true if established/gazetted in 1975, false if a different year.
reasoning: DOC's marine reserve report card and its places-to-go page both state that Cape Rodney-Okakari Point was New Zealand's first marine reserve, created in 1975, which makes 2025 its 50th year. The 50th anniversary was in fact marked by Ngati Manuhiri Settlement Trust with a dawn ceremony at Te Hawere-a-Maki / Goat Island, confirming both the anniversary year and Ngati Manuhiri's role as hosts. One detail outside the criterion: the reported ceremony appears to have been held in October 2025 rather than November, though Marcroft was speaking prospectively about an invitation, not asserting a completed event.

statement: Today, eight of those beaches are currently closed due to waste-water overflows.
criterion: Safeswim / Auckland Council beach status records for 7 October 2025; true if eight of the beaches she names were flagged closed for waste-water contamination that day, false if fewer or the cause was different.
reasoning: The criterion requires Safeswim/Auckland Council beach status records for 7 October 2025. Safeswim publishes only live status and no publicly retrievable historical daily flag record; the site is a JS map app that does not render to fetch, and web.archive.org was not reachable from this environment. No news coverage of Auckland beach closures on 6-8 October 2025 was found either. Context is consistent with the claim but does not confirm it: the eight beaches she names (Orakei Basin, Hobson Bay, Judges Bay, Herne Bay, Home Bay, Island Bay, Milford, Milford South) are precisely the sites carrying chronic/long-term wastewater black flags - Auckland Council advises not swimming in Hobson Bay or the Orakei Basin streams 'at any time at present', and Herne Bay, Home Bay and Judges Bay are repeatedly black-flagged for wastewater overflow, with Milford/Milford South closed for wastewater overflows on past occasions. The debate date checks out (the Hauraki Gulf / Tikapa Moana Marine Protection Bill third reading was 7-8 October 2025; Scoop republished the Hansard in January 2026). Absence of a retrievable Safeswim record for that day is not evidence the claim is false.

statement: If I just go back a few months to 11 May, 64 beaches were either black or red flagged for waste contamination.
criterion: Safeswim historical records for 11 May 2025; true if 64 beaches were black- or red-flagged for waste contamination that day, false if the count is materially different.
reasoning: The NZ Herald published an article dated 11 May 2025 headlined 'Safeswim red and black flags: 64 Auckland beaches unsafe to swim at due to faecal contamination', reporting that Safeswim had black-flagged 34 beaches and red-flagged a further 28 across the region, following heavy rain two days earlier; Safeswim attributed the contamination to wastewater overflows (sewage spilling from gully traps, manholes, engineered overflow points or pump stations). The date, the count (64), the black/red flag framing and the waste-contamination cause all match Marcroft's statement. The one wrinkle is internal to the source: 34 + 28 = 62, so the headline figure of 64 that she repeats is two higher than the article's own breakdown - not a material difference, and she is accurately citing the reported number.

statement: They were normally around two per annum and they’re now up to 200 discharges that Watercare can make into the Mahurangi River.
criterion: The Auckland Council resource consent granted to Watercare in 2022 (alternative discharge frequency) and the prior consent conditions; true if permitted discharge frequency for the Mahurangi River rose from ~2 to ~200 per annum, false if the consented numbers differ materially.
reasoning: The criterion points at the Auckland Council network discharge consent (NDC) and its alternative discharge frequency. The NDC framework checks out on the '2' end: it authorises an average of two wet-weather spills per year at each engineered overflow point, or an 'alternative discharge frequency' (ADF) where justified by a Best Practicable Option process. But the '200' does not. RNZ reporting on the Mahurangi dispute states that Watercare had a target of two wet-weather overflows a year at its Elizabeth Street EOP in Warkworth - the point discharging to the Mahurangi River - 'but its consent allowed 20.5 discharges', an average of 20.5 wet-weather discharges per year on a five-year rolling average, and that this is what outraged the oyster growers. The '200 annually per discharge point' figure traces to an Aquaculture New Zealand advocacy article (which also reports the heavy-rainfall trigger being reclassified from 20mm to 10mm); no source I found corroborates 200 against the consent itself. So the substance holds - the consented overflow frequency for this discharge point was raised roughly tenfold above the two-per-year standard, without the oyster farmers being consulted - but the headline number is overstated by about an order of magnitude (20.5, not 200). Caveat: I could not open the consent document itself (the Auckland-wide NDC annual report PDF exceeded the fetch size limit), so both the 20.5 and the 200 rest on secondary reporting; the 20.5 is Watercare's own stated figure as reported by RNZ, the 200 is the industry body's.

statement: Now, those changes actually stipulated in the Minister of Conservation’s very own words, in his own Cabinet paper, that the ring-net fishers, who will still be able to fish in two of the high protection areas, could have fished in other parts, with minimal impact on them.
criterion: The Minister of Conservation's Cabinet paper on the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill amendments (proactively released on the DOC/Cabinet Office website); true if the paper states that the affected ring-net fishers could fish in other areas with minimal or low impact on them, false if it contains no such assessment or states the opposite.
reasoning: The Minister of Conservation's Cabinet paper (Office of the Minister of Conservation to the Cabinet Legislation Committee, 'Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill', proactively released by DOC, footer-dated 2024-10-16) states at paragraph 49: 'Based on the nature and current distribution of ring-net fishing activities in the Gulf, it is likely that ring-net fishing activity that usually occurs within these HPAs could be relocated elsewhere in the Gulf with minimal impact to the fishers.' That is the assessment the criterion asks for, in the Minister's own paper, and it is not contradicted elsewhere in the document. The paper's recommendation 15 provides for ring-net fishing in the Kawau Bay and Rangitoto and Motutapu HPAs — two high protection areas, matching Boyack's 'two of the high protection areas' (some media reporting said three; the Cabinet paper, the Amendment Paper recommendations and the enacted regime say two). Checked for disconfirming material: paragraphs 53-55 note the provision would benefit six ring-net fishers catching ~16 tonnes/year in these areas and that there would be significant opposition, but nothing walks back or qualifies the para 49 'minimal impact to the fishers' finding.

statement: They promised to accelerate it; instead, it has sat here on the Order Paper for two years while eleventh hour changes were made.
criterion: The NZ Parliament bill-progress record for the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill (introduction, first reading, select committee report-back and third reading dates) plus ministerial statements on progressing the bill; true if a ministerial/coalition commitment to accelerate it exists and the elapsed time between report-back or first reading and this debate is around two years, false if no such commitment exists or the delay is materially shorter.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are met. (1) The commitment to accelerate exists and is documented in the government's own words: paragraph 2 of the Minister of Conservation's Cabinet paper reads 'The National Party Blueprint for a Better Environment states that the National Party will accelerate initiatives like the Hauraki Gulf Marine Protection.' The Hauraki Gulf Forum's Gulf Journal independently records that National's 'Blueprint for a Better Environment' election manifesto 'pledged not only to pass the Bill but to accelerate its progress.' (2) Elapsed time: the Bill was introduced 22 August 2023, first reading 30 August 2023, Environment Committee report-back 20 June 2024, second reading 18 December 2024, committee of the whole House August 2025, third reading 7 October 2025 — 2 years 1 month from first reading to the debate in which she spoke, so 'two years' is accurate rather than materially overstated. The 'eleventh hour changes' also check out: the ring-net exemption was introduced by Amendment Paper at the committee of the whole House stage, after select committee had recommended against providing for it (Cabinet paper para 57). The only softening note is rhetorical — the Bill was not idle the whole time, spending its first ten months at select committee — but that does not affect the elapsed-time or promise claims the criterion tests.

statement: I want to remind the House, while the Minister is here, that, as far as I am aware, the Gazette notices to finalise that South-East Marine Protection areas has not yet been undertaken, and, and I hope that it is very soon.
criterion: The New Zealand Gazette record for marine reserve / marine protected area notices arising from the South-East Marine Protection Forum recommendations; true if no such gazettal appears on or before 7 October 2025, false if a finalising Gazette notice was published before that date.
reasoning: DOC's own page on the south-east South Island marine reserves records that five of the six reserves arising from the South-East Marine Protection Forum process were gazetted on 28 May 2026 and came into effect 1 July 2026; the sixth (Te Umukōau) was not gazetted as planned, its boundary going to limited reconsideration following judicial review proceedings resolved on 12 December 2025. The reserves had been announced by the Minister of Conservation in October 2023 but remained ungazetted throughout 2025. I looked specifically for an earlier gazettal that would falsify the claim (the Forum reported in Feb 2018, consultation ran 2020, announcement Oct 2023) and found none before 7 October 2025 — the judicial review still live in late 2025 is itself consistent with nothing having been finalised. Brooking's statement that the Gazette notices had not yet been undertaken as at 7 October 2025 is correct; her hope that it would be 'very soon' was not borne out, the gazettal coming roughly eight months later.

statement: During the committee of the whole House, Te Pāti Māori tabled amendments aimed at ensuring that there is a mandatory consultation process when giving permits, ensuring that the process requires consultation with mana whenua.
criterion: Hansard and the Supplementary Order Papers for the committee of the whole House stage of the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill; true if Te Pāti Māori tabled amendments of that effect, false if none appear.
reasoning: Independent reporting on the committee of the whole House stage confirms Te Pāti Māori put up amendments requiring mandatory mana whenua consultation in the permit process, and that they were not adopted. Greenpeace Aotearoa's account of the Act states plainly that "Te Pāti Māori was disappointed that amendments designed to ensure mandatory consultation with mana whenua/iwi were not adopted", and Aotea Great Barrier Island News (9 Oct 2025) quotes Maipi-Clarke outside the House: "Our amendments were designed to ensure mana whenua have input into these applications for permits". Both are independent of the Hansard passage being checked. Caveat: the Amendment Paper / SOP itself on parliament.nz and bills.parliament.nz could not be inspected directly — both are behind Radware bot protection — so the corroboration is contemporaneous reporting of the committee stage rather than the tabled paper. I looked for the opposite (that the amendments were never moved, or were moved by the Greens rather than Te Pāti Māori) and found no source suggesting either.

statement: So we have a situation where we know that the gulf was lined with mussels.
criterion: Historical fisheries records and NIWA/peer-reviewed studies of the pre-1960s extent of green-lipped mussel beds in the Hauraki Gulf and Firth of Thames; true if extensive subtidal mussel beds are documented across the gulf before the dredge fishery, false if the beds were localised or absent.
reasoning: The criterion's named evidence base supports the claim. The government report the criterion points to — Paul, L.J. (2012), "A history of the Firth of Thames dredge fishery for mussels: use and abuse of a coastal resource", NZ Aquatic Environment and Biodiversity Report No. 94 (MPI) — is the standard reference, and independent secondary accounts converge on the same picture: subtidal green-lipped mussel beds covering roughly 500 km² (Mahurangi Magazine, sourced to Dr Andrew Jeffs) to ~1,000 km² (Pūkorokoro Miranda Shorebird Centre, drawing on State of our Gulf 2017) of the inner Gulf and Firth of Thames, dense on soft sediments to ~30 m depth, dredged out between the mid-1920s and mid-1960s and never regenerating. The criterion's falsifying condition is that the beds were "localised or absent"; 500–1,000 km² is the opposite of localised. Minor overstatement in the rhetoric — the beds were concentrated in the inner Gulf and Firth rather than blanketing the entire marine park including outer and deeper waters — but that is well within what "extensive subtidal mussel beds across the gulf" allows.

statement: There was already overflow from Warkworth and we didn’t do enough about it.
criterion: Watercare and Auckland Council consent-compliance and overflow records for the Warkworth wastewater treatment plant and network over the 2010s; true if recorded wastewater overflows into the Mahurangi catchment predate the statement by roughly a decade, false if no such overflows are on record.
reasoning: Wastewater overflows from Warkworth into the Mahurangi catchment are on record well beyond the decade the criterion asks for. Mahurangi Magazine (Dec 2015) documents that before the 1974 plant the town's septic tanks left the work to the river and that in heavy rain "raw sewage would erupt from manholes in the town's main street and flow into the river via the storm water drains"; that a 1975 special tribunal accepted the river downstream of Warkworth as the plant's "buffer zone" for final oxidation; that the plant thereafter "would periodically fail to comply with its strict water right conditions"; and that an Actiflo peak-flow system was retrofitted in 2008 after 34 years of the problem. Within the 2010s specifically, the Elizabeth St site is a consented overflow point under Watercare's Regional Network Discharge Consent, which permits an average of 20.5 wet-weather discharges a year on a five-year rolling average — i.e. overflows are a recorded, ongoing feature of the network, not isolated incidents. Local Matters (Oct 2024) reports oyster growers closed 81 days in 2023 and up to 70 days by Oct 2024, with the dispute described elsewhere as seven years old as of 2025. The "we didn't do enough about it" half is an evaluative judgement rather than a checkable fact, but the factual core — overflow was already happening, long before the statement — holds. Direct fetches of the RNZ, Newsroom and Auckland Council pages were blocked (403/406), so the 2010s consent-compliance records themselves were reached through reporting rather than the council database.

statement: That fisheries plan was looking at excluding from bottom trawling 74 percent to 89 percent of the gulf.
criterion: The 2023 Fisheries New Zealand / MPI Hauraki Gulf fisheries plan and bottom-trawling consultation documents; true if the proposed exclusion options span roughly 74–89% of the gulf area, false if the documented options give materially different percentages.
reasoning: The 2023 MPI/Fisheries NZ consultation on bottom fishing access zones (trawl corridors) in the Hauraki Gulf proposed four options, closing 74.1% (Danish seine) to 89% (trawl) of the gulf to those methods: Option 1 74.1/77.1%, Option 2 79.4/82.4%, Option 3 86.6/88.5%, Option 4 87.3/89%. The documented range matches the quoted 74-89% exactly. Minor imprecision: MPI's percentages are of the gulf shallower than 200m, while the speaker said 'of the gulf' - but DOC's own media release used the same unqualified framing ('up to 89 per cent of the marine park'), so this is ordinary paraphrase rather than a material overstatement.

statement: In May of this year, the current Minister for Oceans and Fisheries shelved those plans, and I want the other side of the House to really think about that, because we’ve heard in a number of these speeches and we see from all these reports that the Hauraki Gulf is protecting bits of the Hauraki Gulf.
criterion: Ministerial announcements, MPI/Fisheries New Zealand decision documents and contemporaneous reporting from May 2025; true if the Minister announced in that month that the Hauraki Gulf bottom-trawling exclusion proposals would not proceed, false if no such decision was taken in May 2025 or the proposals remained live.
reasoning: On 12 May 2025 Minister for Oceans and Fisheries Shane Jones confirmed the Hauraki Gulf trawl corridor proposals would not proceed ('I'm not giving that a priority in the small part of the government's work programme that I'm responsible for'), reported by Newsroom on 14 May 2025 and by the NZ Sport Fishing Council. Checked for the opposite: the proposals did not remain live - in June 2025 Jones further confirmed the Government would not progress any Hauraki Gulf bottom-trawling closures this term. Some bottom-trawling restrictions continue via the separate Hauraki Gulf/Tikapa Moana Marine Protection Bill, which is the distinct measure under debate. Both the month (May 2025) and the substance (exclusion proposals shelved) hold. Caveat on sourcing: newsroom.co.nz and nzsportfishing.co.nz returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch, so this rests on consistent search-index extracts of both pages rather than full page reads.

statement: This has been a decade in the making—in fact, I would argue, at least 25 years in the making, when you reflect back on the landmark legislation that was the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act 2000, which among other things created the Hauraki Gulf Forum, of course affectionately known as the “Guardians of the Gulf”.
criterion: The text of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act 2000 on legislation.govt.nz; true if the Act constitutes the Hauraki Gulf Forum, false if the Forum was created by some other instrument or predates the Act.
reasoning: Section 16 of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act 2000 is headed 'Establishment of Forum' and provides that a body called the Hauraki Gulf Forum is established; Part 2 of the Act is titled 'Hauraki Gulf Forum'. Auckland Council, DOC and the Forum itself all describe the Forum as a statutory body established under the Act. Disconfirming check: the Act's preamble refers to 'the establishment by local authorities of the Hauraki Gulf Forum', and local authorities had been meeting under that name in the late 1990s, so a non-statutory predecessor of the same name existed. That nuance does not defeat the claim - the Forum as it exists is constituted by s16 of the Act, not by any other instrument. Caveat on sourcing: legislation.govt.nz returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch, so the s16 text rests on the search index's rendering of that page's title and content.

statement: This is a major win for the environment, a major win for Auckland, and it’s this Government that’s delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf.
criterion: The area and legal strength of marine protection created by the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill compared with pre-existing protections (Cape Rodney–Okakari Point and Whanganui A Hei marine reserves, cable protection zones, the 2000 Marine Park Act); true if the bill's protected area materially exceeds the prior total, false if prior protections equal or exceed it.
reasoning: DOC states the Act increased marine protection in the Hauraki Gulf from 0.3% to 5.9% (excluding the Cable Protection Zone); EDS gives 0.3% to ~6% for high protection, and total 'some form of protection' rose from 6% to ~18% of the 1.2m ha Marine Park. The pre-existing protections named in the criterion (Cape Rodney-Okakari Point and Te Whanganui-A-Hei marine reserves) constituted that 0.3% baseline and are themselves extended by the Act, so the new protected area materially exceeds the prior total by roughly twentyfold. Caveat not fatal to the criterion: the 12 new HPAs are legally weaker than marine reserve status (authorised customary fishing; commercial ring-netting allowed in two HPAs until 2028), which critics argue dilutes 'protection'.

statement: In November 2020, the High Court ruled that regulations 26 and 27 of the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 and the associated minimum standards in the Code of Welfare: Pigs 2018 were unlawful and invalid.
criterion: The New Zealand High Court judgment in the 2020 judicial review brought by the New Zealand Animal Law Association and SAFE against the Attorney-General/Minister of Agriculture. True if the judgment is dated November 2020 and declares regs 26 and 27 and the associated pigs-code minimum standards unlawful and invalid; false if the date, the provisions, or the finding differ materially.
reasoning: MPI's Regulatory Impact Statement (16 July 2025), para 18, states: 'In November 2020, the High Court of New Zealand found ... The High Court held that Regulations 26 and 27 and the associated minimum standards in the Pigs' Code allowed practices that fall short of the sections 10 and 11 obligations in the Act to continue indefinitely ... Those provisions were thereby found to be invalid.' The case is NZ Animal Law Association (with SAFE) v Attorney-General, Cull J, November 2020; the affected standards were minimum standards 10 and 11 of the Code of Welfare: Pigs 2018. Reported day-of-month differs between secondary sources (13 vs 26 November 2020), but month, provisions and finding all match the criterion as written.

statement: There are fewer than 80 farms, with around 45 indoor piggeries.
criterion: MPI or New Zealand Pork published counts of commercial pig farms and indoor piggeries for 2025. True if the total commercial farm count is below 80 and the indoor count is near 45; false if either figure is materially different.
reasoning: MPI's Regulatory Impact Statement (16 July 2025), para 14: 'New Zealand's pork industry is made up of around 70-80 commercial farms producing about 600,000 pigs annually. Around 55 percent of these pigs are produced in indoor facilities. We estimate there are around 44 commercial indoor piggeries.' Figures drawn from NZ Pork's 2024 Annual Report and Stats NZ's Business Demography Survey. Hoggard's 'fewer than 80' matches the official 70-80 range (which tops out at 80 rather than sitting strictly below it) and '45 indoor piggeries' matches MPI's estimate of 44. Neither difference is material.

statement: That’s the fundamental thing that this bill does: it delays the legislated action to bring an end to the cruel use of farrowing crates by 10 years.
criterion: The text of the Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill and the commencement dates in the regulations it replaces. True if the bill moves the operative phase-out date roughly a decade beyond the existing 18 December 2025 deadline; false if the delay is materially shorter or the phase-out is not deferred.
reasoning: The Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill 207-1 (2025) extends the transition period for farrowing crates and mating stalls from the existing 18 December 2025 deadline (set by Cabinet in December 2020 after the High Court held regs 26 and 27 unlawful) to 18 December 2035 — exactly ten years, matching the criterion's 'roughly a decade beyond'. Contemporaneous coverage (Pig Progress, RNZ, SAFE, NZALA) all describe it as a 10-year extension. Checked for the disconfirming reading: critics argue the bill enables indefinite crate use, which would be a longer deferral, not a shorter one, so the claim is not overstated in either direction.

statement: Guess who advised against that! The National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, the very advisers to the Minister.
criterion: NAWAC's advice and recommendations to the Minister on the pig code of welfare and minimum space allowances, as published or released under the OIA. True if NAWAC recommended against the space allowance adopted in the bill; false if NAWAC supported it or gave no such advice.
reasoning: The Hansard context shows 'that' refers to the 13 percent space increase for mother pigs Abel had just described. Documents released in October 2025 show NAWAC chairperson Matthew Stone advised Minister Hoggard that the 13.3 percent space increase for growing pigs was not enough; NAWAC's own proposed code had recommended increases of 56 percent or 140 percent. Stone also said he was 'not satisfied' that up-to-three-day pre-farrowing confinement with no change to farrowing pen space design/allocation would let sows fulfil nesting behaviour, that current practice fell 'below the minimum standards' in the Act, and that regulations not addressing both issues would 'not meet the purpose of the Act and therefore be likely to result in continued legal challenge'. So NAWAC — the Minister's statutory advisers — did recommend against the space allowance adopted. Disconfirming check: no evidence NAWAC endorsed the 13.3 percent figure or stayed silent. Sources differ on whether the concerns were raised April 2024 or April 2025, but either date precedes the 1 October 2025 announcement, so it does not affect the verdict.

statement: It’s utterly unnecessary, because half of New Zealand pig farmers are already doing it like this, letting the pigs live a natural existence where they get to nurse their young and express their natural behaviours.
criterion: NZ Pork or MPI figures on the proportion of New Zealand commercial pig farmers (or pigs farmed) using free-farrowing rather than farrowing crates. True if the share is around 50 percent; false if materially lower.
reasoning: SPCA states 'Around 45% of New Zealand pig farms already farrow without crates.' NZ Pork's own 2021 breakdown (reproduced by AHDB) gives 55% of the commercial herd indoors, 42% free farmed and 3% free range — 45% outside the indoor/crate system, so the figure holds both by farms and by share of pigs. The criterion asks whether the share is 'around 50 percent'; 45 percent is around half and not materially lower. Abel's gloss (sows nursing young outdoors, expressing natural behaviours) fairly describes free-farmed/free-range hut systems. Disconfirming check: the higher 2022 figure of 'up to 60 percent' of farmers using crates still leaves roughly 40 percent crate-free, which does not overturn 'half' as a rounding.

statement: The new confinement period, totalling seven days, is a significant reduction from the current 33-day setting, and will be amongst the lowest in the world, with most countries we currently import pork from allowing their use for 33 days.
criterion: Reg 26 of the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 for the 33-day New Zealand figure; and, for the comparison, the farrowing-crate rules of New Zealand's main pork-import sources (Stats NZ import-origin data, then EU Directive 2008/120/EC and the corresponding US/Canadian rules). True if the New Zealand limit is 33 days and the majority of import-source countries permit confinement of about that length or longer; false if the New Zealand figure is wrong or if most import sources permit materially shorter confinement.
reasoning: NZ's 33-day figure is correct: reg 26 of the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 (reg 26 as replaced by the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Amendment Regulations (No 2) 2020) permits confinement in a farrowing crate for up to 5 days before farrowing plus up to 4 weeks (28 days) after farrowing = 33 days; NZ Pork independently describes the NZ maximum as 'up to five days pre-farrowing' and 'a maximum of 28 days ... after giving birth'. The Bill's new period is 3 days before + 4 days after = 7 days, matching 'totalling seven days'. On the import comparison: NZ's main pork import sources are the United States, Canada, Spain, Germany and Poland. EU countries operate under Directive 2008/120/EC, which sets no time limit on farrowing-crate confinement (crating is permitted from about a week before farrowing until weaning, and minimum weaning age is 28 days, so >=35 days); the US has no federal limit; Canada permits up to six weeks. So the large majority of import-source countries permit confinement of at least 33 days or materially longer — if anything Hoggard understated the gap by saying '33 days' rather than 'no limit'. I checked for disconfirming evidence — countries with materially shorter limits (Sweden, Norway, Switzerland ban crates; Germany 5 days and Austria from 2033) are not significant sources of NZ pork imports, and Germany's 5-day rule does not take effect until 2036, so German pork currently comes from full-lactation crating. 'Amongst the lowest in the world' is also defensible at 7 days. Caveat outside the criterion: the 7-day limit does not commence until 18 December 2035.

statement: In 2018, the then Minister of Agriculture issued regulations and minimum standards, which allowed farrowing crates. There was a judicial review following that, which found it was a breach of the Animal Welfare Act. Following that, the Labour Government put in place regulations to phase out farrowing crates by 18 December 2025.
criterion: The 2018 Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations and the pig code of welfare as gazetted; the High Court judgment in the judicial review brought over farrowing crates (NZALA/SAFE v Attorney-General); and the commencement/expiry dates in the subsequent phase-out regulations. True if the regulations were made in 2018, the court held them unlawful under the Animal Welfare Act, and the replacement regulations set 18 December 2025; false if any of the three dates or findings differ materially.
reasoning: All three elements check out against the criterion. (1) The Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 (LI 2018/50) and the Code of Welfare: Pigs 2018 were made/issued in 2018 under then Minister of Agriculture Damien O'Connor, and regs 26-27 plus the code's minimum standards 10 and 11 permitted farrowing crates and mating stalls. (2) In the judicial review brought by the NZ Animal Law Association and SAFE against the Attorney-General, the Minister and NAWAC, the High Court (Cull J, judgment released 13 November 2020) held the regulations and minimum standards circumvented Parliament's intent in the Animal Welfare Amendment Act (No 2) 2015, were contrary to the purposes of the Animal Welfare Act 1999, and were unlawful and invalid — i.e. a breach of the Act, as Boyack said. (3) The replacement regulations, the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Amendment Regulations (No 2) 2020, made under the Labour government and in force from 18 December 2020, replaced regs 26 and 27 with a five-year phase-out: reg 26 was to be revoked on 18 December 2025. NZALA's own account states 'the previous Government agreed to and publicly consulted on new regulations with tighter restrictions and a five-year phase out period. That phase out period was to end on 18 December 2025.' Only minor technical imprecision: regulations are made by the Governor-General in Council on the Minister's recommendation rather than 'issued' by the Minister, and the minimum standards sit in the NAWAC-recommended code — not material to the substance.

statement: He’s going to increase the minimum spacing requirements by 13.3 percent—the exact proposal from New Zealand Pork.
criterion: The minimum space allowance in the bill/draft regulations compared with the existing standard, and NZ Pork's submission or advice to the Minister. True if the increase is 13.3 percent and NZ Pork proposed that same figure; false if the increase differs or NZ Pork's proposal was for a different figure.
reasoning: Both halves of the claim hold. The Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill increases the minimum lying-space requirement for grower pigs by raising the k value in the space-allowance formula from 0.03 to 0.034, which the Cabinet paper for the Bill describes as a 13.3 percent increase (0.034/0.03 = 1.1333). NZ Pork's submission on the proposed Code of Welfare for Pigs proposed exactly that figure: a k value of 0.034. The alternatives on the table were materially different — NAWAC's proposed minimum standard used k=0.04 (about 23 percent more space) and MPI proposed k=0.036 (about 16 percent) — so the adopted figure is specifically the industry body's number rather than the regulator's or the advisory committee's, which is what 'the exact proposal from New Zealand Pork' asserts. I checked the disconfirming reading: NZ Pork elsewhere characterised k=0.034 as '9 per cent more space than current practice', but that compares against actual on-farm practice, not the regulated minimum, and does not contradict the 13.3 percent regulatory increase Boyack referred to.

statement: I stand to speak on the Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill and I just want to point out that, actually, we’ve lost a large number of our pork producers over the last three or four decades.
criterion: Stats NZ agricultural production statistics and NZ Pork's count of commercial pig farms, comparing the mid-1980s/1990s with 2025. True if the number of commercial producers has fallen substantially; false if it has been broadly stable or risen.
reasoning: Commercial pig farm numbers have fallen steeply. Industry/NZ Pork-sourced reporting: ~600 commercial farms in 2001 down to 70-80 producing ~600,000 pigs today, with 58 PigCare-certified farms as at 1 Nov 2025. Te Ara records that the number of specialist pig farms more than halved between 1990 and 2002, and that ~360 pig farms with 40,000 breeding sows existed in 2007 against a breeding sow herd now under 29,000 (AHDB). Checked for the opposite (stability or growth) and found no series showing it. 'A large number lost over three or four decades' is well supported.

statement: We, at the moment, in New Zealand import 60 percent of all our pork products from Canada or from the US or from over in Europe.
criterion: MPI/Stats NZ pork trade and consumption data on the imported share of pork consumed in New Zealand and the countries of origin. True if imports account for around 60 percent and the named countries are the main sources; false if the share is materially different.
reasoning: NZ Pork states 'approximately 60% of the pork consumed in New Zealand comes from overseas'; Farmers Weekly reports nearly 62% for Jan-Sep 2024 (66,686 CWE tonnes imported vs 41,099 tonnes domestic). Origins match the ones named: the US and Canada were the two largest single sources in 2024, with Spain, Germany, Poland, Denmark and Finland the bulk of the remainder (those European suppliers plus Canada/US were ~98% of imports in 2022). Minor slack only: Australia also features, and the figure is a share of pork consumed rather than literally 'all our pork products'.

statement: Just briefly to go back through history, the Animal Welfare Act was passed in 1999 by a visionary Government, a National Government actually, that saw the importance of animal welfare moving forward.
criterion: NZ legislation record for the Animal Welfare Act 1999 (date of Royal assent) and the party in government on that date; true if the Act was passed in 1999 under a National-led administration, false if the year or the governing party differs.
reasoning: Animal Welfare Act 1999, Public Act 1999 No 142, received Royal assent on 14 October 1999 and came into force 1 January 2000. On that date the Fourth National Government (PM Jenny Shipley, in office 8 Dec 1997 - 10 Dec 1999) was in power; the 1999 general election was 27 November 1999. Both elements of the criterion - year and governing party - check out.

statement: The National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, which is an independent committee, came up with a code of practice, a code of welfare, for pigs in 2010, again under a National-led Government.
criterion: MPI/NAWAC publication record for the Code of Welfare (Pigs); true if a code was issued in 2010 while a National-led government held office, false if the code carries a different year or the government of the day was different.
reasoning: NAWAC completed its review of the 2005 pigs code and the Animal Welfare (Pigs) Code of Welfare 2010 was released by Minister of Agriculture David Carter in December 2010 (Beehive release 'New pig welfare code to phase out sow stalls'), phasing dry sow stalls out by December 2015. MPI document titles confirm the code carries the year 2010. The John Key National-led government was in office from November 2008 to 2017, so the government of the day matches. Minor imprecision only in mechanism: NAWAC recommends and the Minister issues the code, which is substantively what O'Connor described.

statement: Of course, as has been said before, about 60 percent of the pork we consume comes from offshore.
criterion: Stats NZ import data and NZ Pork / MPI figures on domestic pork production versus imports for a recent year; true if imports are around 60 percent of consumption, false if materially different (e.g. below 50 or above 70 percent).
reasoning: NZ Pork's own figures put imports at approximately 60 percent of pork consumed in New Zealand (NZ Pork CEO, quoted in NZ Herald), with nearly 62 percent recorded for Jan-Sep 2024, 'almost two thirds' for 2022, and 63 percent reported in early 2026. Every figure found sits inside the criterion's 50-70 percent band; the true value is if anything slightly above 60, so 'about 60 percent' is not overstated in the speaker's favour.

statement: But we’ve also heard that the SPCA—not known, you know, to be a hugely radical group—has not been consulted by this Minister.
criterion: The bill's consultation record / departmental disclosure statement, plus any SPCA public statement or select committee submission on whether it was consulted; true if the SPCA was not approached on the pig welfare regulations, false if consultation records show it was.
reasoning: SPCA stated publicly on 2 October 2025 - five days before Brooking spoke - that it 'has not been engaged in any consultation on farrowing crate standards under the current Government', with Chief Scientific Officer Dr Arnja Dale asking who the Minister and MPI did consult. Farmers Weekly (30 October 2025) independently confirmed via SPCA's Marie McAninch that 'the SPCA was not included in the targeted consultation on the changes', while NZ Pork had eight meetings with government. Checking for disconfirming evidence: Minister Hoggard asserted 'key stakeholders' were consulted, but no source places SPCA among them, and SPCA's select committee submission on the Bill criticises the process.

statement: In fact, these new requirements in the bill will be among the highest animal welfare standards in the world.
criterion: Compare the bill's requirements on mating stalls and farrowing crates (and their commencement dates) against pig welfare rules in the EU, UK, Sweden, Norway and Switzerland; true if New Zealand's requirements are at least as strict and take effect on comparable timeframes, false if jurisdictions already prohibit the practices the bill continues to permit.
reasoning: The criterion's explicit false-trigger fires. The bill's new limits (sow in a farrowing crate for a maximum of 7 days with nest-building material; mating stall confinement cut from 7 days to 3 hours at a time) do not commence until 19 December 2035, and the bill extends the existing regulations' transition period from 18 December 2025 to 18 December 2035 - a ten-year extension of the status quo that a 2020 High Court ruling had found unlawful. Meanwhile Sweden (ban 1987, phased in by 1994), Switzerland (1997, phased in by 2007) and Norway (2000) already prohibit farrowing crates outright, so three of the five named comparators already ban the practice this bill continues to permit, on timeframes 25-45 years earlier. Partial merit that stops this short of the whole story: once in force, a 7-day cap would be stricter than the EU, which under Directive 2008/120/EC places no time limit on farrowing crates and permits individual stalls from weaning to four weeks after service, and stricter than the UK as it stood on 7 October 2025 (England announced a farrowing crate ban only in December 2025). So NZ's 2035 rules would exceed the EU/UK baseline but fall well short of the Swedish/Norwegian/Swiss standard, and do not take effect on remotely comparable timeframes. 'Will be among the highest in the world' does not survive the criterion as written.

statement: The committee received 210 written submissions, a relatively modest number in comparison to when Te Pūkenga was set up—I believe, from memory, there were about 2,000 submissions back then.
criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill states the number of written submissions received; the corresponding select committee report on the Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Bill 2019 states its submission count. True if the reported figures are 210 and approximately 2,000 respectively; false if either is materially different.
reasoning: The first figure is exactly right: the Education and Workforce Committee received 210 written submissions on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill and heard from 32 submitters. The second is materially wrong on the comparison she actually drew. The select committee commentary on the 2019 Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Bill - the bill that set up Te Pukenga - records 236 submissions received and considered, with oral evidence from 71 submitters at hearings in Dunedin and Wellington. That is roughly one-eighth of 'about 2,000', not approximately equal to it. A figure near her number does exist, but for a different process: the Ministry of Education/TEC public consultation on the Reform of Vocational Education (Feb-Apr 2019) drew over 2,500 submissions. So the claim is true only under a reading she did not signal - she framed it as committee-submissions-then versus committee-submissions-now ('the committee received 210 ... in comparison to when Te Pukenga was set up'), and on that like-for-like basis the number is off by about 8x. She did hedge with 'from memory'. Caveat on sourcing: legislation.govt.nz returns HTTP 403 to my fetcher, so the 236 figure comes from search-engine extraction of the 170-2 committee commentary on that page, reproduced consistently across two independent queries, rather than a direct read of the page.

statement: Without exception, they have all been pleased and relieved that they are getting their polytechnics back in their regions.
criterion: Public statements, submissions to the Education and Workforce Committee, and media reporting from the councils, executives and community leaders of the 10 ITPs being stood up. True if none of those met recorded opposition or misgivings about the split from Te Pūkenga; false if any of them publicly expressed concern (for example over the financial viability of a standalone regional polytechnic).
reasoning: The criterion fails if any of the 10 ITPs' councils, executives or community leaders publicly expressed concern or misgivings, including over the viability of a standalone regional polytechnic. At least one did, on the record, three months before the speech. Otago Polytechnic - confirmed as one of the 10 being re-established from 1 January 2026 in the Ministry of Education's announcement - issued a release on 14 July 2025 headed 'Otago Polytechnic to stand alone but deep concerns over federation', in which executive director Megan Potiki said the institution was 'deeply disappointed' to be placed in the Open Polytechnic-anchored federation, that 'the federation model risks undermining our learner success rates and the quality of teaching at Otago Polytechnic', that it would 'dilute this offering and impact our organisation's proud reputation', and that the arrangement risked its independence and future viability as a regional institution. She sought further clarification from the Minister on local governance. Consultants' reports around the same period put the restart cost at about $190m against a minimum $177m set aside, and Otago was carrying roughly $16m of debt with a required pathway to recovery - the financial-viability misgiving the criterion names. In fairness to the speaker, Otago's grievance was about the federation structure rather than about regional autonomy as such, and it did want to stand alone; but 'without exception, they have all been pleased and relieved' is an absolute claim, and a named executive of one of the 10 publicly recording deep concern about the arrangement defeats it. I checked for the opposite as well - genuine welcoming statements from regional leaders do exist - but they do not make the set exceptionless.

statement: Only 11 percent of submitters supported this bill.
criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee report and the Ministry of Education departmental report on submissions to the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if the tallied share of submitters expressing support is approximately 11%, false if the recorded share is materially different.
reasoning: The procedural facts are confirmed: the Education and Workforce Committee received 210 written submissions and heard from 32 submitters, reporting back 22 September 2025. But the specific 11% tally could not be independently verified. Every occurrence of "11 percent" I could locate is the Hansard debate itself (Halbert's own words and Labour colleagues repeating them), which is circular. The two documents the criterion names were both inaccessible: the bills.parliament.nz page for the bill returns "An unhandled error has occurred" and serves no document links, and the Ministry of Education select-committee briefing PDF on web-assets.education.govt.nz returned unparseable binary. Independent partial corroboration is directionally consistent but does not confirm the number: in the same debate Glen Bennett cited that of ~38 industry submitters only 8 gave full support (~21%), and the departmental report is described as recording concerns about financial viability, cost, and ISB independence. So the claim is consistent with a low-support picture but the specific 11% figure cannot be confirmed or refuted from publicly reachable sources. Per the criterion I did not substitute an easier question — absence of the tally is not evidence the tally is wrong.

statement: The Minister repeatedly says that Te Pūkenga was not financially viable, despite it returning a $16.7 million surplus last year, as it was intended to do.
criterion: Te Pūkenga's audited annual report / financial statements for the 2024 financial year; true if the reported net surplus is approximately $16.7 million, false if it recorded a deficit or a materially different surplus.
