reasoning: Te Pūkenga's Annual Report 2024, tabled in Parliament on 26 June 2025, records a surplus of $16.6 million for the 2024 financial year — its first ever surplus. This was a $54.5m (144%) improvement on the 2023 deficit of $37.9m and a $121.7m (116%) improvement on the 2022 deficit of $105m; revenue grew $68.4m (5%) on 2023. Halbert's $16.7m is $0.1m (about 0.6%) above the reported figure — within the criterion's "approximately $16.7 million" and nowhere near the criterion's falsity conditions (a deficit, or a materially different surplus). I checked for disconfirming evidence: RNZ, ODT, BusinessDesk, The Post and Te Pūkenga's own release all report the same $16.6m figure, and none report a parent-vs-group split that would produce a different headline number. Note the criterion covers only the surplus figure; the rhetorical rider "as it was intended to do" is not tested here, and it is worth flagging that this was the organisation's first surplus after two consecutive large deficits.

statement: We’ve already lost 19,000 construction workers, and last year, 3,700 fewer individuals enrolled in building apprenticeships and there were 9,000 overall fewer apprentice completions across all fields year on year under this National Government.
criterion: Stats NZ construction sector employment series (HLFS/filled jobs) for the period since late 2023, and Tertiary Education Commission industry training and apprenticeship enrolment/completion statistics for 2024 vs 2023; true if each figure matches those series within rounding, false if any is materially overstated or reversed in direction.
reasoning: Three figures, and they do not all hold up equally. (1) "3,700 fewer individuals enrolled in building apprenticeships" is well supported and if anything understated: Education Counts data (via Figure.NZ) shows apprentices in the field of architecture and building falling from 35,660 in 2023 to 31,765 in 2024 — a drop of 3,895. (2) "19,000 construction workers lost" is directionally correct but ahead of what the published series showed on 7 October 2025. Stats NZ HLFS puts construction at ~310,000 in the June 2023 quarter and ~294,000 in June 2025 (~16,000), and Labour's own 28 July 2025 release cited 18,000 since 2023. The 19,300 figure appears only in NZCTU analysis published in March 2026, five months after he spoke — so 19,000 was an overstatement against the data then available, though a modest one given the sector was still shedding roughly 1,000 jobs a month. (3) "9,000 overall fewer apprentice completions across all fields year on year" I could not reconcile with any completions series. Apprentice completions ran about 14,000 in 2024 (Education Counts reports 12,930 in 2025, down 7.7% on 2024), so a 9,000 fall would require roughly 23,000 completions in 2023 — a ~39% single-year collapse that no source reports. What did fall by roughly that order is apprentice headcount, not completions: apprentice numbers fell 9.9% in 2024 (~7,600 fewer people) and trainee numbers 14%. So the third figure looks like a headcount decline mislabelled as completions rather than an invented number. I could not read the Education Counts tables directly (the site returns 403 to automated fetches), so this rests on derived figures and secondary reporting. Overall: the substance — sharp declines in construction employment and in the training pipeline — holds and one figure is confirmed, but one is overstated relative to contemporaneous data and one does not match the series it names.

statement: The Minister, in fact, promised industry a stronger role under these reforms.
criterion: Ministerial press releases, the vocational education reform consultation documents and Cabinet papers issued by Penny Simmonds from 2024 onward; true if she publicly committed to a stronger or leading role for industry in the redesigned system, false if no such commitment is on record.
reasoning: The criterion asked whether Simmonds publicly committed to a stronger or leading role for industry. She did, repeatedly and on the record. Her Beehive release announcing the Te Pūkenga disestablishment states that regional decision-making was restored "and industry put back into the driver's seat for work-based learning", describing the new system as "locally and industry-led, regionally responsive, and future focused". The August 2024 consultation she launched proposed an industry-led model for standards-setting and industry training, and the resulting eight Industry Skills Boards (established 1 Jan 2026, replacing the Workforce Development Councils) were framed as giving industry control over setting standards, developing qualifications, endorsing deliverers and quality assurance. I looked for the disconfirming case — a record where industry's role was described as unchanged or reduced — and found none; every ministerial framing from 2024 onward promises industry a larger role. Halbert's characterisation of the promise is accurate (whether the delivery matched it is a separate question the criterion does not ask).

statement: In fact, the Treasury analysis of this reform said that the newly established ITPs could expect financials that were the same, if not worse, than before Te Pūkenga was established.
criterion: The Treasury / MoE Regulatory Impact Statement and Treasury's advice on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill: true if it states the disestablished ITPs' expected financial position is equal to or worse than pre-2020; false if Treasury forecast improved financials or made no such comparison.
reasoning: Treasury's advice to the Minister, reported from released correspondence in June 2025, states that the proposed future state for ITPs "appears to be similar, if not worse, than the situation faced by ITPs pre-Te Pūkenga" — near-verbatim the phrasing Hernandez used in the House. The context is explicitly financial: Treasury noted the additional funds and grants amount to only about 4.4 percent of the funding Te Pūkenga received in 2024, that the cuts already being progressed were the only change likely to produce significant improvement on the pre-Te Pūkenga state, and that proposed campus-based delivery rates are lower in real terms than pre-Te Pūkenga. Related Treasury material warns that the financial configurations of the new ITPs will directly affect system viability and that the changes may not fully sustain the financial challenges the institutes face. Checking the disconfirming side: I found no Treasury forecast of improved financials for the new ITPs, and the RIS itself concedes the Ministry had not quantified the proposals' likely impacts. Hernandez attributes the line to "the Treasury analysis of this reform" rather than the RIS specifically, which matches the source (Treasury advice/correspondence on the reform).

statement: There were 855 job losses last year and 1,000 are expected in this year.
criterion: TEC/Te Pūkenga workforce reporting and Tertiary Education Union redundancy tallies for 2024 and 2025: true if the 2024 figure is 855 ± rounding and the 2025 forecast is around 1,000; false if the counts are materially different.
reasoning: The 2024 half is exact: OIA documents released to the Greens' vocational education spokesperson show Te Pūkenga staffing dropped by 855 over the year, from 10,480 in 2023 to 9,625 in 2024 — about one in ten roles. The 1,000 figure is also genuinely on the record: a March 2025 Cabinet paper from Simmonds was reported in April 2025 as showing the polytech changes would cost more than 500 courses and about 1,000 jobs. But that ~1,000 is the cost of the disestablishment transition as a whole, not a forecast of a further 1,000 losses within 2025 as Hernandez's "expected in this year" implies. The Cabinet paper's own number was "up to 900 FTE" (alongside ~550 programmes and ~30 delivery sites) from financial improvement plans already underway as of late 2024 — i.e. partly overlapping the 855 he had just counted separately. Later proactively released figures put the 2025-specific loss at about 620 FTE with 257 qualifications paused or closed, and the union's own estimate mid-2025 was around another 400 roles in scope. So both numbers exist and neither is invented, but presenting them as consecutive annual totals stacks a transition-wide figure on top of a year that it partly contains, materially overstating the forward-looking number.

statement: Anyway, Labour established Te Pūkenga, as we know, by merging 16 polytechs and nine workplace training providers, and that only really started operating at the beginning of 2023.
criterion: TEC / Te Pūkenga establishment records and the Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Act 2020: true if 16 institutes of technology and polytechnics and nine industry training organisations' training arms were merged into Te Pūkenga, and if it began operating as a single unified entity at the start of 2023; false if the counts differ materially or the unified operating date is a different year.
reasoning: Te Pūkenga was established 1 April 2020 by the Sixth Labour Government under the Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Act 2020, merging the 16 institutes of technology and polytechnics and taking over industry/apprenticeship training from nine industry training organisations. Both counts match exactly. The 16 ITPs continued as subsidiaries until they were disestablished on 1 January 2023, when Te Pūkenga began operating as a single unified entity — matching Foster's 'only really started operating at the beginning of 2023'. Checked for a contrary count (e.g. 11 ITOs) and found the transferring work-based learning divisions consistently reported as nine.

statement: Te Pūkenga was based in Hamilton.
criterion: Te Pūkenga's registered head office address in the Companies Office / Crown entity records and its annual report: true if the national office was located in Hamilton, false if it was in Wellington or elsewhere.
reasoning: NZIST announced on 15 May 2020 that its head office would be located in Hamilton, after a joint bid from Hamilton City Council, Te Waka, Waikato-Tainui and the Waikato Chamber of Commerce. The registered/national office address is Wintec House, cnr Anglesea and Nisbet Streets, Hamilton 3204, and official Te Pūkenga OIA correspondence gives the Office of the Chief Executive at that address. Checked the disconfirming possibility (Wellington) and found no evidence for it; the only qualification in the record is that most national-office roles were distributed around the country rather than physically in Hamilton, which does not change the office's location.

statement: We hear very little about this, but we know from what's been in the media recently that there has been a release of information that shows that this is going to cost a lot more than what they were absolutely telling us it was going to cost.
criterion: Media reporting (RNZ/NZ Herald) in September–October 2025 on an official information release covering the cost of the Te Pūkenga disestablishment/transition, compared against the Government's earlier published transition cost estimate; true if the released figure materially exceeds the earlier stated figure, false if no such release exists or it is at or below the earlier figure.
reasoning: A qualifying information release exists in the window: Te Pūkenga proactively released the Regional ITP Viability reports (commissioned by TEC in November 2024) in August–September 2025, and RNZ reported on 27 September 2025 that about $190m would be needed to recapitalise the 16 polytechnics being spun out, including write-offs of internal Te Pūkenga loans. That exceeds the Government's earlier published figure — the $157.449m contingency set aside in Budget 2024 for disestablishing Te Pūkenga and transitioning to new institutional arrangements — by roughly 21%, which is material. It falls short of fully true because the RNZ reporting does not itself draw that comparison or frame the figure as exceeding what the Government had stated, and a consultants' recapitalisation estimate is not strictly like-for-like with a transition-cost contingency; the comparison is inferred rather than reported. Tinetti's 'a lot more than what they were absolutely telling us' is therefore substantively supported but rhetorically stronger than the released evidence establishes.

statement: We do know that the Government has withdrawn from proposals to close the Tokoroa and Taupō campuses, thanks to the efforts made by communities.
criterion: Toi Ohomai / Te Pūkenga change-proposal decision documents and Ministry of Education announcements for 2025: true if the final decisions retain the Tokoroa and Taupō campuses after they had been proposed for closure; false if closure proceeded or was never proposed.
reasoning: Toi Ohomai proposed in July 2025 to cease campus-based delivery in Taupō and Tokoroa from 2026 (166.7 FTE roles disestablished). After consultation it reversed that decision, announced ~9-11 September 2025: Taupō trades delivery retained, Tokoroa retention contingent on a new government 'strategically important provision' fund. NZ Herald (10 Oct 2025) reports Toi Ohomai confirmed TEC strategic funding had come through, allowing face-to-face learning to continue in Tokoroa. So the final decisions retain both campuses after they had been proposed for closure — the criterion's 'true' branch. Caveat the criterion does not test: the closure proposal was Toi Ohomai's, not the Government's; Hernandez attributes the withdrawal to 'the Government', whose actual role was the funding decision that made retention viable, alongside the community campaign he credits. At the moment he spoke (7 Oct 2025) Tokoroa's funding was on the brink of confirmation rather than confirmed.

statement: This Government has talked about how they want to reduce the amount of people—particularly young people—going on to be beneficiaries, but the free TAFE programme in Australia shows that when someone has gone through the free TAFE programme, they’re 37 percent less likely to end up on the benefit, and over half of those people who have gone through the free TAFE programme have actually seen their incomes increase.
criterion: Australian Department of Employment and Workplace Relations Free TAFE evaluation/outcome reporting and NCVER student outcomes surveys: true if a published evaluation reports a ~37% lower rate of income-support receipt and >50% of completers with increased income; false if the published figures differ materially or no such finding exists.
reasoning: Searched DEWR's Free TAFE pages and quarterly snapshots, the Victorian Auditor-General's Free TAFE audit, Jobs and Skills Australia's VET National Data Asset, the Karmel/Holmesglen 'initial look at Fee-Free TAFE' paper, and the AEU's 2025 'Unlocking the full potential of TAFE'. None reports a '37 percent less likely to end up on the benefit' finding for Free TAFE. Closest published figures: AEU 2025 — among VET graduates who received income support before study, 39% are no longer on income support two years after completion; JSA VNDA — 48% income-support exit rate one year after completion, and a median income uplift of $14,100 for graduates (a positive median does imply over half saw incomes rise, so that half of the claim is defensible). The substance therefore holds, but the specific statistic is materially different from anything published: it is an exit rate rather than a relative-risk reduction, and it covers VET graduates generally, not Free TAFE participants specifically. Disconfirming evidence checked: the Victorian Auditor-General found Free TAFE students had outcomes similar to students in non-Free-TAFE courses and to students doing the same courses at private providers, which undercuts attributing an income-support effect to the fee waiver itself. The criterion's 'true' branch (a published evaluation reporting ~37% lower income-support receipt AND >50% of completers with increased income) is not met; the figures found differ materially in construction while pointing the same direction, so this sits between the branches rather than being a clean false.

statement: Look, the Minister talks about how this is an industry-centred reform, but, actually, of the around 38 industry submitters, only eight of them gave their full support to the changes.
criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's published submissions on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill: true if roughly 38 industry submissions were received and about 8 recorded unqualified support; false if the counts differ materially.
reasoning: The Education and Workforce Committee received 210 written submissions on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill (submissions closed 18 June 2025) and heard from 32 submitters; it reported back on 22 September 2025, with the third reading on 15 October 2025 — consistent with the 7 October 2025 speech being the second reading. But neither the committee report nor the Ministry of Education's published material breaks submitters down by sector or records a tally of who gave 'full support', so there is no published source stating ~38 industry submitters with 8 supportive. The primary documents (individual submissions on parliament.nz) would in principle allow the count, but parliament.nz's submissions and bill pages are behind a bot-verification wall and returned errors/404s on every attempt, and 'industry submitter' and 'full support' are the speaker's own categorisations rather than fields in the record. Web searches for the 38/8 figures returned only reports of Hernandez's own speeches (Scoop's Hansard reprints), i.e. circular sourcing. Corroborating but non-verifying context: BusinessNZ and DairyNZ both criticised the bill to the committee, and the Ministry's departmental report is described as recording industry themes that the Industry Skills Boards are not independent or industry-led enough — consistent with the thrust, but not evidence for the specific counts.

statement: The member for Northland said, in an RNZ article, that the Government has no intention whatsoever to close NorthTec, and he promises that.
criterion: RNZ coverage of the vocational education reforms in 2025 quoting the MP for Northland on NorthTec's future; true if he is quoted saying the Government has no intention of closing NorthTec, false if no such quote appears or the quote is materially different.
reasoning: RNZ published an article headlined "Government has 'no intention whatsoever' to close NorthTec, Northland MP promises", quoting Grant McCallum, the National MP for the Northland electorate, saying the government has "no intention whatsoever" of closing NorthTec — this despite NorthTec being on the list of institutes facing possible closure or merger in the Te Pūkenga break-up. The criterion asked for RNZ coverage of the 2025 vocational education reforms quoting the MP for Northland to that effect; it exists and the quoted words match Prime's rendition, including the framing that he promises it. I could not fetch the article body directly (RNZ returns 403 to the fetcher and no Wayback snapshot exists), but the headline itself carries the quoted phrase and the search-indexed body text confirms the attribution and the surrounding context ("Northland needs vocational training and NorthTec's got an important part to play in that, but it's got to be able to stand up on its own two feet and be credible"). Checked for disconfirming evidence: no source suggests McCallum said the opposite or that the quote is misattributed; later coverage is consistent, with McCallum going on to announce NorthTec's re-establishment as a standalone regional polytechnic from 1 January 2027.

statement: There was 11 percent support for this.
criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on the bill, or the departmental report's summary of submissions; true if the proportion of submitters recorded as supporting the proposal is approximately 11 percent, false if materially different.
reasoning: The criterion names the Education and Workforce Committee's report on the bill, or the departmental report's summary of submissions, as the source to check. I could not reach either. The committee reported back on 22 September 2025 and the commentary is carried in the reprinted bill (150-2) on legislation.govt.nz, which returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher, as did bills.parliament.nz (unhandled error) and web.archive.org (blocked in this environment). The Ministry of Education's proactive-release page lists two summary-of-submissions reports (the 2024 VET consultation and the 2025 work-based learning consultation) but neither is the departmental report on this bill, and the PDF I retrieved was not machine-readable. What I can establish is only that the figure circulates within the debate itself: the committee received 210 written submissions and heard 32 submitters, and Shanan Halbert stated in this same second reading that "Only 11 percent of submitters supported this bill", later refined to "only 11 percent of submitters unconditionally backed these reforms"; Prime then used the same figure. Every search result reporting 11 percent traces back to these Hansard speeches rather than to an independent document, so confirming it would be circular. The refinement to "unconditionally" hints at a real underlying tally (support / support with changes / oppose), and a related datapoint from the same debate is directionally consistent (Francisco Hernandez: of roughly 38 industry submitters, only eight gave full support — about 21%), but that is a different denominator and cannot substitute for the named source. I looked for disconfirming evidence too — no source anywhere states a materially different support proportion, and no government speaker contested the number in the debate. Not being able to open the document is not evidence the claim is false, so this is uncheckable rather than false.

statement: As of last year, some 900 fulltime-equivalents, 500 programmes, and approximately 30 delivery sites have been cut—cut, cut, cut.
criterion: Tertiary Education Commission and Te Pūkenga / polytechnic reporting on staffing, programme and site reductions during 2024, or the Tertiary Education Union's tally; true if the aggregate figures are close to 900 FTE, 500 programmes and 30 sites, false if materially lower.
reasoning: A Cabinet paper by Vocational Education Minister Penny Simmonds, reported by RNZ and the NZ Herald, states that polytechnics "have begun implementing their financial improvement plans, which as of late 2024 indicated reductions of approximately 550 programmes, up to 900 FTE and approximately 30 delivery sites." That matches Prime's three figures: 900 FTE exactly, ~30 delivery sites exactly, and 500 programmes against an actual ~550 — an understatement, and one that runs against her own argument rather than inflating it, so it is not materially lower in the direction the criterion guards against. Jan Tinetti used the same line with 550 in the same debate, indicating a shared Labour talking point drawn from the Cabinet paper. Two nuances worth recording: the source describes reductions "indicated" in financial improvement plans and "up to" 900 FTE, i.e. planned figures, whereas Prime says they "have been cut" — a modest overstatement of how far the cuts had been executed, though contemporaneous reporting that Te Pūkenga lost 855 staff and over $80m in funding ahead of disestablishment supports the cuts having largely materialised. The criterion turns on whether the aggregate figures are close to the stated numbers, and they are.

statement: In fact, we saw in yet another article, the RNZ article, that there's an estimate of about $190 million, more than the total amount allocated to the Government for transition.
criterion: RNZ reporting in 2025 on the cost of disestablishing Te Pūkenga, checked against the transition funding appropriated in Budget 2024/2025; true if a figure of approximately $190 million is reported and exceeds the appropriation, false if no such figure appears or it is within the allocated amount.
reasoning: RNZ published "About $190m needed to restart polytechnics - consultants reports" on 27 September 2025 (article 574336), reporting that consultants' reports commissioned by the Tertiary Education Commission found recapitalising the 16 institutes being removed from Te Pūkenga could require about $190m, including write-offs of internal Te Pūkenga loans. The transition money appropriated for the disestablishment was a $157.4m contingency established in Budget 2024 (RNZ and subsequent Newsroom reporting on the same contingency, of which $56.1m had been appropriated and $24.9m paid by July 2026). $190m exceeds $157.4m, and the RNZ article itself sets the two figures against each other. Checked for disconfirming evidence: Budget 2025 vocational items (a $10m one-off Industry Skills Board establishment cost, $30m/yr ongoing ISB standards-setting funding, and the later $325m transfer of Te Pūkenga's own reserves to the standalone ITPs) are not Crown transition appropriations for the disestablishment, so they do not lift the allocated transition total above $190m. Minister Simmonds disputed the $190m as a dated snapshot based on late-2024 assumptions, but the criterion asks only whether such a figure is reported and exceeds the appropriation — both hold.

statement: So we heard Andy Foster say that they were ideological.
criterion: The Hansard record of Andy Foster's speech on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, 7 October 2025: true if he characterises workforce development councils as ideological as his own view; false if he only reports that others told him they were ideological.
reasoning: The Hansard record of the 7 October 2025 second reading shows Andy Foster (NZ First) said: "I also heard that the WDCs, the workforce development councils, were often overly political and ideological." When challenged across the House by Shanan Halbert he clarified: "These are the things, Shanan Halbert, that I actually heard from people in the comments" — i.e. he was relaying submitters'/stakeholders' feedback, not stating his own assessment. Brooking herself acknowledged the correction later in the same debate: "Oh, he's correcting me. He said that people told him that workforce development councils were ideological, not that he thinks that they were ideological—but he still said it in his speech." The criterion is explicit that it is false if he only reports that others told him they were ideological, which is what the record shows. Note the residual nuance: the words were spoken by Foster in his own speech, so Brooking's paraphrase has a literal surface basis, but under the criterion as written the attribution of the view to Foster does not hold.

statement: I know that because I recall her huge opposition to the mergers of the polytechs. She was very vocal about that.
criterion: Contemporaneous public record 2018–2020 — select committee submissions on the Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Bill, SIT media releases, and news coverage: true if the SIT chief executive is on record repeatedly opposing the merger, false if no such public opposition is documented.
reasoning: Context in the same speech makes clear Brooking's "her" is Penny Simmonds, SIT chief executive for roughly two decades (1997–October 2020). The contemporaneous 2018–2020 record documents repeated public opposition while she held that role: she pushed back on the February 2019 Hipkins proposal at the time of announcement; on the 1 August 2019 confirmation she said publicly "It is hugely disappointing for SIT and Southland community but we will let the Southland community speak on that so we can focus on our staff and students", saying she had been blindsided after expecting SIT to retain autonomy; the ODT describes her as having, alongside Otago Polytechnic colleagues, "staged a vociferous but ultimately unsuccessful southern campaign against the creation of Te Pūkenga", viewing the reforms as an attack on institutional autonomy and a punishment for high performers; the Southland Tribune states she "was a vocal critic of the vocational reform which was led by the Labour-led Government in 2019 when Simmonds was still at the helm of the SIT" and "fired many verbal shots" at the Minister; and her 2020 election campaign, run while still SIT CE, featured opposing the merging of New Zealand's polytechnics as a stated policy. Checked for disconfirming evidence: no record of SIT or Simmonds supporting or acquiescing to the merger was found; the surrounding Invercargill campaign (Mayor Tim Shadbolt, a "Save SIT" petition) is consistent with, not a substitute for, her own opposition. The only qualification is that her loudest sustained campaigning came after she entered Parliament in late 2020, but the criterion's test — the SIT chief executive on record repeatedly opposing the merger — is met within the 2018–2020 window.

statement: So it seems that this Government is down on Dunedin, it is down on jobs, and we’ve had reports in the Otago Daily Times that the polytech might have to decrease their land area by 60 percent.
criterion: Otago Daily Times reporting during 2025 on Otago Polytechnic's campus footprint: true if an ODT article reports a prospective reduction of roughly 60 percent in the polytechnic's land area, false if no such figure appears or the reported figure is materially different.
reasoning: The criterion asked for ODT reporting during 2025 of a roughly 60 percent reduction in Otago Polytechnic's land area. The ODT article "'Wide-scale divestment' urged for Otago Polytech" (Matthew Littlewood, 29 September 2025) reports that Deloitte, reporting for the Tertiary Education Commission's viability process, recommends Otago Polytechnic reduce its land area by 60% and its built area by about 50%, potentially including sale of the category-2-listed Ralph Hotere Cottage. RNZ's coverage of the same consultants' reports independently records Otago Polytechnic as able to reduce land area by 60 percent. The article predates Brooking's 7 October statement, and she characterised it accurately and with appropriate hedging ("might have to"). Checked for a materially different figure (e.g. a built-area 50% figure being confused for land) and the 60% land figure is the one reported.

statement: The select committee also recommended that a new section is inserted to ensure that implied warranties, which are an existing consumer protection mechanism under the Building Act, continue to be applied, because, of course, we also need to make sure that we are protecting consumers, protecting those people who will become the owners of these properties, as well.
criterion: The Building Act 2004 (subpart 6 of Part 4A, the implied warranties provisions, ss 362I–362K) and the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the Building and Construction (Small Standalone Dwellings) Amendment Bill. True if implied warranties are an existing Building Act consumer-protection mechanism AND the committee's report recommends a new section preserving their application; false if either limb is absent from those documents.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are satisfied in the named documents. I read the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill directly. Its "Implied warranties" section states: "Section 362I of the Act provides a list of implied warranties for building work. Subsection (1)(a)(ii) states that part of the contract is that the building work will be carried out in accordance with the plans and specifications set out in the contract." It then notes that because the bill allows non-consented dwellings, plans and specifications would not exist and "this language would not apply", and recommends "inserting new clause 21A, which would amend section 362I to provide that, in relation to a non-consented small stand-alone dwelling, building work would have to be carried out in accordance with the final design plans." So implied warranties are an existing Building Act consumer-protection mechanism, and the committee did recommend a new provision preserving their application. One imprecision: the report recommends a new *clause* (21A) in the bill amending existing s 362I, not a "new section" in the Act; this is drafting terminology and does not change the substance. Report presented by the Transport and Infrastructure Committee (Chair Andy Foster), bill referred 22 May 2025, report-back deadline 23 September 2025.

statement: It resulted in $300 million going down the gurgler—$300 million down the Labour fiscal drain.
criterion: Te Pūkenga's audited annual reports 2020–2024 and Tertiary Education Commission funding/deficit records: true if cumulative operating deficits plus establishment/transition costs attributable to Te Pūkenga total approximately $300 million; false if the audited figure is materially lower.
reasoning: The criterion asks whether cumulative operating deficits plus establishment/transition costs attributable to Te Pukenga total approximately $300 million. The audited results fall materially short. Te Pukenga's reported annual results: 2021 surplus $7.6m; 2022 deficit $105m (as restated in the 2024 report; originally reported as ~$80m); 2023 operating deficit $37.9m; 2024 surplus $16.6m. That is about $143m in gross deficits and roughly $119m net. Treasury estimates show establishment and transition appropriations of the order of $90-100m ($10m for establishment/subsidiary transition plus ~$90.2m phased over three years), which takes the outside total to roughly $240m gross - real money, and the right order of magnitude, but not $300m. No source I found supports the specific $300m figure as Te Pukenga's cost: the nearest ministerial number was Penny Simmonds' "$250 million deficit", which Te Pukenga executives publicly disputed as about one-fifth of that; the $330m/$422.6m figures are funding *requests* that were not granted, not money spent; and the $297m figure that appears in reporting is a *forecast* of polytechnic losses over four years under the disestablishment plan, i.e. attributable to the current Government's reform rather than the merger Butterick was criticising. Verdict is partly_true rather than false because the substance - large sums consumed by a merger that was reversed - holds, but the figure is materially overstated relative to the audited record.

statement: You know, we’ve seen 20,000 jobs in building and construction gone since the day of the election.
criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs / Household Labour Force Survey employment for the construction industry, comparing October 2023 with the most recent quarter before October 2025; true if the fall is approximately 20,000, false if materially smaller or if employment rose.
reasoning: Construction employment did fall substantially since the Oct 2023 election, but by materially less than 20,000 on the series the criterion names, as at the statement date. HLFS/OECD construction employment: 307,646 (Sep 2023 qtr, the election quarter) and 301,614 (Dec 2023 qtr) vs 292,401 in the Jun 2025 quarter — the most recent quarter available on 7 Oct 2025 — a fall of ~15,200 (or ~9,200 from Dec 2023). Stats NZ business employment data reported by RNZ in Sep 2025: 16,000 fewer filled jobs in construction between Dec 2023 and the Jun 2025 quarter. Labour's own releases escalated from 18,000 (28 Jul 2025) to 20,000 (29 Sep 2025) without citing a series. The larger 19,300 figure only appears later (NZCTU, Mar 2026), after further declines. So the substance — a large, sustained fall — holds, but the 20,000 figure overstates the ~15,000-16,000 supported by the data at the time.

statement: We’re also seeing more and more young New Zealanders who could be taking up those opportunities and building apprenticeships and getting into building, from whatever walk of life they are from, either leaving our shores—200 young New Zealanders a day—or not able to get into those jobs in building and construction.
criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for New Zealand citizen departures in the year to the date of the statement, restricted to the younger age bands the claim refers to (broadly under 30); true if that subset averages about 200 a day, false if the 200-a-day figure only holds for citizen departures of all ages combined or is materially lower.
reasoning: The 200-a-day figure matches NZ citizen departures of ALL ages, not young people. Stats NZ: 71,800 NZ citizen migrant departures in the June 2025 year (197/day) and 73,900 in the August 2025 year (202/day). Restricting to the younger age bands the claim refers to, migrants aged 18-30 made up 27,200 (38%) of those 71,800 departures — about 75 a day, and 27,200 (39%) of 70,000 in the March 2025 year. That is the exact condition the criterion specifies as false: the 200-a-day number only holds for citizen departures of all ages combined, and the young-adult subset is materially lower (roughly one-third of the claimed rate). The underlying phenomenon (record youth outflow, ~3 in 5 to Australia) is real, but the specific quantity attached to 'young New Zealanders' is wrong.

statement: That’s really important, and I’d say that this Government has kind of done the opposite, really, by cancelling a bunch of State homes that would have been built over the last few years that would have helped address the housing shortage but also would have kept builders and construction companies employed during this time.
criterion: Kāinga Ora build programme records and Budget 2024/2025 documents on planned public housing places: true if a material number of previously committed/planned state house builds were cancelled or removed from the programme after October 2023; false if the programme was maintained or expanded with no cancellations.
reasoning: A material number of previously committed/planned state house builds were removed from the Kainga Ora programme after October 2023. On 24 June 2025 Kainga Ora announced it was cancelling 212 planned housing projects that would have delivered almost 3,500 state homes, alongside selling 20% of its vacant land holdings, and writing off $190-220m in sunk scoping/planning costs. Of the consented-but-uncontracted projects scheduled to start before 30 June 2025, 172 of 284 (60%) were dropped, removing 1,019 units. Named cancellations include 259 homes in Onehunga, 322 in Whangarei, 245 across nine Palmerston North projects, a 108-home Christchurch village, and a 16-storey Manukau tower. This followed the Bill English review and Housing Minister Chris Bishop's directive for a turnaround plan. I checked for the disconfirming case — that the programme was maintained or expanded — and found the opposite: the build programme was cut back and refocused, with delivery shifted toward community housing providers. Genter's causal framing (that the builds would have kept construction firms employed) is an inference rather than a verified fact, but the factual core of the claim is correct.

statement: Well, I’m assuming most of the members know that the head office for Te Pūkenga actually is in the Waikato, in Hamilton. It’s not about bringing everything back to Wellington, like we’ve been talking about; it’s actually about it being out in the regions.
criterion: Te Pūkenga's annual reports and Crown entity registration records for its registered/head office address: true if the head office is recorded in Hamilton, Waikato; false if recorded in Wellington or elsewhere.
reasoning: Te Pūkenga/NZIST announced on 15 May 2020 that its head office would be located in Hamilton, and the address is consistently recorded as Level 2, Wintec House, Cnr Anglesea and Nisbet Streets, Hamilton 3204 — in Te Pūkenga Work Based Learning's annual report and on the letterhead of a Te Pūkenga OIA response dated November 2025, i.e. contemporaneous with the speech. Checking for the disconfirming case, no source records a Wellington head/registered office; Wellington appears only as one of several regional campus locations. The head office is in Hamilton, Waikato, as stated.

statement: In fact, they’ve been bailed out twice by the Government over the last 20 years.
criterion: Tertiary Education Commission and Ministry of Education records of exceptional financial assistance, Crown loans or capital injections to WITT since about 2005, plus WITT's annual reports: true if two or more such interventions are recorded; false if fewer.
reasoning: Context confirms 'they' = WITT (Bennett's speech on the vocational education bill). The record shows one clearly documented rescue episode: WITT received Crown loans totalling $18 million 'over a number of years of financial difficulties', its Council was replaced by a Commissioner in December 2006, and in 2007 Tertiary Education Minister Pete Hodgson announced the Crown debt would be written off / converted to equity over five years subject to recovery-plan targets. That can be read as two interventions (the lending, then the write-off), which is the reading that makes 'twice' defensible, but it is a single crisis and much of the lending predates the 2005–2025 window. Searching for a second, separate bailout in that window turned up nothing: the intervening TEC event (2015) was WITT being required to repay $3.7m of funding after an investigation — the opposite of a bailout — and the $2m TEC grant plus mooted $30.8m recapitalisation for standalone status both postdate the October 2025 speech. Note I could not open the TEC page or RNZ articles directly (403 / empty fetch), so the Beehive release details rest on search-engine extracts of that page. Substance holds — WITT has a real history of exceptional Crown assistance — but 'twice ... over the last 20 years' is materially overstated as a count of distinct interventions inside that window.

statement: As Chris Penk has previously stated in the House, it is around 50 percent more expensive to build a stand-alone house in New Zealand than in Australia.
criterion: Trans-Tasman residential construction cost comparisons (NZ Infrastructure Commission / former Productivity Commission housing affordability work, MBIE build-cost analysis, or Rider Levett Bucknall / CoreLogic cost indices) for stand-alone dwellings: true if New Zealand per-square-metre or per-dwelling build costs are around 50 percent above the Australian equivalent; false if the gap is materially smaller or reversed.
reasoning: The attribution is accurate: Chris Penk has repeatedly stated 'It is 50% more expensive to build a standalone home in New Zealand than in Australia,' including in July 2025 and August 2025 announcements — and in none of them is a study cited for the figure. On the underlying fact the evidence splits by methodology. It roughly reproduces from aggregate official statistics: Stats NZ average build cost for standalone houses is about NZ$3,200–3,270/m² (March 2026 quarter ~NZ$3,229/m²) against roughly A$1,970/m² derived from ABS building-activity data, which is about 50% higher once currency-adjusted. But that is not a like-for-like comparison. Deloitte Access Economics, for Fletcher Building, found per-square-metre housing construction costs 'very similar and in some cases cheaper' in New Zealand for the same house design, with Australia's lower final cost coming from standardised designs, GST of 8% vs NZ's 12%, and lighter seismic/fire/façade requirements; BRANZ work (Ian Page) put the same-house gap at about 10%, and a builder operating in both markets costed an identical home at about three-quarters the NZ price in Australia (~33%). Materials-only premiums have been estimated at ~55% (exchange-rate adjusted) and ~24% (Productivity Commission, materials in place). Looking for the disconfirming case as the rules require, there is real published analysis pointing to a materially smaller construction-cost gap, and no published government analysis supporting the 50% figure could be located. So: directionally correct and defensible under one aggregate reading of the criterion, but overstated as a statement about the cost of building the same house.

statement: This is also important in the context of councils’ consenting systems because, at the moment, council consents are at the lowest they have been over the last seven years, and I think there’s a lot of different reasons for that, but this takes some of that out.
criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued series (annual/rolling-year new dwellings consented) to the quarter ending nearest October 2025: true if the current level is lower than in each of the preceding six years, false if any of those years was lower.
reasoning: Criterion asks whether the current rolling-year new dwellings consented is lower than each of the preceding six years. The latest Stats NZ data available on 2025-10-07 was the August 2025 release: 34,078 homes consented in the year ended August 2025, UP 1.3% on the year ended August 2024 (~33,640). The next release (September 2025) showed 34,882, up 3.6% year-on-year and described as the highest monthly figure in more than two years. So at least one of the preceding six years (2024) was lower, which fails the criterion's strict test. The substance is nonetheless close to right: annual totals through mid-2025 sat around the second-lowest for any month since end-2018 and about a third below the mid-2022 peak of ~51,000, so consenting was near multi-year lows — but 'the lowest in seven years' overstates it, and the series had already turned up.

statement: They do not even have aerial trucks—lots of them don’t have trucks in general, and won’t be able to come out and service the fires if they happen in these granny flats.
criterion: FENZ fleet and appliance-allocation records plus the NZPFU/FENZ appliance availability reporting: true if a substantial share of brigades have no operational appliance and aerial appliances are unavailable across most of the network, false if brigades are generally appliance-equipped and aerial appliances are stationed per the standard urban coverage model.
reasoning: Two claims. (a) Aerial appliances: true for volunteer/rural brigades. FENZ's aerial fleet is roughly 25 vehicles (18 Type 4 heavy aerial pumps, 5 hydraulic elevating platforms, 2 turntable ladders) across 637 stations, stationed at main-centre career stations, so brigades outside the main urban centres have none. NZPFU further documents genuine availability failures: Auckland's region down from 5 heavy aerials to 2, Christchurch without its 32m appliance for a week with a spare that has health-and-safety issues, Parnell running a 22-year-old spare, and every metropolitan city affected by a faulty aerial. (b) 'Lots of them don't have trucks in general': not supported. The pump fleet is ~852 (352 light, 250 medium, 250 heavy) plus ~179 rural appliances for 637 stations, so brigades are generally appliance-equipped. NZPFU's complaint is about age and reliability (25-40-year-old cascaded trucks, repeated failures, one rural brigade of 15,000 people having three vehicles removed), not about brigades having no appliance at all. The criterion's 'true' condition (a substantial share of brigades with no operational appliance) fails; its 'false' condition holds on the appliance side but not cleanly on aerial availability. Substance right on aerials, materially overstated on trucks.

statement: Section 72 allows councils to grant consent for building. Section 67 allows councils to take a liberalised view of a project and allow something to happen.
criterion: The text of ss 67 and 72 of the Building Act 2004 on the NZ Legislation website. True if s 72 empowers a territorial authority to grant a building consent in the circumstances it covers and s 67 confers a discretion to relax the ordinary requirements; false if either section does something materially different from the power described (e.g. if it imposes a duty on a party other than the council, or confers no consenting discretion at all).
reasoning: Checked against the criterion's named source, the Building Act 2004 on legislation.govt.nz. Section 67 is titled 'Territorial authority may grant building consent subject to waivers or modifications of building code' and provides that a BCA that is a territorial authority may grant a consent subject to a waiver or modification of the Building Code, on any conditions it considers appropriate (excluding access for people with disabilities). That is a discretion for the council to relax the ordinary requirements — matching 'take a liberalised view of a project and allow something to happen'. Section 72 is titled 'Building consent for building on land subject to natural hazards must be granted in certain cases': despite s 71, the territorial authority must grant the consent where the work will not accelerate, worsen or result in a natural hazard, the land is or is likely to be subject to one or more natural hazards, and it is reasonable to grant a waiver or modification of the Building Code for that hazard. So s 72 does operate as a power for councils to consent building in the circumstances it covers. Two caveats that stop short of falsifying it under the criterion: s 72 is framed as a duty to grant rather than a bare permission, and it is confined to natural-hazard land, not a general consenting power. Neither exclusion in the criterion applies — the duty is on the council itself, and s 67 plainly confers consenting discretion.

statement: That cost councils a fortune, and that was the outcome of the last time the Government decided to massively deregulate the building sector in order to, supposedly, achieve productivity, make it cheaper, make it easier to build more homes.
criterion: The Hunn Report (2002), the Weathertight Homes Resolution Service / Financial Assistance Package records, and PwC's cost estimates for the leaky homes crisis: true if councils carried a substantial share of remediation cost (e.g. the 25% council share under the FAP, plus litigation settlements) and if official inquiries attribute the failure in part to the deregulatory 1991 Building Act regime; false if councils bore negligible cost or if the inquiries attribute the crisis to unrelated causes.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion are satisfied. Cost: the DBH/PwC 2009 report 'Weathertightness — Estimating the Cost' estimated $11.3b total economic cost for the 42,000-dwelling consensus forecast and found the cost was being borne 69% by owners, ~25% by territorial authorities and 4% by other parties; courts generally assigned around one third of liability to local authorities as the solvent 'last man standing'; and the 2011 Financial Assistance Package set a 25% council contribution where the council had certified the work. That is a substantial, multi-billion-dollar council/ratepayer share, not a negligible one. Attribution: the Hunn Report (Oct 2002) was commissioned to examine whether the failures were attributable to the Building Act 1991, its regulations, or their administration, and the 2003 parliamentary inquiry into weathertightness concluded that 'changes to the building control regime brought about by the Building Act, and too greater reliance of market competitiveness have… contributed to the systemic failure of the building industry'. The 1991 Act was the deregulatory, performance-based/self-certification reform, and was repealed and replaced by the tighter Building Act 2004 in response. Genter's 'massively' is rhetorical intensity, but the substance — councils paid heavily, and official inquiries blamed the deregulated regime in part — holds.

statement: From the regulatory impact statement, it’s estimating approximately 7,800 additional granny flats—maybe the numbers are up a little bit.
criterion: The MBIE regulatory impact statement for the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill: true if its central estimate of additional dwellings is approximately 7,800; false if the estimate is materially different (e.g. 13,000).
reasoning: The 7,800 figure is genuine but superseded. MBIE's Supplementary Analysis (4 March 2025), the regulatory impact analysis supporting the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill, states directly: 'Allowing granny flats up to 70 square metres to be built without a building consent is estimated to increase the supply of granny flats by around 13,000 units over 10 years. We note that this differs from our December 2024 conclusion which estimated that an additional 7,866 granny flats up to 60 square metres would be built.' The cost-benefit tables and the induced-demand table give the operative number as 13,138 additional granny flats cumulative to FY2035 (on top of 15,750 under the status quo). So Genter accurately quoted the earlier December 2024 RIS for the 60m2 proposal, and she signalled awareness of a revision ('maybe the numbers are up a little bit'), but the estimate attached to the bill actually before the House is 13,138 — 67% higher, which the criterion names explicitly as the materially-different case. True only under a reading (the superseded 60m2 RIS) that she flagged only faintly, and the understatement is material to the argument she was making about the bill's modest benefit.

statement: That’s not to criticise this bill—it’s to say it’s a good first step, but there are probably other elements that we have to consider as well as to why it is that the construction sector has been the hardest hit by job losses.
criterion: Stats NZ employment/filled-jobs by industry (HLFS and Business Employment Data) over 2024–2025: true if construction recorded the largest absolute or proportional fall in employment of any industry over that period, false if another industry fell further.
reasoning: Stats NZ employment indicators for the year to June 2025 (the most recent data available when Paul spoke on 7 October 2025) show construction filled jobs down 12,169, or 6%, against a total fall across all industries of 27,850 (1.2%) — construction alone accounted for roughly 44% of the entire net national decline in filled jobs. The next-largest faller, manufacturing, was down 5,850 (2.5%), less than half construction's absolute loss and well under half its rate. Over the longer 2024–2025 window construction is down about 16,000 jobs since December 2023 (and ~14,500, or 6.8%, from its February 2024 peak of 213,000), versus manufacturing -8,700 and retail -6,000. Construction therefore leads on both the absolute and the proportional test in the criterion, and the criterion requires only one. Checking for disconfirmation: the public-sector cuts are the obvious rival, but public administration and safety's worst reported print was -4,247 (-2.5%) in a single quarter and was partly election-related temporary roles, well short of construction. Caveat: I did not locate a complete ANZSIC-level table for the period, so a small industry could in principle show a larger percentage fall; across all industries actually reported, construction is the hardest hit on both measures.

statement: The uncertainty in the construction sector has meant that a lot of construction companies haven’t received the same levels of work that they would expect or that they had been used to expecting.
criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued for new dwellings and construction industry activity/GDP series for 2023–2025, plus construction-sector liquidation and employment data; true if construction work volumes fell materially below the preceding years' levels, false if activity was flat or rising.
reasoning: Stats NZ shows construction activity fell materially below preceding years: construction GDP −1.8% in the June 2025 quarter, value of building work put in place −2.2%, construction filled jobs −1.3%, and a ~9.4% annual fall in construction activity. Construction sales fell 3.1% in the June 2025 quarter. Sector employment fell from 213,475 (2023) to 207,825 (2024 annual average), and construction liquidations reached 751 firms in 2025 (up 13%), with Q4 2025 the worst quarter since Deloitte began sector collection in 2022. New-dwelling consents fell from a ~51,000 peak (year to May 2022) to the low-to-mid 33,000s through 2024–mid 2025. Checked for the opposite: consents had begun rising annually by mid-2025 (+3.6% year to September 2025), but the claim is about work companies actually received, and building work put in place and construction employment were still contracting at the time of the statement. The claim is also modestly framed ('haven't received the same levels of work'), which the data supports.

statement: As I said in my first reading speaking, I’m really looking forward to how this is going to help the over 50 percent of migrants in my community now that we’ve got the parent visa up and running.
criterion: 2023 Census overseas-born share of usual residents for the speaker's electorate (Takanini) — true if above 50%, false if materially below; and Immigration NZ records on whether the Parent Boost Visa was open for and accepting applications on 7 October 2025.
reasoning: Both limbs of the criterion hold. 2023 Census: 51.6% of usual residents of the Takanini electorate were born overseas, against 28.8% nationally — above 50%, though only narrowly (a ~1.6pp margin, so the claim is true but has little headroom). Rima Nakhle has been the National MP for Takanini since 14 October 2023, so 'my community' maps to that electorate. On the visa: Immigration NZ opened the Parent Boost Visitor Visa for applications on 29 September 2025, eight days before the 7 October 2025 statement, so it was indeed 'up and running'. Checked for disconfirmation: no evidence of a delayed opening, suspension, or pause in the intake between 29 September and 7 October 2025.

statement: The National Government, as we’ve heard tonight, have made decisions that absolutely have caused a dramatic slowdown in new builds, and we’ve seen that manifest in various ways right across New Zealand.
criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued for new dwellings, comparing the period from October 2023 onward with the preceding years; true if new-dwelling consents/starts fell materially over that period AND the fall can be traced to identifiable government decisions rather than pre-existing drivers, false if the decline predates the government's decisions or is attributable to interest rates and the construction cycle.
reasoning: The criterion requires both a material fall in new-dwelling consents/starts from October 2023 onward AND that the fall be traceable to identifiable government decisions rather than pre-existing drivers. The first limb partly holds: consents fell from 37,239 (2023) to roughly 33,500–33,800 across 2024 and early 2025 (year to January 2025 −7.2%, year to April 2025 −5.2%). But the second limb largely fails. The collapse began from the ~51,000 peak in the year to May 2022 — well before the government took office in November 2023 — and contemporaneous analysis attributes it to rising interest rates, higher build and material costs, tighter lending and falling house prices, i.e. the construction cycle. There is one identifiable government decision that genuinely cut new builds: the Kāinga Ora turnaround plan cancelled 212 projects covering almost 3,500 state homes and halted growth in state housing stock, so the public-housing component of the claim is real. Disconfirming evidence also matters for the 'dramatic slowdown' framing: by the date of the statement consents had turned upward — the year to June 2025 was up 1% (first annual growth in two years) and the year to September 2025 was up 3.6%, with September the strongest month in over two years. Substance holds for public housing and for 2024, but 'absolutely have caused a dramatic slowdown' materially overstates the government's causal share and ignores that new-build consents were already recovering.

statement: This bill delivers on a part of the coalition agreement. It was something that New Zealand First specifically campaigned on, so we are delighted that we're now actually able to deliver this campaign promise.
criterion: The National–New Zealand First coalition agreement (published December 2023) and NZ First's 2023 election policy material. True if the agreement contains a commitment matching this bill's subject (consent-free small stand-alone dwellings / granny flats) and NZ First's published 2023 policy includes it; false if the commitment appears only in the National–ACT agreement, only in a post-election work programme, or has no NZ First campaign counterpart.
reasoning: The coalition-agreement half is confirmed: the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report on the bill quotes the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement commitment to "amend the Building Act and the Resource Consent system to make it easier to build granny flats or other small structures up to 60sqm", so the commitment is in the NZ First agreement (not the National–ACT one) and this bill delivers it. The campaign half is not supported: NZ First's own 2023 Election Policies page lists its housing platform (Ministry of Infrastructure land unlocking, RMA/intensification repeal, Housing Commission, prefabrication, restoring tax deductibility, seniors/public housing, first-home select committee inquiry) with no mention of granny flats, minor or small stand-alone dwellings, or a consent exemption for structures up to 60 m². interest.co.nz's independent compilation of NZ First's 2023 housing policy matches that list and also omits it, and interest.co.nz's contemporaneous reporting attributes the promise to the post-election deal: "Making it easier to build these small dwellings was promised in the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement late last year." I checked for disconfirming evidence (NZ First press releases and campaign coverage from 2023) and found no granny-flat campaign announcement; the nearest thing is Shane Jones's later statement that he had "been working on these changes for two decades", which is a personal long-standing interest, not published 2023 campaign policy. So: coalition agreement yes, NZ First 2023 campaign promise no.

statement: This started off talking about 60 square-metre buildings. After consultation—there was consultation before the legislation was introduced—it was raised to 70 square metres.
criterion: MBIE's pre-introduction discussion document on consent-free granny flats and the bill as introduced. True if the discussion document proposes a 60 m² limit and the bill as introduced sets 70 m²; false if either figure differs, or if the increase happened at a different stage (e.g. at select committee rather than before introduction).
reasoning: MBIE's pre-introduction discussion document 'Making it easier to build granny flats' (consultation 17 June – 12 August 2024, 1,970 submissions) proposed a new Schedule to the Building Act exempting simple stand-alone dwellings of up to 60 square metres, matching the 60 m² coalition-agreement figure. The Beehive release of 5 April 2025 announced that after consultation the maximum was "increased to be 70 sq m rather than the earlier proposed 60 sq m", and said the Building Act amendment would be introduced in the middle of 2025. The Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill was introduced on 22 May 2025 with the 70 m² limit in clause 1 of new Schedule 1A. So the increase happened after consultation and before introduction, exactly as stated — not at select committee. The select committee report independently confirms the sequence: "We understand that the Government decided to increase this to 70 square metres following public consultation in 2024."

statement: Of course, the size of the building is defined and, as we’ve heard, initially the policy position was going to be that it’s 60 square metres and now it’s 70 as the bill was introduced, and that hasn’t changed.
criterion: The MBIE granny-flat discussion document / Cabinet paper and the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill as introduced, plus the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report-back version. True if the consultation proposal specified a 60 m² maximum floor area and the bill as introduced and reported back specifies 70 m²; false if either figure differs or the reported-back bill altered the 70 m² limit.
reasoning: Both halves of the criterion hold. The consultation proposal was 60 m²: MBIE's June 2024 discussion document proposed a Building Act exemption for simple stand-alone dwellings up to 60 square metres, and the 5 April 2025 Beehive announcement records the increase to 70 m² after consultation. The bill as introduced (166-1, introduced 22 May 2025) sets 70 square metres, defined in clause 1 of new Schedule 1A. The reported-back version did not alter it: the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report states the bill "is intended to reduce the time and cost of building stand-alone dwellings that are 70 square metres or less" and its recommended amendments concern definitions of design plans, project information memoranda, information territorial authorities must keep, implied warranties, liability protections, mezzanine floors and plumbing/drainage specifications — none touch the floor-area limit. I specifically looked for a committee-stage or SOP change to the area and found none, so Brooking's "that hasn't changed" is accurate as at 7 October 2025.

statement: If we look at the statistics that are readily available for anybody to check in to, specific statistics that were released in April this year show that 33,595 new homes consented in the year to February this year—February 2025—and that was down 7.4 percent from the year before.
criterion: Stats NZ 'Building consents issued' release for February 2025 (published April 2025): true if the number of new dwellings consented in the year ended February 2025 is 33,595 (± rounding to the nearest hundred) and the annual change is -7.4%; false if either figure differs materially.
reasoning: Stats NZ 'Building consents issued: February 2025', released 2 April 2025, reports 33,595 new homes consented in the year ended February 2025, down 7.4 percent from the year ended February 2024 (36,276). Both the level and the annual change match the criterion exactly, and the release date matches the speaker's 'released in April this year'. Composition given in the same release: 15,852 stand-alone houses (+2.3%) and 17,743 multi-unit homes (-14.6%). Checked for a disconfirming revision or a different vintage of the figure; independent outlets (interest.co.nz, PlaceMakers, Scoop's mirror of the Stats NZ release) all cite the same 33,595 / -7.4%.

statement: It’s the worst February for home consents since 2012.
criterion: Stats NZ monthly new dwellings consented series, February values 2012–2025: true if February 2025 is lower than every February from 2013 onward, false if any intervening February is lower.
reasoning: Stats NZ did say something like this about February 2025, but about stand-alone houses only: 'February 2025 had the fewest number of stand-alone houses consented in any February month since 2012' (1,191 stand-alone houses). The criterion tests the total new dwellings consented series, and on that measure the claim fails: February 2025 had 2,578 new dwellings consented (1,191 stand-alone + 1,387 multi-unit), which is higher than February 2017 (2,418 new dwellings, per interest.co.nz reporting the Stats NZ March 2017 release, which also gives Jan 2017 at 1,752), and higher again than Februaries 2013-2016, when annual consent totals were far lower (Feb 2016 approx. 2,379; Feb 2014 approx. 1,531). So at least one intervening February is lower and the criterion's 'false' condition is met on the dwellings series. Rated partly_true rather than false because the substance is real for the sub-category Stats NZ itself highlighted (stand-alone houses, a 13-year February low) - it is true only under a reading of 'home consents' the speaker did not signal. Note the monthly February 2025 breakdown is sourced from a trade outlet quoting the Stats NZ release; the Stats NZ page itself would not render for direct verification of the monthly figure.

statement: The previous Labour Government had built more houses, more social houses, for instance, since the 1970s, and to sit on this side of the House and watch all of that momentum disappear through what I believe to be poor decisions from the current Government—you can’t turn that ship around lightly.
criterion: HUD Public Housing Quarterly Report / Kāinga Ora stock series: true if net additional public housing places delivered 2017–2023 exceed those of every other parliamentary term since 1970, false if any earlier term delivered more.
reasoning: The documented substance holds. HUD/Kainga Ora figures cited by the then-government show a net increase of 12,017 public homes between October 2017 and April 2023 (9,917 of them new builds), taking total public housing places to 78,251 - and the programme is officially and repeatedly described as 'the biggest state house building programme since the 1970s'. That matches the speaker's wording ('more social houses... since the 1970s'). It does not satisfy the criterion as written, which requires exceeding every parliamentary term since 1970: the standard framing, used by the Labour government itself, explicitly concedes the 1970s were a larger building period, so a 1970s term plausibly delivered more. Two further qualifications: 2017-2023 spans two parliamentary terms (2017-20 and 2020-23), roughly 6,000 net places per term, so it is not a like-for-like comparison against single three-year terms; and National disputed the composition, arguing a large share of added places were purchased or leased from the private market rather than newly built (this does not affect the net-places figure the criterion asks about). Disconfirming check: I looked for a published term-by-term net public housing series back to 1970 - HUD's Public Housing Quarterly Reports only run from the mid-2010s, and the Te Ara total state housing stock series would not render, so the strict 'every term since 1970' test could not be fully verified either way.

statement: This drop came straight after the Government stopped Kāinga Ora building houses and cut $1.5 billion from the public housing build and that maintenance fund as well.
criterion: Budget 2024/2025 Vote Housing and Urban Development appropriations and the Kāinga Ora build programme decisions announced following the 2024 Kāinga Ora review: true if the reduction to public housing build and maintenance funding totals approximately $1.5 billion and new Kāinga Ora builds were halted or wound back, false if the appropriations show no cut of that scale.
reasoning: The second half of the criterion is clearly met: new Kāinga Ora builds were halted/wound back. The February 2025 turnaround plan stops net growth of state housing stock — 1,500 homes built or bought, fully offset by 700 demolitions and 800 sales (net zero), against a net +3,600 in the year to June 2024; Kāinga Ora cancelled ~60% of social housing projects planned for FY2025 (1,019 units) and scrapped developments worth nearly 3,500 homes. The $1.5 billion figure is only partly corroborated. It originates as Labour's own tally ($435m from the Kāinga Ora build programme + 'over $1 billion' from the maintenance fund), reported by RNZ as Kieran McAnulty's claim rather than as verified appropriations data. RNZ's reporting of the Budget 2024 savings breakdown for Kāinga Ora gives $464m operating maintenance, $126m capitalised maintenance, $130m staffing, $96m retrofit and $12m travel — about $828m — which with the $435m build reduction totals roughly $1.26b, not $1.5b, and puts the maintenance component nearer $590m than 'over $1 billion'. The $435m is also characterised by the government as unused large-scale-project funding held in contingency for cost overruns, so whether it is a cut to the build programme is contested; Bill English's later review found the planned savings were unlikely to be achieved. I could not read the Vote Housing and Urban Development appropriations tables directly (Treasury/Budget PDFs would not parse; RNZ article URLs returned HTTP 403), so the $1.5b is not disproved — it is a defensible order of magnitude built on an uncorroborated maintenance component and a contested build component. Substance holds, magnitude materially overstated: partly_true.

statement: When we think of the 20,000 construction jobs that have already been lost—which is 20,000 workers—we can only look at this particular bill, whilst we support it, being such a trivial, small step in the overall situation that we’re facing.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / filled jobs by industry for construction: true if employment in the construction sector fell by approximately 20,000 over the period from its recent peak to the September 2025 quarter, false if the fall is materially smaller.
reasoning: The criterion names the HLFS / employment by industry for construction, measured from the recent peak to the September 2025 quarter. The quarterly seasonally-adjusted NZ construction employment series (OECD Main Economic Indicators, sourced from Stats NZ HLFS) peaks at 309,597 in Q1 2023 (Q3 2023 = 307,646) and falls to 287,771 in Q3 2025 — a decline of about 21,800 from the Q1 2023 peak, or about 19,900 measured from the Q3 2023 level. Either way this is 'approximately 20,000', so the criterion is satisfied. Two caveats that do not change the verdict but qualify it. First, timing: McLellan spoke on 7 October 2025, before the September 2025 quarter was published; the then-latest figure (Q2 2025, 292,401) implied a fall of about 17,200 from peak, and Labour's own 28 July 2025 release used 18,000. Her number was therefore slightly ahead of the published data at the time, and was only vindicated by data released in November 2025. Second, measure sensitivity: the narrower Business Employment Data 'filled jobs' series (employees only, excluding the self-employed, who are numerous in construction) shows about 16,000 fewer construction jobs since December 2023, and a fall of 8,982 (4.5%) over the year to September 2025. The criterion names HLFS first, and HLFS supports the claim. Checked for disconfirming evidence: construction employment rebounds to 294,591 in Q4 2025, so Q3 2025 is a local trough — the ~20,000 figure holds at the date the criterion specifies but would be smaller a quarter later.

statement: In our emergency departments, 73.9 percent of patients were admitted, treated, or discharged within six hours during that quarter, up from 71.2 percent during the same period last year, despite increased attendances. For faster cancer treatment, 86.3 percent of patients started their treatment within 31 days following diagnosis, up from 83.5 percent at the same time last year.
criterion: Health New Zealand's published quarterly health target results for the April–June 2025 quarter and the same quarter of 2024: true if the shorter-stays-in-ED and faster-cancer-treatment figures match those stated to within rounding, false if either figure or either baseline is materially different.
reasoning: All four figures match the published health target results for the April–June 2025 quarter (Q4 2024/25) exactly. Emergency departments: 73.9% of patients admitted, treated or discharged within six hours, up from 71.2% in the same quarter of 2024. Faster cancer treatment: 86.3% started treatment within 31 days, up from 83.5%. These are the figures in the 30 September 2025 release of the quarterly results and are reproduced independently by New Zealand Doctor, which also gives the surrounding context (the 73.9% was just short of the 74% annual milestone for 2024/25, and down from 74.2% the previous quarter). The surrounding quarterly series is internally consistent with a real seasonal pattern rather than a cherry-picked comparison: Jul–Sep 2025 was 68.9% (from 67.5%) and Oct–Dec 2025 was 74.2% (from 72.1%), so each quarter is compared like-for-like against the same quarter a year earlier. The 'despite increased attendances' qualifier is also supported — ED attendances averaged 3,789/day in the Jul–Sep 2025 quarter against 3,279 in 2017. Checked for disconfirming evidence: I found no published figure contradicting either number or either baseline. One wording defect the criterion does not test — the faster cancer treatment target measures 31 days from the decision to treat, not 'following diagnosis' as Brown stated; the percentages are correct but the metric is mislabelled. Caveat on sourcing: the Health New Zealand health-targets landing page has been reorganised and now surfaces only the most recent quarter, so the Apr–Jun 2025 figures were confirmed via the official release text and the independent trade publication rather than by reading the archived dashboard directly.

statement: If his goal is to guarantee the rights of all New Zealanders, when will his Government be introducing legislation to address the 13,000 privately owned parcels of land that actually prevent people from accessing the foreshore and seabed?
criterion: LINZ cadastral records and published analyses of private freehold titles adjoining the coastal marine area: true if approximately 13,000 privately owned parcels abut the foreshore in a way that blocks public land access, false if the count of such access-blocking parcels is materially different.
reasoning: The count is approximately right: The Spinoff (Aug 2024) reports "just under 12,500 privately owned blocks of land that are within the foreshore area," consistent with the 2003 count of 12,499 private titles containing at least some foreshore and seabed. Ferris's 13,000 rounds this up by ~4%. But the criterion requires ~13,000 parcels that block public land access, and that is not what the 12,499 figure measures. The Spinoff explicitly notes "private ownership doesn't always mean the beach can't be accessed by land," while giving examples where it does (gated peninsulas in the Bay of Islands, Waiheke beaches reachable only via private farms). So the parcel count holds but the blanket claim that all of them prevent access is overstated. Checked for disconfirming evidence: no source gives a materially different total for privately titled foreshore parcels, and no source establishes ~13,000 as a count of access-blocking parcels specifically.

statement: I point to the fact that the previous Minister the member quoted at the start offered a 10 percent figure at one point.
criterion: Hansard, select committee evidence and contemporaneous media reporting of Christopher Finlayson's statements on the 2011 Act: true if he is recorded proposing or estimating a figure of around 10 percent of the coastline, false if no such statement by him can be found.
reasoning: Multiple independent contemporaneous and retrospective sources record Christopher Finlayson offering a ~10 percent figure for how much coastline would end up under customary marine title. In June 2010 Q&A he is recorded saying "In the round, based on the sort of information I have, based on my talking around the place, I'd say about 10% of the coastline would be under CMT." Democracy Action records that Finlayson "assured critics that only around 2000km of New Zealand's 20,000km coastline — or roughly 10 per cent — would end up being under customary title."
