The Democracy Project's account of the 2011 Act states "the then treaty negotiations minister, Chris Finlayson, predicted 10 percent." Goldsmith's claim is narrow — that Finlayson "offered a 10 percent figure at one point" — and is directly met. Looked for disconfirming evidence: no source suggests Finlayson never offered such a figure; the criticism in the sources is that his prediction proved far too low (later court decisions put close to 100% of the coastline in the frame), which concerns the accuracy of Finlayson's estimate, not whether he made it.

statement: You cannot increase spending by 84 percent, drive up inflation, drive up interest rates, put the economy into recession, and raise unemployment.
criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses series: compare total core Crown expenditure in 2017/18 with 2023/24 (or the last Labour-set Budget). True if the increase is approximately 84%, false if materially different.
reasoning: Treasury actuals for core Crown expenses: $76.3b (year ended 30 June 2017), $80.6b (2017/18), $139.0b (2023/24, the last Labour-set Budget year). The criterion's named comparison, 2017/18 vs 2023/24, gives +72.5% — materially below 84%. The most favourable legitimate alternative baseline, 2016/17 (last fully National-set year, since Labour took office in Oct 2017) to 2023/24, gives +82.2%, close to but still under 84%. Total Crown expenses ($104.0b in 2017/18 to $180.1b in 2023/24) give +73.2%. No standard Treasury series over Labour's term produces 84%. Searched for disconfirming evidence — i.e. a National/Treasury derivation that does yield 84% — and could not find the figure sourced in National Party or Treasury material; National's own "Labour Can't Stop Spending" page cites $116.1b promised vs $139b actual and departmental increases (72% MBIE, 137% MfE, 62% MCH), not an 84% aggregate. Substance (a very large spending increase, 72–82%) holds; the 84% figure is overstated. The causal claims about inflation, interest rates, recession and unemployment are outside the criterion and were not assessed.

statement: Yeah, it’s difficult, unemployment has ticked up a bit, but it’s the same as what it has been over a 30-year average, it’s significantly below what it has been over the last 15 years, and—unlike that member—we’re just not happy to actually be the party of people who don’t work.
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate for the September 2025 quarter compared with the mean of the series over the preceding 30 years and over the preceding 15 years. True only if it matches the 30-year mean and sits materially below the 15-year mean.
reasoning: Stats NZ/OECD-harmonised HLFS unemployment was 5.3% in the September 2025 quarter (5.2% in the June 2025 quarter, the latest print available when Luxon spoke). Computed from the quarterly series: the mean over 1995Q3-2025Q3 (~30 years) is 5.16%, so 'the same as the 30-year average' is accurate. But the mean over 2010Q4-2025Q3 (15 years) is 4.89% — unemployment was ABOVE the 15-year mean, not 'significantly below' it. The criterion required both halves; only the first holds. The claim would only work against the 15-year peak (6.7%, 2012Q3), which is not what was said.

statement: If the dire current state of the New Zealand economy is all someone else’s fault, why is it that the New Zealand economy shrunk by almost 1 percent at a time when other economies around the world that have been hit harder by Donald Trump’s tariffs—many of whom had a higher rate of inflation at the peak of the global pandemic—have been growing faster than New Zealand?
criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP for the June 2025 quarter (true if a contraction of approximately 0.9–1.0%), and OECD quarterly GDP growth for the same quarter across members with higher US tariff exposure and higher 2022 peak CPI. False if the contraction is materially smaller or if those comparators did not grow.
reasoning: Stats NZ reported GDP fell 0.9% in the June 2025 quarter (released 18 Sept 2025), far worse than the -0.3% consensus — matching 'almost 1 percent'. For the comparator half: OECD-wide Q2 2025 growth was +0.4%; economies with equal-or-greater US tariff exposure and higher 2022 peak CPI than NZ's 7.3% mostly grew — euro area +0.1%, UK +0.3%, Australia +0.6%, US +0.7%, France +0.3%, Japan +0.3%. Disconfirming check: Germany (-0.3%), Italy (-0.1%) and Canada (growth halted) did not grow, but none contracted anywhere near 0.9%, and the claim was 'many of whom', not all. Criterion met on both limbs.

statement: The committee has decided to reduce the OCR by 50 basis points. This is the 8th OCR reduction since August last year. At that time, the OCR was 5.5 percent. It is now at 2.5 percent.
criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Review of 8 October 2025 and the published OCR decision history: true if the 8 October decision was −50bp, the OCR is 2.5%, and there have been eight reductions since August 2024.
reasoning: RBNZ's 8 October 2025 Monetary Policy Review cut the OCR by 50 basis points to 2.5%, a larger move than the 25bp markets expected. The OCR was 5.5% before the easing cycle began in August 2024. Counting the reductions since: Aug 2024 (5.25), Oct 2024 (4.75), Nov 2024 (4.25), Feb 2025 (3.75), Apr 2025 (3.50), May 2025 (3.25), Aug 2025 (3.00), Oct 2025 (2.50) — exactly eight. All three components of the statement check out.

statement: Assuming today's reduction is passed on in full, a family with a 25-year $500,000 mortgage would have minimum repayments of $400 less a fortnight than they were in the middle of last year.
criterion: RBNZ floating first-mortgage rate series for June 2024 and October 2025 (adjusted for a full pass-through of the 50bp cut); compute the standard amortising repayment on $500,000 over 25 years at each rate. True if the fortnightly difference is approximately $400.
reasoning: Rate endpoints verified from ANZ's own rate-change announcements: the floating home loan rate was 8.64% in mid-2024 (ANZ's July 2024 release cut it by 15bp TO 8.49%, implying 8.64% prior, i.e. the rate prevailing in June 2024), and 6.29% immediately before the 8 October 2025 OCR cut (ANZ's October 2025 release cut floating by 40bp TO 5.89%, implying 6.29% prior). Applying the full 50bp pass-through Willis explicitly stipulated gives 5.79%. Standard amortisation of $500,000 over 25 years: at 8.64% the monthly repayment is $4,073 and at 5.79% it is $3,157, a difference of $916/month, or ~$423 per fortnight on a 12/26 fortnightly-equivalent basis. Computing a true fortnightly schedule (650 periods) instead gives $1,879 vs $1,451 = $428/fortnight. Checked the disconfirming direction: a smaller gap would require either a lower mid-2024 rate or a higher post-cut rate, but ANZ's mid-2024 floating rate was at its cycle peak of 8.64% and other major banks were clustered at 6.24-6.34% pre-cut, so the average would give ~5.77% under full pass-through and an even slightly larger saving. Every reasonable fortnightly convention (12/26, true fortnightly, monthly/2) yields at least $400. Contemporary reporting records Willis saying 'more than $400', and the arithmetic supports that stronger form. Claim holds and is if anything mildly conservative.

statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his cuts to jobseeker will impact over 2,000 18- and 19-year-olds who may be disabled, sick, or experiencing severe mental ill health, and, if so, how does he justify this?
criterion: MSD benefit statistics and the regulatory impact statement for the 18/19-year-old jobseeker parental assistance test: the estimated number of affected 18- and 19-year-old recipients recorded with a health condition or disability. True if above 2,000.
reasoning: The criterion asks for the number of affected 18- and 19-year-old recipients recorded with a health condition or disability, true if above 2,000. Two independent sources clear that bar. First, MSD confirmed to RNZ that 2,685 18- and 19-year-olds were receiving Jobseeker Support Health Condition Disability as at 30 June 2025. Second, the Regulatory Impact Statement 'Tightening access to Jobseeker Support and Emergency Benefit for 18 and 19 year olds' (MSD, finalised 10 September 2025) states at para 7 that approximately 15,060 Jobseeker Support recipients were 18 or 19 as of June 2025, and at para 26 that 'As of June 2025, roughly one-fifth of Jobseeker Support recipients aged 18 and 19 were receiving Jobseeker Support - Health Condition, Injury or Disability' - about 3,000. The RIS confirms the design point that makes the claim bite: the Parental Assistance Test applies to all Jobseeker sub-types, not just Work Ready, so HCD recipients are in scope (para 26: 'Because the changes will be applied to all of the different sub-types of Jobseeker Support... disabled people are more likely to be affected'). I checked the disconfirming reading: if 'impact' meant 'certain to lose the benefit' rather than 'subject to the new test', the number would be lower, since the RIS estimates ~4,300 across all sub-types become ineligible in 2027/28 under the revised parental income limit (vs 9,205 under the Budget 2025 design), and one-fifth of 4,300 is ~860. But Swarbrick's wording was 'impact', and the hedged 'who may be disabled, sick, or experiencing severe mental ill health' matches the exposure reading; on that reading the figure is 2,685, comfortably above 2,000.

statement: Why are there 10,000 more unemployed young people and 36,000 fewer jobs in this country since he took office, if not because of his Government’s billions of dollars of cuts to investment?
criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployed count for the 15–24 age group, and the Monthly Employment Indicators filled-jobs series, comparing November 2023 with the latest release before October 2025. True if the changes are approximately +10,000 and −36,000.
reasoning: Both legs check out against the series named in the criterion. Youth unemployment (HLFS 15-24 unemployed, unadjusted, via the OECD/FRED mirror of the Stats NZ series): Sep 2023 quarter 49,000; Dec 2023 quarter 54,900; Jun 2025 quarter 62,800 (the June 2025 quarter is the latest release before October 2025, since the September 2025 quarter was not published until November 2025). Luxon took office 27 November 2023, which falls between the Sep and Dec 2023 quarters; interpolating to November gives ~52,900, hence ~+9,900 - essentially exactly the 10,000 claimed. I validated the 62,800 figure independently against interest.co.nz's breakdown of the June 2025 quarter (37,100 unemployed aged 15-19 plus 25,700 aged 20-24 = 62,800), which confirms the OECD series matches Stats NZ HLFS. Filled jobs (Monthly Employment Indicators, seasonally adjusted): November 2023 was ~2.385m (the December 2023 release reported December up 4,746 to 2.39m from November); August 2025 was 2.35m (up 4,814 on July). That is a fall of roughly 35,000, consistent with the 36,000 claimed. Disconfirming check on the youth leg, which is the more baseline-sensitive of the two: using the Dec 2023 quarter alone as the baseline gives only +7,900, while the seasonally adjusted series gives +14,100 (52,848 to 66,939). The claim's own stated baseline is when the government took office, i.e. November 2023, and on that baseline the figure lands at ~10,000; the alternative baselines bracket rather than contradict it. Both numbers are within ordinary rounding of the claim.

statement: Growing and strengthening the education workforce is exactly what this Government is doing, and, as I’ve already told the member on numerous occasions, the schooling teacher workforce grew by 2.5 percent in 2024, delivering 864 new teachers—the largest year-on-year increase since records began in 2009.
criterion: Ministry of Education Teacher Workforce / Education Counts staffing series for calendar 2024: true if the year-on-year change is ~2.5% and ~864 FTE/headcount teachers, and no year from 2009 onward shows a larger increase; false if the growth figure differs materially or an earlier year in the series exceeds it.
reasoning: The Ministry of Education / Beehive figure is 1,864 new teachers in 2024, not 864. The 2.5% growth rate is correct (workforce 75,968 in 2024, up from ~74,100) and the Ministry does state this was the largest year-on-year increase since the series began in 2009; the breakdown is 1,128 primary + 736 secondary = 1,864. The count as quoted is materially wrong and internally inconsistent with the 2.5% in the same sentence (2.5% of ~76,000 is ~1,875). Substance and record claim hold; the headline number does not.

statement: On provisional figures for 2025, there’s been a 30 percent increase in domestic students enrolling in initial teacher education for the first time.
criterion: Ministry of Education / Tertiary Education Commission provisional 2025 enrolment data for first-time domestic initial teacher education students: true if the increase on 2024 is ~30%, false if materially different or if the comparison base is not first-time domestic enrolments.
reasoning: Ministry of Education data reported September 2025: 3,525 first-time domestic enrolments in initial teacher education year-to-date 2025 vs 2,715 in the same period of 2024, a 29.8% increase. The comparison base is first-time domestic ITE enrolments, exactly as the criterion requires, and the figures were provisional/year-to-date as Stanford signalled. Breakdown: primary +31%, secondary +28%, ECE +24%. Disconfirming check: the separate 6.3% figure (3,400 to 3,615) is the 2024 full-year number, not a revision; the Ministry was still citing the 30% figure for 2025 in a February 2026 release.

statement: Why were teachers offered a pay rise of less than inflation when Crown board members are getting up to an 80 percent increase?
criterion: (a) The NZEI/PPTA collective offer on the table in October 2025 compared against the Stats NZ CPI annual rate for the September 2025 quarter — true if the offered annual increase is below that rate; (b) the Cabinet Fees Framework / Public Service Commission 2025 fee determinations for Crown entity boards — true if any published increase reaches ~80%.
reasoning: (a) Stats NZ CPI annual inflation to the September 2025 quarter was 3.0%. The teacher offers around October 2025 were 1% per year for three years (rejected August 2025) and then an improved 2.5% plus 2.1% over two years (~2.3%/year annualised) — both below 3.0%. PPTA stated the offer was 'below current and projected rates of inflation.' (b) The Cabinet Fees Framework effective 1 July 2025 lifted Group 3 (Crown entities, autonomous Crown entities, TEIs) fee ranges by 80%, with the top chair fee moving from $90,000 to $160,000. Disconfirming check on whether this was only a nominal range change: actual ministerial approvals reached or exceeded 80% — EPA chair $53,000 to $96,700 (+82.5%), NZ Artificial Limb Service chair +80.2%, Antarctica NZ chair +118%. Both halves of the comparison hold as stated.

statement: Does the Prime Minister understand, then, the basic maths that if there are four job seekers to every job that is available in this country, all of his cuts to jobseeker support couldn’t hope to possibly punish people into ghost jobs but will only deepen poverty and homelessness?
criterion: Ratio of MSD jobseeker support recipients (or HLFS unemployed) to online job vacancies (MBIE Jobs Online / Seek listings) at September 2025. True if approximately 4:1.
reasoning: RNZ ran this exact calculation on 7 October 2025, the day before Swarbrick spoke. Using MSD Work Ready Jobseeker recipients against online job ads, it found 'just under four people for every job ad, nationwide' — down from about nine in 2020, roughly twice the 2021-22 rate, and steady since. On the alternative measure the criterion also allows (HLFS unemployed per job ad) the ratio was five to one, so Swarbrick's figure is if anything conservative. Regional detail in the same piece (e.g. Hawke's Bay: 7,359 jobseekers, 568 Seek listings ≈ 13:1) is consistent. Checked for disconfirming evidence: the only way to get a materially lower ratio is to count all vacancies rather than online ads, but the criterion specifies online job vacancies (MBIE Jobs Online / Seek), and on that basis ~4:1 holds at September/October 2025. Note MBIE's Jobs Online is an index rather than a count, so the RNZ ratio rests on Seek/Trade Me ad counts.

statement: In the last administration, with 3.2 to 3.5 percent unemployment, the Labour-Greens Government drove a 50 percent increase and put 60,000 more people on jobseeker benefit.
criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets: jobseeker support recipient counts at the start and end of the 2017–2023 period, and the Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate over that period. True if the rise is approximately 60,000 and approximately 50%.
reasoning: The two headline numbers check out almost exactly. MSD's September 2018 benefit fact sheet reports working-age Jobseeker Support rose by 8,917 to 129,643, implying ~120,726 at September 2017. MSD data via Figure.NZ gives 181,509 at 2023 Q3 (and 189,795 at 2023 Q4). September 2017 to September 2023 is therefore +60,783, or +50.3% — 'a 50 percent increase and 60,000 more people' is accurate, and a Beehive release citing '~70,000' suggests the December 2023 endpoint would make it larger still. What does not hold is the framing 'with 3.2 to 3.5 percent unemployment'. Stats NZ HLFS: unemployment was ~4.6% when Labour took office in 2017, peaked at 5.3% in 2020, hit its record low of 3.2% only in the December 2021 quarter, and was 3.9% in the September 2023 quarter. The 3.2-3.5% band describes 2021-22 alone, not 'the last administration'; much of the benefit rise is the 2020 COVID spike, when unemployment was well above that range. 'Labour-Greens Government' is also loose — the Greens held a confidence-and-supply agreement (2017-20) and a cooperation agreement (2020-23), not coalition seats. Substance holds; the conditioning clause is materially overstated.

statement: This is a Government that is—I’ll tell you what the landlord cut did create: rents have gone down $5 a week, instead of up $180 a week.
criterion: MBIE tenancy bond data / Stats NZ rental price index: change in median weekly rent over the year to September 2025. True if the median fell by approximately $5 a week; false if rents rose. The $180 counterfactual should be checked against whatever projection it is drawn from.
reasoning: Rents were falling, so the claim is not false in direction. The most recent Tenancy Services bond data available on 8 October 2025 (July 2025 month, reported by interest.co.nz on 19 September 2025) put the national median at $590/week, down $5 from June's $595 — an exact match for Luxon's figure, but month-on-month. On an annual basis: HUD's rental price index had nationwide rents for new tenancies down 0.4% year-on-year at September 2025 (about -$2.40 on a ~$590 median), for the third month running; the bond median for Q3 2025 was $590 against $600 in Q2; and by November 2025 the bond median was $595, a $5/0.8% drop year-on-year. realestate.co.nz later recorded the first annual fall in average weekly rent in a decade ($638 to $627). So 'down about $5 a week' is defensible depending on series, and rents certainly did not rise. The $180 counterfactual is also a real number — it is National's own MBIE bond-database figure for the cumulative rise across Labour's six years, median $400/week to $580/week — but it is a six-year total set against a one-month (or at best one-year) $5 fall, a comparison the phrasing does not signal. The causal attribution to 'the landlord cut' (restored interest deductibility) is not established: the fall is generally attributed to collapsed net migration (down 74% year to March 2025) and increased rental supply, with bonds lodged up year-on-year for five straight quarters.

statement: We are determined to reverse the trend we inherited, which saw people under the age of 25 on jobseeker spend an average of 18 more years on benefit. This has been 49 percent longer than in 2017.
criterion: MSD benefit system actuarial valuation / future years on benefit projections for jobseeker recipients aged under 25, comparing the latest valuation with the 2017 valuation: true if the average is ~18 years and the increase on 2017 is ~49%, false if either figure differs materially or the 2017 comparison uses a different cohort definition.
reasoning: Both figures trace to MSD's Social Outcomes Model / Benefit System Insights report released October 2024, which the Minister has cited repeatedly: people under 25 on Jobseeker Support are projected to spend an average of about 18 more years on a benefit over their lifetimes — 49 per cent longer than in 2017. The wording in the quote matches the published source almost exactly. Corroborating MSD material shows the same series moving in that direction (future years on benefit for under-25 Jobseeker recipients: 16.7 years at Sept 2021, 18.9 years at Sept 2022), so ~18 years is the right order of magnitude and the 2017 baseline comparison is MSD's own, not a re-cut cohort. Caveat noted but not disqualifying: the underlying 2017 valuation table was not directly readable (the MSD/Beehive PDF would not render), so the 49% is confirmed via MSD's published statement of it rather than by recomputing from the raw valuation. Also, the figures are from the Oct 2024 report, a year before this Oct 2025 statement, and the framing 'the trend we inherited' is rhetorical — but the criterion tests the numbers, and the numbers hold.

statement: Why has she made it so that two parents who are both working 27 hours each on the minimum wage can now work 11 hours less a week and yet be financially better off?
criterion: Modelling of the parental income test threshold combined with Working for Families abatement and the jobseeker entitlement for an 18–19-year-old, at the April 2025 minimum wage: true if net household income at 2×16 hours exceeds that at 2×27 hours, false if it does not.
reasoning: The abatement cliff she is pointing at is real and well documented, but the specific scenario as stated does not clear the criterion's test. At the April 2025 minimum wage of $23.50/hr, two parents at 27 hours each earn $65,988/yr, just above the $65,529 parental income cut-out (The Spinoff independently makes this exact calculation: 27 hours each reaches the threshold, 26.5 hours each stays under). Dropping to 16 hours each gives $39,104/yr. Household take-home falls by roughly $21,700 (approx. $55,500 net at 2x27 vs approx. $33,800 at 2x16), while the gain is the 18-19-year-old's Jobseeker Support at $268.13/wk after tax = approx. $13,900/yr. Adding the largest plausible Working for Families offset (abatement at 27% above $42,700 on the approx. $23,300 of income given up = approx. $6,300) still leaves the household behind, and only unusually large Accommodation Supplement gains for a renting family with additional dependent children could close it. So net household income at 2x16 hours does NOT exceed that at 2x27 hours in the general case. It does work under a different reading — 11 hours less across the household combined (approx. 5.5 hrs each, approx. 21.5 hrs each = $52,546) leaves them roughly $3,000/yr ahead — but she said '27 hours each' and then omitted 'each' from the 11, so that reading is not one she signalled. Commentators including Auckland academics confirm the underlying perverse incentive (a sole parent on $75,000 is under $1,000 in the hand better off for her last $20,000 of earnings, and the 'logical thing' is to stop earning it), which is why this is overstated rather than false.

statement: How can she claim that this change will incentivise young people when her Government has increased university fees, increased youth unemployment, cut the Apprenticeship Boost, and made life even harder for working Kiwi families struggling with the cost of living crisis?
criterion: (a) TEC annual maximum fee movement settings for 2024 and 2025; (b) Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate for 15–24-year-olds, September 2023 quarter versus the most recent quarter before October 2025; (c) Budget 2024/2025 appropriations and eligibility settings for Apprenticeship Boost. True if all three moved in the stated direction, false if any did not.
reasoning: All three testable legs moved in the stated direction. (a) University fees: the TEC Annual Maximum Fee Movement was set at 2.8% for 2024 and raised to 6.0% for 2025 (Gazette notices 2023-go2541 and 2024-go3199), more than doubling the permitted increase; separately, first-year Fees Free ended in 2024 and was replaced from 1 January 2025 by a final-year scheme paid only on completion from 2026, so first-year students now pay fees they previously did not. The Tertiary Education Union reports the cost of tertiary education rose 19% over two years. (b) Youth unemployment: the 15-24 rate was approx. 10.7% on an annual-average basis in 2023 (overall unemployment was 3.9% in the Sept 2023 quarter), and had risen to 13.1% by the September 2024 quarter and 15.2% by September 2025 — so the most recent quarter before October 2025 (June 2025) sits around 14%, unambiguously higher than September 2023. (c) Apprenticeship Boost: from 1 January 2025 only first-year apprentices in targeted industry areas remain eligible for the $500/month subsidy; second-year apprentice support ended 31 December 2024. That is a narrowing of eligibility, i.e. a cut. The trailing 'cost of living crisis' clause is rhetorical characterisation rather than a checkable figure and was not assessed. One framing caveat: government does not set university fees directly, it sets the cap universities charge within — but it raised that cap and removed first-year Fees Free, so the direction is the speaker's.

statement: The 4.7 percent that is on the table at the moment is a fair and reasonable offer that we hope the New Zealand Educational Institute and Post Primary Teachers’ Association members will take seriously.
criterion: The pay offer documents / union and Ministry of Education bargaining updates current at 8 October 2025: true if the headline offer to NZEI and PPTA members is 4.7%, false if the figure differs or applies only to part of the term.
reasoning: The 4.7% figure is genuine and is the Government's own published number, but it is the top-of-scale figure rather than a member-wide headline, and it is a within-12-months figure inside a longer agreement term. The Public Service Commission's revised primary teachers' offer of 6 September 2025 (the offer live on 8 October) states the 4.7% increase applies to 'teachers at the top of the pay scale' within 12 months, while teachers not yet at the top instead receive built-in progression of 3.9%-7.7%. On the secondary side, the Ministry's STCA negotiation page shows the offer chronology (16 July, 5 September, 10 October 2025 — so the September offer was the one on the table on 8 October) and records that the eventual settlement gave a cumulative 4.7% only to secondary teachers on the top two trained-scale steps (9 and 10), with 4.6% for the remainder. So the number is not invented and is defensible as the headline, but 'the 4.7 percent that is on the table' materially overstates what most NZEI and PPTA members were being offered, and it describes a 12-month increase rather than the whole term. Checked for disconfirming evidence: no source shows a different headline percentage or shows 4.7% applying uniformly to all members.

statement: Does the Minister for the Public Service’s comments that people are striking just to have a long weekend increase or decrease the likelihood of strike action?
criterion: Public record of Judith Collins' statements as Minister for the Public Service in the weeks before 8 October 2025 (media transcripts, press conference recordings, Hansard): true if she is recorded characterising strike action as being for a long weekend, false if no such remark exists in the record.
reasoning: Judged against the criterion's window ('in the weeks before 8 October 2025'), no record was found of Judith Collins characterising strike action as being for a long weekend. Collins IS on record with a long-weekend framing, but roughly a fortnight AFTER this question: in her open letter of ~19-22 October 2025 about the 23 October mega-strike, she urged parents to ask 'why their union arranged a strike in a week when many schools already have teacher-only days, followed by Labour Day on Monday.' Even that later remark criticises the strike's timing relative to Labour Weekend; it does not say people are striking 'just to have a long weekend.' Her documented commentary before 8 October is different in kind — a 'political stunt' with 'no genuine engagement' by the PPTA (August), 'unfair, unproductive and unnecessary,' a 'coordinated attack' on students, and accusing teachers of using kids 'like footballs.' Searched for disconfirming evidence specifically: the Public Service Commission's own chronology of public sector industrial action (Aug 8, Aug 13, Aug 20, Sep 6, Sep 8, Sep 12, then Oct 14-17) contains no such Collins statement, and repeated searches of Beehive releases and RNZ/1News/NZ Herald coverage of the August and September strike rounds surfaced nothing. Caveat on confidence: beehive.govt.nz, rnz.co.nz, scoop and the Newstalk ZB audio pages all returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch, so this rests on search-index snippets plus the Public Service Commission page; an unindexed radio or press-conference remark cannot be completely excluded, and the substance (Collins disparaging strikers, and later invoking Labour Weekend) is partially supported.

statement: Our Government has turned around the delivery of school property, we’ve halved the cost of building new classrooms, and children deserve to live in safe, warm, dry classrooms and we’re delivering just that.
criterion: Ministry of Education per-classroom capital cost figures for standard classroom builds, comparing the pre-2023 average with the 2025 average: true if the average unit cost has fallen by ~50%, false if the reduction is materially smaller or the comparison relies on a different classroom specification.
reasoning: The ~50% magnitude checks out against the Ministry's own figures, but the comparison relies on a changed classroom specification, which the criterion names as a failure condition. On magnitude: the June 2024 Ministerial Inquiry into School Property recorded that the average cost of a new classroom had reached $1.2 million (bespoke, architecturally designed open-plan buildings having become standard by end-2023), with projections of $1.8m for projects started Oct 2023-June 2026; the 2025 average is ~$620,000, a ~48% fall. Stanford's own formulation nine days after this quote is 'We've halved the cost of delivering new classrooms from $1.2 million to $620,000.' On specification: the saving comes precisely from changing what is built — Stanford attributes it to 'offsite manufacturing, modular classrooms, repeatable designs, simple and standard solutions,' i.e. bespoke architect-designed open-plan builds replaced by standardised modular ones. That is not a like-for-like unit-cost reduction on the same product. The inquiry also notes site works budgeted at roughly $500,000 per teaching space, which sit outside the quoted unit cost, and I encountered one framing of the fall as a 28% reduction against the end-of-2023 figure, which I could not trace to a primary source. Searched specifically for disconfirming evidence and for any independent fact-check of the like-for-like question; none was found either confirming or rebutting it. Note: rnz.co.nz, beehive.govt.nz and newsroom.co.nz returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch, so parts rest on search-index snippets; the national.org.nz mirror of Stanford's 17 October release was fetched directly.

statement: This survey follows an identical survey in 2022, and most critically, it shows that in nearly every single measure for nearly every type of person, attitudes to attendance are improving.
criterion: The ERO report 'Back to class: How are attitudes to attendance changing?' and its 2022 predecessor: true if the questions are materially the same and the large majority of measures moved favourably across respondent groups, false if the instruments differ materially or a substantial share of measures were flat or worse.
reasoning: The second half of the criterion fails. ERO's Part 5 opening (report p55) states the opposite of Seymour's characterisation: 'We found mixed results. Parents' overall attitudes to attendance have improved, but attitudes to daily attendance haven't changed much, and attitudes about "justified" absences have worsened.' Finding 4 is headed 'However, parents are not yet taking daily attendance more seriously' and Finding 5 'Parents are increasingly content for children to miss school for some justified reasons.' A substantial share of measures moved unfavourably: parents comfortable with their child missing a couple of days rose 50%->59%; willing to allow absence for out-of-school events 41%->58%; for family/cultural events 67%->76%; for a one-or-two-day family holiday 46%->47% (flat); parents' view that school is important for their child's future 92%->93% (flat). Two respondent groups are explicit exceptions: Maori students are 'the only group of students whose attitudes to daily attendance have not improved' (67%), and Maori parents' attitudes 'have declined the most, down 5 percentage points since 2022.' The student-side measures did improve broadly (school important for future 78%->82%, daily attendance important 67%->73%, never want to miss school 15%->28%, low socio-economic +12pp), and two parent measures improved (comfort with week-plus absence 41%->31%, law as a reason 58%->65%), so the underlying direction Seymour describes is real but materially overstated. On the first half of the criterion: the instruments are closely linked but not 'identical' as stated. The report says the review 'builds on ERO's previous research, including our 2022 study,' and that Term 2 2025 timing 'was chosen to link up as closely as practical with our last data collection on this topic which spanned both Terms 2 and 3 in 2022.' Enough items were repeated verbatim to support the 2022-vs-2025 percentage-point comparisons in Parts 4 and 5, but ERO nowhere describes the survey as identical, the collection window differs, and 2025 adds large new sections (school actions, rewards and consequences, closures, roles and responsibilities).

statement: Critically, 82 percent of students from poorer families said that going to school is important for their future. That compares with 84 percent of students from wealthier families.
criterion: The Education Review Office 2025 attendance survey report: true if it records approximately 82% of students from lower-decile/poorer households and 84% from wealthier households agreeing that school attendance matters for their future; false if the figures or the gap are materially different.
reasoning: Exact match to the source. ERO, 'Back to class: How are attitudes to attendance changing?' (October 2025), summary report p3: 'Students in low socio-economic communities now think school is just as important for their future as students in high socio-economic communities (82 percent and 84 percent respectively). Low socio-economic students' attitudes were previously 10 percentage points lower than high socio-economic students.' Both figures and the 2-point gap are as Seymour stated. Two small wording notes that do not change the verdict: ERO classifies by the socio-economic level of the school's community (Equity Index), not by household income directly, and the measure is 'school is important for their future' rather than the narrower 'going to school' (the separate daily-attendance measure is 78% low vs 73% high socio-economic, Figure 3). The criterion explicitly admits a lower-decile reading, and decile/Equity Index is a school-level measure, so this is within what was asked. Checked for disconfirming evidence: no other figures in the report contradict these, and the corresponding 2022 baseline (a 10-point gap) is consistent with the direction Seymour was describing.

statement: Three years ago, it was four out of 10 parents who thought it was OK for their children to miss a week of school.
criterion: The 2022 Education Review Office attendance survey of parents: true if roughly 40% of parents reported being comfortable with their child missing a week or more of school; false if the reported proportion is materially different.
reasoning: Confirmed against the source in two places. ERO summary report p4, Finding 3: 'Now only three in ten parents (31 percent) are comfortable with keeping their child off school for a week or more in a term compared to four in ten (41 percent) in 2022.' The full research report repeats this at p56 and charts it as Figure 28 ('Percent of parents reporting on their comfort with their child missing a week or more of school in a term, 2022 and 2025': 41% in 2022, 31% in 2025), with p58 adding 'down from more than two in five (41 percent) in 2022.' Seymour spoke on 2025-10-08, so 'three years ago' correctly identifies the 2022 comparison year, and 41% is squarely 'four out of 10.' His paraphrase 'thought it was OK for their children to miss a week of school' fairly renders ERO's 'comfortable with keeping their child off school for a week or more in a term.' A related 2022 measure points the same way: 35% of parents were willing to keep their child off for holidays of a week or more, down to 28% in 2025.

statement: An analysis of 22 scientific articles that are relevant shows that piglet mortality risk is 14 percent higher in systems that do not confine sows after farrowing.
criterion: The review of 22 studies underlying MPI's advice on the draft pig welfare code: true if it reports piglet mortality risk approximately 14% higher in non-confinement farrowing systems; false if the cited review reports no such difference or a materially different effect size.
reasoning: The review is Glencorse, Plush, Hazel et al. 2019 (Animals 9(11):957), a systematic review and meta-analysis retaining 22 publications, which reports a 14% increase in the relative risk of piglet mortality in farrowing pens compared with crates (p=0.0015), mainly from crushing. MPI's own Literature compendium on the draft Code of Welfare: Pigs cites exactly this figure and study count, confirming it is the review underlying the advice named in the criterion. Study count and effect size both match the quote. Caveat on strength, not accuracy: the same paper found no difference in stillbirths or piglets weaned, and roughly 40% of individual studies found higher mortality in crates.

statement: Most of the rest of the world is at 33 days; we are reducing down to seven.
criterion: Comparative regulation of post-farrowing sow confinement in major pig-producing jurisdictions (EU Council Directive 2008/120/EC, plus Sweden, Norway, Switzerland, Australia, the United States): true if the modal permitted confinement period across those jurisdictions is about 33 days; false if most permit indefinite confinement or prohibit crates outright, either of which would make '33 days' unrepresentative.
reasoning: 33 days is New Zealand's own current maximum (being cut to 7 days, max 4 post-farrowing); no other jurisdiction sets a 33-day limit. EU Directive 2008/120/EC requires group housing only from 4 weeks after service until 1 week before expected farrowing, then permits crating through weaning with no cap (~35 days in practice — the figure Germany is replacing with a 5-day maximum from 2036). Australia and the US set no legal limit either. Sweden (1987), Switzerland (1997) and Norway (2000, 7-day temporary crating only) prohibit crates; Austria and Finland are phasing them out. The criterion's falsifier is therefore met on the legal reading: most named jurisdictions either allow indefinite confinement until weaning or ban crates outright. The claim holds only as a description of typical practice in the major producing jurisdictions (~5 weeks), a reading the speaker did not signal.

statement: Is he aware that it is a profound behavioural need of mother pigs to build a nest 24 hours before giving birth, and if they are caged it is deeply distressing for them, they will literally paw the ground, often bloodying their snouts, trying to build a nest?
criterion: Peer-reviewed animal-behaviour literature on pre-partum nest-building in domestic sows (e.g. Applied Animal Behaviour Science reviews, NAWAC's code review evidence): true if nest-building is documented as a strongly motivated behaviour occurring roughly 24 hours before parturition and if thwarting it in crates is associated with stress indicators including snout abrasion from bar-directed rooting; false if the literature does not support the timing or the distress response.
reasoning: The peer-reviewed literature supports each element. Nest-building is triggered by the pre-partum progesterone drop and prolactin rise and begins approximately 24 h before parturition, with the sow rooting and pawing to dig a hollow before gathering material; it is internally motivated and performed regardless of substrate availability. Confinement across that 24-h window disrupts it, producing elevated plasma cortisol, bar-biting and repetitive pressing/rooting of the snout against crate fixtures. The specific injury is documented: sows wear down front hooves and suffer snout abrasions from performing the behaviour against crate materials, and a comparative study found fewer frustration behaviours in loose sows (bar biting 3.3±2.12 crated vs 0.5±0.29 non-crated) and fewer facial injuries after farrowing. Disconfirming check: one review notes increased nosing of crate features but not bar biting during farrowing itself, which narrows the timing of some indicators but does not contradict the pre-farrowing pattern.

statement: How does he justify extending the use of cruel farrowing crates indefinitely when every animal welfare organisation in New Zealand, including the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee [NAWAC], and 73 percent of New Zealanders oppose the use of farrowing crates because of worse welfare outcomes for mother pigs and piglets?
criterion: Two checks: (a) NAWAC's published advice and its reconsideration on the draft pig code — true if NAWAC's standing position opposes farrowing crates, false if it accepted limited post-farrowing crating; (b) the published polling behind the 73% figure (SPCA/Horizon or similar) — true if a national poll found approximately 73% opposition, false if no such poll exists or found materially different support.
reasoning: (b) holds: a nationally representative Verian poll commissioned by SAFE in September 2025 found 74% of New Zealanders oppose the use of farrowing crates and 73% support a complete ban, so the 73% figure is real and correctly scaled (a separate Horizon/SPCA poll of 10-16 Oct 2025 found 75% wanting a phase-out, but that postdates the quote). (a) does not hold as stated. NAWAC did disagree with the Government's reforms - chair Matthew Stone advised Minister Hoggard he was 'not satisfied' that three days' pre-farrowing confinement met nesting needs and that current crate practices fell 'below the minimum standards' of the Animal Welfare Act - so NAWAC opposed the indefinite extension. But NAWAC's own position is not blanket opposition to farrowing crates: its proposed code and consultation options permitted confinement for up to 72 hours post-farrowing, and the draft allowed up to 5 days pre-farrowing and 4 weeks lactation confinement transitionally. Under the criterion as written ('false if it accepted limited post-farrowing crating'), that check fails. The blanket 'every animal welfare organisation in New Zealand' is also not verifiable as an absolute. Substance holds - the polling number is accurate and NAWAC did oppose the Government's move - but the NAWAC characterisation is materially overstated.

statement: Over the next four years, we have budgeted to invest a record $61.8 billion in public infrastructure, and this number is only set to grow with new capital earmarked for allocation and is a huge step up from the $50.6 billion the previous Government invested between 2019 and 2023.
criterion: Budget 2025 capital allowance and the National Infrastructure Pipeline / Treasury capital investment figures: true if the four-year budgeted public infrastructure capital total is approximately $61.8b and the comparable 2019–2023 figure is approximately $50.6b on a like-for-like basis; false if the two figures are drawn from different bases or are materially different.
reasoning: The $61.8b is a real, sourced government figure: Willis's own Budget 2025 speech (22 May 2025) states 'Government infrastructure investment over the forecast period now totals around $61.8 billion.' Two problems against the criterion. First, the period: $61.8b covers the BEFU 2025 forecast period, and Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop subsequently described the same $61.8b as 'central government capital investment expected over the next five years' (November 2025), not four - so 'over the next four years' compresses the window. Second, the comparator: I could not locate the $50.6b figure for 2019-2023 in any Treasury, Beehive, Budget or Infrastructure Commission source, and its framing ('the previous Government invested') describes actual past spend measured against a budgeted forward forecast - different bases, which the criterion treats as disqualifying. Note also that Labour's own Budget 2022 projected $61.9b of Crown infrastructure spending from 2022 to 2026 on a comparable forward-plan basis, which sits awkwardly with 'record.' Headline number substantiated; the four-year framing and the like-for-like comparison are not.

statement: The private sector builds a significant amount of New Zealand’s infrastructure, and when private sector projects like Auckland port and major housing developments can’t even get a consent, that holds it back, which is why fast track is so important, and which is why today’s 50-basis-point Official Cash Rate reduction is also pretty important.
criterion: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand Monetary Policy Review of 8 October 2025: true if the OCR was cut by 50 basis points on that date; false if the cut was a different size or no cut was made.
reasoning: The criterion asks only about the RBNZ Monetary Policy Review of 8 October 2025. On Wednesday 8 October 2025 the RBNZ Monetary Policy Committee reached consensus to reduce the Official Cash Rate by 50 basis points, from 3.00% to 2.50%. The RBNZ's own release is titled 'OCR reduced to 2.5%' and RNZ's report is headlined 'Reserve Bank slashes Official Cash Rate by 50 basis points.' I checked for the disconfirming possibility of a 25bp cut: markets and economists were split 25/50 beforehand, and the RBNZ explicitly said it considered a smaller cut but chose the larger one; the 25bp cut to 2.25% was the separate November 2025 decision. Willis's characterisation of the cut's size and date is correct.

statement: In fact, we built more classrooms in the last year than the last Government did. We built more social housing in our last 23 months than that Government did in its last three years.
criterion: Ministry of Education school property delivery figures for new teaching spaces by year, and HUD/Kāinga Ora public housing supply reports: true if classrooms delivered in the year to mid-2025 exceed the highest comparable year under the 2017–2023 Government, and if net public housing places added over the 23 months to October 2025 exceed those added in the three years to October 2023; false on either count if the comparison reverses, and false if the housing figure counts gross builds against the predecessor's net additions.
reasoning: Two conjoined claims, each directionally supported but materially overstated by an unsignalled framing. CLASSROOMS: MoE/ministerial figures support a year-on-year comparison — the average classroom cost was cut 28% (from ~$1.2m at end-2023 to ~$620k in 2025), allowing roughly 30-31% more classrooms delivered in 2024 than in 2023, and ~641 new classrooms were planned for 2024. So 'more classrooms than the last Government' holds only against the predecessor's FINAL YEAR. Said flat, the phrase reads as more than the last Government built at all, which is plainly false — the 2017-2023 government delivered thousands of teaching spaces over six years. I could not obtain an independent MoE per-year delivery series to test the criterion's 'highest comparable year under 2017-2023' test; the 30-31% figure is the government's own. HOUSING: the coalition's own figure (Beehive/HUD, 11 Sept 2025) is 'over 6,800 net new social homes' by Kainga Ora and CHPs since November 2023 (~22 months). The predecessor's comparable net additions: total public housing places were 74,337 at 30 Jun 2021, 76,253 at 30 Jun 2022 and 78,251 at Apr 2023 — about +2,000/yr, giving roughly 6,000-6,500 net over Labour's last three years (~73,000 in late 2020 to ~79,000 in late 2023). So 6,800 vs ~6,250 is a margin of well under 10%, inside the noise between series, not the clear win the quote asserts. It is also not like-for-like: the coalition's number is a delivery count of newly funded IRRS places (including CHP acquisitions of existing homes) over a period when Kainga Ora's own managed stock went backwards — 78,204 in 2024-25 falling to a forecast 78,027, a net loss of 177 — with ~3,500 planned homes cancelled. The criterion's explicit falsifier (gross builds counted against the predecessor's net additions) is not cleanly triggered, since the 6,800 is labelled 'net new', so I do not rate it false; but neither count clearly exceeds the predecessor on a common measure. Substance holds, materially overstated.

statement: Isn’t the point that the damage is done, with 20,000 jobs gone after he decided to stop and pause infrastructure builds?
criterion: Stats NZ construction sector employment (HLFS or filled jobs) change between the December 2023 quarter and the June 2025 quarter: true if the fall is approximately 20,000; false if materially smaller or if the figure covers a different industry base.
reasoning: The direction and the general magnitude are right — construction employment fell sharply — but no Stats NZ series supports 20,000 as at October 2025. Business employment (filled jobs) data for the June 2025 quarter shows construction down 16,000 since December 2023 (construction lost a further 2,315 jobs, or 1.3%, in that quarter alone, part of a 10,000-job fall across the economy in three months and 50,000 fewer jobs than December 2023 overall). The HLFS-based measure gives the same answer from a different angle: 310,000 employed in construction in June 2023 falling to 294,000 in June 2025, again -16,000. A later Stats NZ reading (December 2025 quarter, 295,100) puts the fall from the mid-2023 peak of ~308,500 at about 13,400. Labour's own releases used 13,000 (Edmonds, post-Budget) and 18,000 at different times, never 20,000. So the true figure on the criterion's named source is ~16,000, an overstatement of about 25% — the substance holds but the number is materially inflated. Separately, the causal clause ('after he decided to stop and pause infrastructure builds') attributes the whole fall to one decision; the sector downturn is broad-based (total construction activity fell from $63b in 2023 to $58.1b in 2024 and $55.7b in 2025), so the attribution is not established by the employment data either way.

statement: Does he know that, to build his infrastructure pipeline, he will need the 761 private sector construction employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people in the last year, and how does he plan to stop the liquidations of two construction firms every day on his watch?
criterion: Companies Office liquidation records and Centrix credit reporting for construction-sector insolvencies in the 12 months to September 2025: true if approximately 761 construction employers ceased trading and the liquidation rate averages about two firms per day; false if either figure is materially different.
reasoning: Both numbers match the criterion. Centrix's September 2025 Credit Indicator Report (covering the 12 months to August 2025 — the most recent data available when the question was asked on 8 October 2025) reports construction as the largest single contributor to company liquidations, with 761 firms liquidated in the past year, a 38% increase. That is the 761 figure, on the timeframe the criterion names, from the reporting source it names. The 'two construction firms every day' claim is the same number restated: 761/365 = 2.08 per day. Disconfirming check: neighbouring Centrix periods give 751 for calendar 2025 (up 13%) and 768 for the year to March 2026, so 761 is not a cherry-picked outlier but sits in a stable band, and the rate stayed at roughly two a day either side of the quote. One caveat that does not change the verdict: the Centrix count is of company liquidations, so 'employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people' is a fair but slightly loose gloss — not every liquidated construction company had employees, and the 761 represent about 0.9% of all registered construction companies.

statement: If the economy is recovering, then why are 200 New Zealanders leaving every day, including thousands of builders, heading to Australia instead of staying here to build in New Zealand?
criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for New Zealand citizen departures to Australia in the year to mid-2025: true if departures average approximately 200 per day (about 73,000 a year); false if materially lower, or if the figure conflates all citizen departures with departures to Australia.
reasoning: The 200/day figure is accurate only for total NZ-citizen departures to ALL destinations: Stats NZ recorded a record 72,700 NZ-citizen migrant departures in the September 2025 year (199/day). Departures to Australia specifically are materially lower: in calendar 2025, 47,500 people departed NZ for Australia, of whom 40,700 were NZ citizens (86%) — about 111 NZ citizens per day, or 130/day counting all citizenships. Net loss to Australia was 28,500 (78/day). Australia took ~58-60% of NZ-citizen departures in the March 2025 year, so attaching 'heading to Australia' to the 200/day figure is precisely the conflation the criterion identified in advance, and overstates the Australia-bound flow by roughly 80%. The substance holds — record numbers of New Zealanders are leaving and Australia is by far the largest destination — but the number is true only under an all-destinations reading the speaker did not signal. The secondary 'thousands of builders' element is outside the criterion but is broadly supported: construction lost an estimated 18,000 jobs between mid-2022 and late 2024, with industry reporting staff moving to Australia for higher wages.

statement: But, again, some of those basic facts: there are 36,000 fewer jobs and there are 10,000 more unemployed young people in the two years since this Government came to office and implemented their economic policies of firing up the shredder and cutting billions of dollars of investment in our economy and in our people.
criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / Business Employment Data comparing the December 2023 quarter with the September 2025 quarter: true if total filled jobs fell by approximately 36,000 and the number of unemployed 15–24 year-olds rose by approximately 10,000 over that period; false if either figure is materially different or moves in the opposite direction.
reasoning: Both legs check out in direction and order of magnitude, and if anything understate the official series. Jobs: HLFS seasonally adjusted employment was 2,917,000 in the December 2023 quarter and 2,872,000 in the June 2025 quarter (the latest available when she spoke on 8 Oct 2025) — a fall of about 45,000; the September 2025 quarter was 2,871,000 (-46,000). Monthly filled jobs agree: the seasonally adjusted series peaked at 2,395,596 in October 2023 and was about 2.35m in August 2025. The NZCTU later put the two-year fall at 41,465 filled jobs. So '36,000 fewer jobs' is conservative against every series, and is consistent with a monthly filled-jobs comparison from the government's late-November 2023 start. Youth unemployment: unemployed 15-24 year-olds rose from 52,848 in the December 2023 quarter to 66,939 in the June 2025 quarter (+14,091), and to 69,059 by the September 2025 quarter (+16,211). Her '10,000 more' again understates rather than overstates. Because neither figure is inflated — partly_true is reserved for overstatement — the claim stands as true, with the caveat that the real numbers are somewhat larger than she stated.

statement: That probably explains why New Zealanders are, unfortunately, leaving in boatloads to the tune of approximately 200 every single day to Australia, because that is this Government’s policy on where the jobs are.
criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for departures of New Zealand citizens to Australia in the 12 months to October 2025: true if the rate averages approximately 200 per day (about 73,000 a year) to Australia specifically; false if the Australia-bound figure is materially lower (e.g. if 200/day is only reached by counting all destinations).
reasoning: Same underlying statistic as the Williams claim, and it fails the same way. Stats NZ recorded 72,700 NZ-citizen migrant departures in the September 2025 year — a record, and 199 per day — but that is to all destinations. Australia-bound flows are materially lower: 47,500 total departures to Australia in calendar 2025, of which 40,700 (86%) were NZ citizens, i.e. about 111 NZ citizens per day; net migration loss to Australia was 28,500 (78/day), itself down from 31,100 in 2024. In the March 2025 year, ~58-60% of NZ-citizen departures went to Australia. Saying 'approximately 200 every single day to Australia' therefore reaches 200 only by counting all destinations — the exact conflation the criterion pre-committed to as the failing condition — overstating the Australia-bound rate by roughly 80%. The core substance (record departures, Australia the dominant destination) is sound, so the claim is materially overstated rather than fabricated.

statement: They have scaled back infrastructure in hospitals, resulting in 15,000 fewer construction sector jobs.
criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs for the construction industry over the period since the change of government: true if construction employment fell by approximately 15,000; false if materially different. The attribution to hospital projects would additionally require Health NZ/Treasury records of deferred or cancelled hospital builds.
reasoning: The magnitude is supportable but the causal attribution is not. Stats NZ shows construction employment fell ~16,000 from June 2023 (310,000) to June 2025 (294,000), and monthly filled jobs in construction fell 4.5% (~9,000) in the year to September 2025; Labour cited 18,000 lost since 2023 in July 2025. So '15,000 fewer construction sector jobs' as at 8 Oct 2025 is within range and if anything conservative. However, the criterion also requires the attribution to hospital projects to hold. Health NZ records do show hospital scale-backs (the Dunedin Hospital rebuild was cut back in Sept 2024 and rescoped to 351 beds vs the old hospital's 396), but the sector-wide decline is overwhelmingly residential and private: consents fell to a six-year low (33,600 in the year to Dec 2024, lowest since 2018), residential activity is down ~14% from its 2021 peak and fell in six of seven quarters, and industry analysts attribute it to high interest rates, falling house prices, high build costs and slower population growth. Hospital construction is far too small a share of the ~190,000-strong construction workforce to account for 15,000 jobs, and the decline predates the change of government. The number is roughly right; the stated cause is materially overstated.

statement: In his own words, he is “wealthy and sorted”.
criterion: The recorded interview or media transcript being referred to: true if Luxon described himself as 'wealthy and sorted' (or in materially equivalent words) on the record; false if no such quotation exists or the words are materially misreported.
reasoning: The quotation exists on the record. In September 2024, questioned about the sale of his Wellington apartment (sold for $975,000, a $180,000 capital gain), Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said: 'Let me be clear: I'm wealthy, I'm — you know — sorted.' The remark was widely reported (Stuff headlined it 'I'm wealthy and I'm sorted') and drew the highest number of nominations for Massey University's Quote of the Year 2024. I looked for a disconfirming account — a claim the phrase was fabricated, clipped or misattributed — and found none; multiple independent outlets (Stuff, RNZ, NZ Herald, ODT, Newstalk ZB) carry the same wording. Edmonds' third-person rendering 'he is wealthy and sorted' is materially equivalent to Luxon's own words.

statement: It’s quite interesting to see, today, the Minister of Finance saying, “I didn’t take any credit for it”, despite, in the first question before that, saying the Government takes credit for it.
criterion: The Hansard record of oral questions for 8 October 2025: true if the Minister of Finance both claimed Government credit for the fall in interest rates in an earlier question and said she took no credit for it in a later one; false if the record does not show both, or if the earlier answer claimed credit for something other than the interest rate fall.
reasoning: Checked against the Hansard record of oral questions for 8 October 2025. The second limb is confirmed: in Question No. 4, Edmonds asked 'If she is taking credit for the latest interest rate cut, will she also take responsibility that this cut is because of a stagnating economy caused by her Government's inaction?' and Hon Nicola Willis replied 'I've taken no such credit.' The first limb does not hold as stated. The earlier finance question (No. 2, Nancy Lu) shows Willis attributing the 50bp OCR cut to the Reserve Bank's monetary policy committee, and explicitly saying macroeconomic stabilisation 'should almost always be left to monetary policy run by the independent Reserve Bank.' Her credit claim was narrower: 'through its spending decisions, the Government of the day can help that task or it can hinder it... This Government is helping. We have introduced discipline to Government spending,' contrasted with a previous Government 'keeping inflation higher for longer and preventing reductions in interest rates.' That is a claim to have created the conditions for lower rates — an implicit credit claim that gives Edmonds a genuine basis — but she did not say the Government takes credit for the rate fall itself. The substance of the inconsistency Edmonds points to is real but materially overstated.
